V

1 On the tables and counters are hundreds of wax heads' more or less finished, and looking very strange apart from their bodies. In another part of the room is a pile of bodies, legs, and armsall heaped up together and if you take a glance into that bag in the corner you will be somewhat surprised, for it is full of doll's eyes looking up at you with a horribly glassy stare. A number of men and women are busy'. A large pin of wax is placed in a still larger pan containing water heated by means of gas. As the water gets hot the wax, of course, melts, and into the moulton wax a workman now drops the colouring matter, generally rouge, to give the dolls that beautiful complexion which we all delight to see. The plaster moulds for the heads, made in three pieces, ate then firmly tied together, and the mould thus formed is carefully filled with the liquid wax. After a certain time the greater part of the wax is poured back, but a portion coming into contaCt with the cold plaster mould has already set. The mould is now untied and removed, and there we have a was bead nicely formed, and looking almost as natural, and some. times as large, as life. Wax'bodies, arms, and legs are ,made in a similar manner.

Two boles are cut in the wax head for the eyes which in the case of the more expensive dolls, have to be placed into their sockets very carefully. In the cheaper kinds the eyes are first warmed and then forced into their, place, being finally cemented with a little wax. Although our dull is now possessed of a pair of eyes much still remains to be /lone. Eyebrows are required, and these are generally paintOd on, but some- times real hair is stuck into the wax carefully and slowly, a few hairs at a time,until the whole is complete Now what do you think? Dolly's face is also ironed! With a speciAlly-constructed iron tool the workman fobs at the wax until the face is quite smooth and polished. The lips and nostrils are painted, the teeth put in, without the aid of a dentist, and finally, the head ?si carried to another part of the factory to gave the hair fixed by women, who, if they do not use real hair for this purpose, use a specially-prepared material which looks as good as real, and that, after all, is the main thing. Boaies and limbs are now added by other workponple, until the doll is completed and ready for Santa Claus's bag.

All the larger and more substantial toys, such as rocking-horses, wheelbarrows, dolls' houses, perambu- latorP, and the endless variety of really handsome toys which are nowadays offered in such profusion, are made principally in our own country, For the cheaper toys of all descriptions Santa Claus depends largely upon, the efforts of his German, Swiss, and French workpeople.—From " The Liverpool Daily Post."

div.head: MR. SEDDON AT PENKETH.
div.p: MR. SEDDON AT PENKETH.
The Labour Party and Increment Value.

Mr Seddon M.P., is now in his constituency working up the enthusiasm of the electors, arid if the meeting held on Thursday evening in the Sankey Sunday school is anything to go by his return to Parliament is assured for the Newton division. Mr. J. Haley pre- sided and was supported on the platform by Messrs. A. Rudd, G. Faulkner, B. Marshall, W. Moores, J.Midwood and Forshaw(divisional secretary of the Labour Party). Mr. Seddon, who had an enthusiastic reception, said they were there that night under the shadow of the greatest political crisis that had been known in this country for many a long year. Up to the last General Election we had had ten years of Tory rule and he thought that the result of that election confirmed the idea that the Conservative Party had outstayed their welcome. (Hear, bear.) On that occasion a great cry was made by the Liberal Party and they as the Labour' party endorsed it,that the Conservatives had not merely muddled things, but they hat been guilty of a ghastly war, which properly, managed could have saved 20,000 lives and millions of poriuds.Whatever might have been the merits or demerits of the Budget we were now con- fronted by an irresponsible body. They need not conjure with their own winds, to manufacture con- demnation of them, for the record of the House of Lords was their own condemnation. The House of Lords had been condemned by their friends, in Lords Macaulay and Beaconsfield, and now their action was condemned by Lords Rosebery, James of Hereford, and Balfour of Burleigh. So far aithe claim of the Lords was concerned woat did they say? They bad killed the Budget—they bad "hung it up." It reminded him of n man who had banged another man and tried to explain that he had not killed him, but only hung him up. (Laughter). For 300 years it had been the inviolable right to levy taxation and the House of Lords had no right to take the action they bad. (Applause). The constitutional issue was plain. Whether the Budget was good or not was not the point. The point was whether we were going to allow an irresponsible chamber to leave their pleasures and their pursuits as on that occasion and come down to the House of Lords to destroy something which had only got a yearly life and, if the voice of the country was against their action, to allow it to pass. He was not a single chamber man so he would have a second chamber composed of statesmen, poets, artists, pro-consuls, business men and of those who had given evidence of ability and who would be elected by the will of the people so that the will of the people would prevail. He contended that the Budget was the fairest Budget we had ever had. It put taxes upon the rich and not on the necessities of life. Referring to the tax of 20 per cent, on the increment value he said it was too modest. If the Laboer party had had the building of the Budget they would have taken 80 per cent. and if the dokes had howled as much as they had up to the present time they would taken the lot. (Laughter and applause.) The increment was created by the people, and.therefore the people were entitled to it. (Applause.) Mr. Seddon dealt with some of the proposals of the Budget and Tariff Reform. He said that in any period of seven years during the last forty sears they found a startling fact. When the imports of manufactured goods was high, the percentage of unemployment was low, and when the imports of manufactured goods was low the percentage of unemployment was high. That proved ft sound economic truth that iuternational trade was international exchange. (Applause). Mr. Midwood moved the following resolution: That this meeting thanks Mr.Seddon for the work lie has done in the House of Commons during the past four years and pledges itself to do everything possible to secure his return at the next election.
Mr. Faulkner seconded, and arter the Chairman and Mr. Rudd had spoken it was carried with enthusiasm.

div.head: Warrington Band of Hope Union.
div.p: Warrington Band of Hope Union.

During the last few weeks a number of Elementary schools in the district covered by the above Union have been visited by the expert lecturer of the Lancashire and Cheshire Band of Hope Union. That these lecturers are doing good wolk amongst our schools is evident from the encouragement given by the managers of education from the Board of Education downwards, whi'st the scholars are delighted pith the simple experiments demonstrating the nature of alcohol, and they look forward with interest to the certificate which is awarded to all those who submit satisfactory essays. At the lectures given at Penketh, Great Sankey, Burtonwood, Winwick, Croft. Orford, Padgate, Woolston, and Martinscroft schools, 29 teachers and 569 scholars were present. As a result, 286 essays were submitted, of which 207 possessed sufficient merit to obtain a certificate.

div.head: SANTA CLAUS'S WORKSHOPS.
div.p: SANTA CLAUS'S WORKSHOPS.
About the Manufacture of Toys.

What wonderful places are our Warrington shops just now! Palaces of light and glitter they are these dark nights, enchanting the real children and astonish- I ing those of older growth. Without doubt our old friend Santa Clause is one of the largest employers of labour in the whole world. His workshops are to be found in nearly every country and thousands—nay, hundreds of thousands—of men, women and even children are busy all the year round making millions of toys of all kinds and sizes to fill the capacious bag which their genial master carries about. with him on-Christmas Eve. When you think of the vast number of children why are constantly supplied with toys, you will wonder for a moment where all the playthings come from and how they are made. The first thing Santa Claus does is to send for the inventors, to whom he gives instructions to make up some new designs for toys to amuse his young friends. The inventota have only to think, but thinking is hard work sometimes, and in this case their work is more difficult than the actual manufacture of the article, for 1 so many novelties have already been invented that it is not an easy matter by any means to invent an entirely new idea for a toy. It is said that now and agiin an inventor will awake in the middle of the night with a great idea for a new toy, and jumping out of bed, will commit the idea to paper so tbat it shall not escape him. 3 hen in the morning off he goes to Santa Claus with a drawing of his idea.and if it is considered likely to be a popular one with children Santa Claus will give orders for an immense quantity to be manufactured to meet the enormous demand which he knows from his experience there will be long before Christmas. The moat popular toy is, of course, the doll, and when you consider the number of girls who possess at least one, and sometimes a whole family of dolls. you will be able to understand that many thousands of workpeople are employed making this one kind of toy. There are wax dolls and rag dolls made in England, china-faced dolls made in France, and Dutch dolls, which are not Dutch at all, but only called so because they are principally shipped from Dutch ports. The best member of the doll family is the wax doll and the best wax dolls first see the light of day in the great city of London. Let us take a peep into some of the rooms of a toy factory er workshop, and see for ourselves how some of our favourites are made.

div.head: MR. CLARKE ON "THE LORD'S SUPPER."
div.p: MR. CLARKE ON "THE LORD'S SUPPER."

In connection with the mission now being held at the Parr Hall, Mr. George Clarke, the evangelist, delivered a lecture on Sunday afternoon entitled "The Lord's Supper—what it means and teaches." The Hall was full and amongst those on the platform was the Mayor (Alderman W. J. Forshaw.) Mr. CLARKE at the commencement of his lecture alluded to the fact that when his late father lived he was accounted the greatest authority on all questions connected with Jewish customs and Church history. He said that when Jesus Christ instituted the Lord's Supper—as we called it—he was not instituting a new feast at all, be was merely partaking of the passover feast. There were no difficulties in understanding the Lord's Supper excepting those difficulties that had been entirely made by what we cslled priestcraftism and sacerdotalism. Those difficulties were such that no student of Church history could accept them. The Lecturer then proceeded to give an account of the circumstances connected with the institution of the Lord's Supper. He said that Jesus who was with his disciples on the other side of the Mount of Olives sent Peter and John into Jerusalem to prepare the psssover. Peter and John left Jesus and the rest, of the disciples between five and six in the morning to spend the whole day in fasting and in prayer. It must have been a very solemn time for Jesus Christ, knowing of everything that was being done and that he was to be the prime actor and finisher of all. The disciples left Him alone with His God as He spent the day thinking of what was coming. They purchased a lamb of the first year without spot or blemish, to be sacrificed. Then they joined the crowd which was wending its way to the Temple, each representative of his family leading a lamb which was to be slain. The lamb had to be presented Ws the priest at the Temple before one o'clock and by two o'clock the priest had to take the lamb and kill it as a sin offering for the sins of the people which it repre- sented. At 2.30 the body of the lamb was lain upon the fire as a burnt offering unto God. It must have been a solemn time for Jesus, as seated undeik the shadow of some rock or tree, He watched the smoke from the sacrificial lamb in the Temple ascending to Heaven. He knew in a few' abort boors that He, the Lamb of God, would be slain—the fulfilmentof all the types in the Temple—His blood would be shed for the remission of sins, and on a Cross on Calvary He would hang, cursed and forsaken of God whilst bearing the sins and iniquities of the whole world. At five in the evening He arose and told His waiting disciples that they must eat of the Passover once more with Him before He suffered. He went foreard calmly to accomplish His death in Jerusalem. To his disciples be spoke words of cheer-and hope., As he went into the city he beheld the crowd coming down from the Temple Mount bearing upon their shoulders the already sacrified lamb. Amongst them were Peter and John. He joined Himself to their company and went with them to the house where they were to eat the Passover. The Lord did not institute the Lord's Supper until after the Passover Supper itself was completed. At 6 o clock Jesus sat down with His disciples and feasted, after which Jesus washed the disciples feet. Then what we now call the Lord's Sapper commenced. The Lord's Supper did not mean an atoning sacrifice, but a feast of praise for people whose sins were already atoned for, and who had therefore come into the presence of their risen and glorified Redeemer to be partakers with Him of the feast as a memorial as he commanded them. He said it was only the converted who could really partake of the Lord's Supper. During the week Mr. Clarke has preached each after- noon excepting Monday on the 23rd Psalm. The

div.head: Warrington Beat Hull.
div.p: Warrington Beat Hull.

As a result of the heavy rains, the match between Warrington and Hull was to a gre tt extent spoiled. A crowd of quite 6,000 people assembled and witnessed an exciting game notwithstanding the mud and water with which the ground was nearly covered. Warrington had four prominint players a.visent in Tilley, Jenkins, Shugars, and O'Neill, while the visitors came strongly represented and determined to maintain their sequence of successes. Stunts, made his first appearance in Northern League football and- was accorded a great reception. The teams were: Warrington-4. Taylor, back; Fish, Dickinson, Fraw- ley, and Stunts, three-quarter backs ; Brooks and Lloyd, half backs • O'Malley, Thomas, Boardman, Bolton, Cheaters, arid Naylor, forwards. Hull—H. Taylor, back; E. Rogers, G. Rogers, Deveraux, and Morton, three-quarter backs; Anderson and Wallace, half backs; Florridge,—Fulton, Wilma; Holder, Walton, and Taylor, forwards. Referee, Mr. G. F. Dickinson, Halifax. Touch judges, Messrs. W. Mainwaring (Salford) and W. Gregory (Runcorn). s Anderson set the ball in motion, and the visitors at once tried the passing game, but with the slippery ball and turf they made little headway against the watchful Warrington defence. Fish was early prominent with a short sprint and kick which took the ball past Taylor. There was a fine rush by the home forwards and the ball was carried over but reached the rails too soon. Warrington now operated in the Hull half, and Frawley made a fine dodgy run which carried play to the line. The Australian passed to Dickenson when tackled and a long throw to Fish saw the left-winger race over near the corner. Thomas just failed at goal from a difficult angle. Hull responded finely and in some hot work near the line, Brooks collided heavily with a Hull forward and took no further part in the game. For some minutes the Warrington defence was highly tried. Rogers and Anderson both being held up on the line. Rogers next got away at centre but was overhauled and tackled by Stuntz,who was showing any amount of keenness. Thomas and O'Mally led a fine rush to the other end where Taylor made a weak clearance,and Boardman charged the ball down, scoring a fine try near the pest, Fish adding a goal. The visitors were by no means daunted and they went straight to the Warring- ton line, where Lloyd and Dickenson were to the fore in good defensive work. Devereaux made a splendid effort to break through, but found Frawley a stumbling block. Half-time: Warrington, one goal two tries (eight points) ; Hull, nil. After a short interval, during which many of the Warrington team had complete changes, the visitors attacked as a result of a misunderstanding between Stunts and Taylor, and for the space of five minutes the railway goal was jeopardised. The Tykes failed to penetrate the defence and eventually Frawley raced .well down the open and dribbled up to Taylor, who was i lucky to save. with O'Malley and Thomas n attendance the latter now operating at the base of the pack in place of Brooks. Warrington made further progress when Lloyd got smartly away, and rushing past Ander- son and Wallace, Frawley was placed in possession. The Colonial ran well for the line and immediately drawing Taylor passed to Stunts who romped over at the corner. His success was bailed with tremendous cheers. Thomas failed to convert. Hull now took up a menacing position, and Rogers tricked Stunts and kicking across to Morton that player soon made traclis for the line and recorded the visitors' only score of the afternoon. Repeatedly Anderson got well away, but received little support, and on one occasion the line appeared at the mercy of the visitors, but Stunts never gave up hope and reaching the ball first succeeded in kicking it dead. Several dashing rushes by the Hull vanguard wore ably met by Lloyd and Thomas, who showed rare pluck in going down for the ball. Stunts made another com- mendable effort near the close, but nothing accrued, and the close of a hard game was as follows : Warrington, one goal three tries (11 points); Hull, one try (three points).
A SHOCK FOR RUNCORN.

At Runcorn, before 2,000 spectators. Padbury was a notable absentee on the Runcorn side, the visitors also having several changes. The opening stages were all in favour of Widnes, Lally and Noon making consider- able headway. Kennedy made a brilliant effort, but Jones returned. Hughes got possession, and after a short run kicked over the Widnes line, and appeared to ground the ball, but the referee ruled otherwise. At half-time there was no score. After the interval Widnes, adopting the kick and rush style, soon had Runcorn on the defensive and following a scramble Reid scored, but Daintith failed at goal. Immediately after Reid again got possession and scored, for Daintith to add a goal. Hughes then put in a fine kick for Runcorn, and following up grounded the ball at the corner, Batterworth failing with the goal kick. Another rush by the Widnes forwards saw Runcorn in difficulties, and Reid smartly ran over, .Daintith failing to improve. liesuming, Ince got possession, and ridded a further try, Aspey failing. A desperate attack by Runcorn followed, and Watton forced his way through, and scored, Richardson being unsuccessful with the goal kick. Result : Widnes 1 goal and 4 tries (14 points), Runcorn 2 tries (6 points.) Teams and officials : Runcorn—Ricbardson, back; Hughes, Moran, Butter- worth and Deakin, three-quarter backs : White and WAton, half backs ; Walker, Kennedy, Williams, Langley, McDonald and Dixon, forwards, - Widnes—Jones, back ; Daintith, Reid, Lally and Ince, three-quarter backs; Noon and O'Garra, half- backs ; S. Aspey, G. Aspey, Colgrove, Rigby, McCarthy and Rigby, forwards. , Referee, Mr. NV. H. Wool, Huddersfield. Touch judges, Messrs. A. Lee, Leigh and W. Nevins, War- rington. ST. HELENS' GREAT WIN AT HUNSLET.

St. Helens found Hunslet short of four of the best men on Saturday, and inflicted a severe reverse on the Parksida Club. Hunslet were the first to attack. A sprint up the wing by Farrar placed Hunslet in a good position, and Grayson landed a goal from a penalty kick. Two minutes after this score was registered, M. Creevey got over the line for the visitors, after Barton had cleverly bluffed Parkinson. Turtill kicked the goal. Some fine open play followed, and Quinn, after receiving the ball from Jenkirson, scored. Grayson failed at goal. There was no doubting St. Helens' supremacy from this stage.. The forwards heeled not. on every occa,ion to the helves, who in tt.rn kr pt t e backs con,tantly supplied with work. As a result, the three-quarters had eutberous chance', and tt.ey put them ti practicil use, their passing tasieg cpitttlly executed. The visitors were credited with two tries in the spa-e of five minutes, Barton rcoring niter a clever cross-kick, and Ft tnnagan frarn a well-judged pass by Greenw )od. C. Creevey felled the goal points. Before the interval arrived Quinn who thronghout plajed a good belm° for Hunslet, again scored after a sharp sprint, but Grayson failed at goal. Half-time score— St. Helens 3 goals and 3 tries (15 points), Hunslet 1 goal Ind 2 tries 8 points). In the second half Jonkinsen reluctantly had to retire, and w:th the defence thus weakened, St. Helens pierced it three times. Mavitty got over tc% ice, and C. Creevey also scored, all as the outcome of smart passing exchanges. None of the goal shots were successful, C. Creevey failing at one and Barton with the otter two attempts. Result :—St. Helens, 3 goals and 6 tries (24 points) ; Hunslet, 1 goal and 2 tries (8 points). Teams an officials : Hunslet—G. Grayson, back; F. Farrar, J. S. Parkin- son, P. Quinn, and A. Jonkinson, three-quarter backs'; F. Whittaker and S. 'freer, half backs; H. Wilson, .1. W. Higson, J. Randall, W. Fowler, S. R )binson and Brooks, forwards. St. Helens —Turtill, hack ; Barton (captain), C Creevey, J. Greenwood, and J. Fiannagan, three-quarter backs; A. Kelly and M. Creevey, half hicks; Briers, Bradley, Pope, Al rvitty, Ifelsby rind Lee, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. Pnestley, Salford. Touch judge', Messrs. F. W. Tattersall, Wakefield, and I'. W. Smith, Keighley.

div.head: NOTES BY " OVALIST."
div.p: NOTES BY " OVALIST."

The interesting item of the week has once more to do with Stuntz. He has established another record by being the first Northern Union pl:iyer to be fined £25. This sum, the N.U. says he must pay to Barrow for breach of agreement before Ito can play again for Warrington.

"It turns out to b • correct tint Barrow approached the Australian before Warrington, and received a cable from him accepting their terms. Subsequently Warrington came into the market with an offer of £25 More. Stunt z wisely closed with the stronger club. The Union seems to lave constituted itself a court of law and decided that Barrow were entitled to £25 damages front Stuntz•—a somewhat questionable decision. The only hold they have over Stuntz is that they can prevent him playing, and it remains' a question for Warrington to consider whether Stuntz's service's are worth another £2. The Warrington Club is held to be blainsles; in the matter, but it is they who will have to ply the piper apparently. Stnntz has paid his footing already in extra gate- money.

• Last Saturday's match saw Warrington in line form again, and the strong hull team were forced to bow the knee to a superior side. It was a great feat on Warrington's part to w in the match after losing the services of Brooks at quarter-time, and Hull did not take kindly to the reverse by 11 points to 3. War- rington's winning superiority lay in the front rank. The five forwards revelled in the mud, and though beaten often for possession,- they carried all before them in loose play. Thomas was a sort of forward half-back, and shile giving L'oyd valuable help he was irresistible in the rushes of the front rank men. Hull played the passing game rather better than did Warrington, but it was no day for effective com- bination, and the methods of the locals proved better suited to the conditions. Rarely has the Warrington ground been in such a state. Pools of water lay in every hollow, and the men were drenched from head to foot after the first ten minutes football, while the ball was like-a buttered bladder. c

A feature of the match was that each side had two Australian three-quarters playing, and these men were the best on their respective sides. Great interest was taken locally in the first appearance of Frawley and Stuntz as Warrington's ight-wing pair, and they did excellent service. Frawley played a grand game from start to finish, and was the most conspicuous back on the field. He had a hand in two of Warring- ton's three tries, and made a perfect opening for Stuntz to score his first Northern League point. There is every hope that the two Australians will become a power in the Warrington ranks when they have had some practice together. Both are speedy beyond the ordinary, and Stuntz a regular flier. Fish scored one good try, but did little afterwards and threw a great deal of work on Taylor. The latter fulfilled a heavy task in capital style, his safe catching being a feature. While I still look to Mclntyre as the future Warring- ton full_ back, I was glad to set Taylor filling the Position of rear-guard on Saturday. It was no day for young full backs.

On the Hull side, the halves were very tricky, and the three-quarters speedy. With a dry ball I think they would have beaten Warrington after Brooks had retired. Their ecnnhination was good even under such terrible conditions. -

The League table shows that Warrington have again climbed to the third place, which they should Maintain if not improve upon. I think Warrington Will finish up above Salford, well as the Reds seem tq be playing.

WARRLNOTON "A "'S FIRST DEFEAT.

Warrington "A" took a strong side to Leigh on Saturday, though the absence of Lloyd, Chesters and Naylor was severely felt. Leigh Shamrocks revelled in the mud, and beating Warrington forwards they inflicted the first reverse of the season on the champions. In the initial stages Warrington were sorely pressed and after good passing by the backs Naughton scored and Riley placed a goal. This reverse roused the visitors, and Jordan and Daintith were to the fore in some concerted play. The defence prevailed and it was not until near the close that the " Wirepuliers "gained anything tangible, Daintith pla,:ing a penalty goal. In the second half Warrington hal much the better of it, but failed at finishing essays, Daintith, Bradshaw and Jordan all being held up near the line. Final : Leigh Shamrocks, one goal one try (five points) : Warring- ton, one goal (two points).

div.head: Warrington and the Registration of Stuntz
div.p: Warrington and the Registration of Stuntz
THE AUSTRALIAN FINED.

A meeting of the Emergency Committee of the Northern Union was held in Manchester, on Tuesday evening, Mr. J. H. Houghton (St. Helens) occupying the chair. The Barrow club made an objection to the registratiou of John Stunts with the Warrington club on the ground that it (Barrow) had definitely arranged terms with Stuntz prior to his accepting terms to play for Warrington. The committee, in the evidence tendered, was of opinion that a distinct breach of agreement had been made by Stunts in respect to the Barrow club, and such breach was made by the player named having received an extra offer of £25 from Warrington. The committeg decided that the Warrington club bad not acted in any way improperly and the registration of Stun i Stunts by that club was quite n order. It further ordered Stunts to pay to Barrow club the sum of £25 as damages for his breach of agreement before being again allowed to play Northern Union football.

WARRINGTON ALBIONS V. SUTTON COMMERCIAL. Last Saturday Warrington Albions met Sutton Com- mercial in a match for the Liverpool and County Cup on Walker's Brewery ground, Padgate-lane, thinking— before they began—that football could be indulged in, in a comfortable moiler. However, it was not to Le, for on arriving at Padgate-lane the ground was in an awful state. The game was to have commenced at 2.30 p.m., but it was 3.15 before the ball was in play. The Albions were short of E. Whitfleld,and played wii h one full back. On such a ground Scientific craft was out of the question,and almost throughout the match- -30 minutes each way—the ball was flying from one end of the field to the other, the backs being called upon very frequently. The only goal scored was by Thomas (Albions), from a shot close in, 15 minutes after the start.

div.head: FOOTBALL GOSSIP.
div.p: FOOTBALL GOSSIP.
BY B. BENNISON.
ILLUSTRATED BY JACK DODWORTII.

To the old stager the march of Accrington Stanley into the first round proper of the Eng- lish Cup competition, by reason of their con- quest in their match with Brentford, is particu- larly interesting. There was a time, as all those steeped in foOtball lore remember, :when Ac- crington boasted of a First League team, and a good one, too. Men 'like George Howarth and Whitehead, who were honoured by their coun- try—and old Torn Hay, the goalkeeper, pretty nearly good enough to play for England, are some of the players one will always associate with the history of Lancashire football. The local lad in those days had a chance. Accrington did not care very much for hunting through Scotland for recruits, and their games with Blackburn Rovers, Preston North End, and Bol- ton Wanderers were something to remember. Round about Accrington there are still' good
Accrington Stanley have reached the first round proper of the English ties.

footballers by the dozen, but the town when the game developed into such a big and serious busi- ness could not hold its end up, and Accrington Stanley are left to carry on the football story of i the bustling, hustling place where everyone s a keen sportsman.

Selling their Birthright. And, writing about the Cup, I would again hammer at what, to every good and thinking sportsman, is an unmitigated evil. I refer to the selling and buying of the right to play at home. For many reasons, and perhaps more than anything else because of sentiment, the English Cup represents a competition that ap- peals to all those interested in good, hard games. You will get a man at a Cup-tie who would not dream of attending any other match, just because the game, to a ‘T...r-y---large extent, has been built upon and made by the Football Cup. The central idea is to throw open to all and sundry a competition in which everybody shall have an equal chance, and in winch merit, and merit alone, shall be the deciding factor; if this is not so, why is there a draw for choice of grounds? There may not be anything in the rules to prevent any team disposing of their right to play at home; but the spirit of Cup fighting is that there shall be no bartering for this or that privilege; the idea of the power of the purse creeping in cannot be too severely condemned. A paltry SUM of £75 induced Tun- bridge to forego their right of playing on their own ground to Workington, and they were beaten all ends up. Tunbridge may say that if they had held to their territorial advantage given to them by the draw they could not have beaten such a side. Such a contention carries no weight at all. Tunbridge should have taken their chances not only of winning but of, having a, decent "gate" if they had remained at home. We shall soon be in the thick of the Clip-ties, and one would be very pleased if the Football Association stepped in and decreed that there shall be no more swapping and trucking. If the buying of privileges is to be continued, then it follows as a matter of elementary logic that the richest clubs are sure to have the best chances of making progress, if, indeed, they do not make their appearance in the final assured. If the Football Association do not care to frame a rule that will stop clubs from going in for the CuP simply on the off-chance of making money by the luck of the draw, why cannot the ties be sold outright to the highest bidder? New Blood for Chelsea. So Chelsea, after a meet commendable fashion, have turned their attention to the

div.head: Chelsea Team now includes a schoolmaster.
div.p: The Chelsea Team now includes a schoolmaster.

amafeurs, in the hope of adding to their strength. W. J. Williams, the Portsmouth schoolmaster, who is a left - wing forward of unquestionable merit, has consented to assist the London club. It was hoped that he would play against Bristol City a_week ago, but he had promieed to take part in a game at home, so that his appearance, looked. forward to with much interest, has been deferred. I have not had the pleasure of seeing for myself what man- ner of player Williams is, but my friends speak highly of him. If he settles down at Chelsea he will have a fine opportunity of making a big name, for presumably he will have Windridge for his partner, one, of the cleverest, inside-lefts since Bache of Aston Villa was at his very best. Chelsea are delighted with Woodward, who in his first game at Stamford Bridge not only scored two goals, but made it plain that his very presence will have a good effect on the whole of the teams.

Unhappy Bolton. When a team are doing badly the lot of the manager and directors is an extremely unhappy one. The people at Bolton are saying things, and the supporters, with every good intention, no doubt, but with little practical knowledge of how best to run a football team, have been putting their heads together, and one gathers that there is much unrest in the neighbourhood of Burnden Park. That Bolton Wanderers have been dreadfully disappointing, and that their position at the bottom of the table is out of all keeping with the liberal support which they re- ceive—l doubt whether the gates have ever been larger in the history of the club than they eye Wllar-70aanot be denied. Bat one met
Iton .s' suppor, . have been making suggestions to the club management.

always doubt whether it is wise for any body of supporters to be up in arms. As I have said, the followers of Bolton, who have clamoured for a team manager and have suggested other reforms, have by their -recent meeting given anything but confidence to their players, and unless there is a general settling dawn the Wan- derers will continue to have a bad time. Matches between neighbours"" have always been a doubtful blessing to my mind. They pro- duce little good football, and, for some reason or other produce a lot of bad blood. They do no good at all. The only effect is that they prci- duce a lot of money. The match between Tot- cennam and Voolwicli A rsonai was tne last word in wild and hartith-searum football, and I should say that neither the people who/looked on nor the players want such another game in a hurry.

QUALIT3r OF MILK.--A subject to which attention might reasonably be paid by the farmer is as regards the quality of his milk, says "Farm and Home." Very interesting tests were some time ago instituted on the farms supplying milk to a northern dairy company. A representative visited each farm and took with him a Gerber apperatus for the determination of butter fat. A sample of butter was taken from each cow, night and morning, together with the weight of each meal. The samples were then analysed, and a record made of the quantity and quality of each cow's milk, taking due regard to the distance from calving-time. The process was repeated at intervals of three months, and gradually animals giving milk of poor quality were marked down for sale. The interest taken by the farmers in the experiment was most gratifying, and greater attention is now being given on their part to this matter.

div.head: WARRINGTON BRIDGE.
div.p: WARRINGTON BRIDGE.
LIVELY DISCUSSION AT THE. COUNCIL MEETING.
Councillor Roberts' Violent Attack on Councillor Pemberton.

There was a lively discussion at the Warrington Town Council meeting on Tuesday evening witli reference to Mr. J. J. Webster's appointment to adjudicate upon the plans and Betas engineer to super- intend the construction of the 'now Warrington Bridge. The General Purposes Committee had receivedlaa lettcr from Mr. Webster accepting the appointment and laying down the conditiorKi under which he would undertake the duties. The remuneratioa for hi 4 services was to be at the rate of 5 per cent. on the cost of the work, exclusive of travelling expenses. It wan resolved that the terms and conditions ooutainel in the letter be agreed to; thr.t the designs, specifications, bills of nuantitirr, and all papers other than thei tenders received from teuderers, be sent to Mr. J. J.. Webster for his adjudicati9n and report; and that the, Nlayor, Deputy-mayor, -with the Town Clerk and. Lrough Surveyor, be appointed a committee to opent the sealed packets, to extract the tenders, and to for- ward all the other papers to Mr. J. J. Webster, and that a list of the persons who had out in tenders bo sent to each member of the Council.
Councillor PEMBERTON bad given notice that be+ would move :

That so much of tho following resolution passed the Council on the 26th October, 1909 as relates to the appointment of Mr. J. J. Webster as engineer to superintedd the construction of Warrington Bridge, be rescinded :

" Resolved, that on the recommendation of the Borough Surveyor, 11Ir. J. .3, Webster be appointed engineer to adjudicate and report on the plans, speci- fications and bills of quantities and also engineer to superintend the carrying out of the work." lie moved the suspension of standing orders so that this motion might he taken 'before the question was considered as part of the iminutes of the General Purposes Committee. Councillor ROBERTS objected on the ground that there was not the slightest necessity to take such a course. Councillor Pemberlon's object was to defeat the proposition to attach the common seal of the Corporation to a certain document and he was at liberty to move that that particular minute be expunged. Councillor PEmuEirrcit The difference is that I won't have the right to repf.7. The motion to suspend was defeated, only eight members voting for and the rest of the Council against.

Councillur PENIFMRTON intimated that he intended to move several amendments to the minutes, but was told by the Mayor and the Town Clerk that be could not speak more than once to the same minutes. Several members, including Councillor Roberts, held that although a member could not speak twice to the same minutes, he was entitled, to move a second amendment when the first had been disposed of, and a vote being taken it was decided that Councillor Pemberton could proceed with his case by meana of separate amendments. Councillor PEMBERTON remarked that it ought to be a matter of right and not of privilege. Councillor PEMBERTON then asked whether any part of the accounts "ordered for payment,' in the minutes and amounting to £653 2s. 9d., included any payment in respect of the Parliamentary Bill they were seeking for the erection of the bridge and other matters.
The TOWN CLERK replied that the amount included £lOO to be paid to the Parliamentary agents in respect of theßill.

Councillor PEMBERTON then moved that that pay- ment and the minute that "the Town Clerk laid before the committee the draft Parliamentary notice of the proposed Bill and the same was amended," be not con- firmed. He said he had supported the proposal to build a ferro-concrete bridge on the assurnce that fifty years would be allowed for repayment of the loan. Now, however, it appeared that the Board would allow only fifteen years. It was a singular thing that although he had attended all the meetings regularly the Council meeting at which this matter was dealt with took place when he could not attend. Notice was given by Alderman Smethurst to deal with the com- munication front the Local Government Board and pass resolutions thereon although that communication did not. come to hand until five days after Alderman Smethurst bad given his notice to deal with it: The communication was to the effect that only fifteen years would be allowed to repay the loan. Toe matter was considered in committee—although be did not know why there should be any secrecy—and it was resolved that they should go to Parliament for a Bill under which they could got a longer terra and that Mr. J. J. Webster be appointed to adjudicate upon desigra and tenders sent in—and also act as engineer to superintend the carrying out of the vr ork. The latter part was not recommended by the Surveyor but was added by the Committee. Councillor ROBERTS: He did recommend it. Councillor PEMBERTON : Ask him.

Mr. LONGDIN said he recommended the appointment of Mr. Webster as adjudicator, as the minute recorded; "and also engineer to carry out the work" was added by the committee. Councillor PEMBERTON : That is exactly what I say. Continuing,he said special resolutions couldnot be altered and the one of which notice w.fs given by Alderman Smethurst referred to Warrington Bridge only. He wanted to know how they came to pass a resolution to the effect that the Town Clerk proceed by Bill for the Bridge " and other matters." Councillor RonEnTs : Because, Mr. Mayor - Mr. PEMBERTON: I object to Councillor Roberts interrupting. Councillor ROBERTS: I rise to a point of order. Councillor PEMBERTON : It is a question for the Town Clerk.

The MAYOR: He has risen to a point of order. You shall have fair play. Councillor RODKRTS said the resolution of which notice was given by Alderman Smethurst was to cen- alder the communication from the Local Government Board and "pass resolutions thereon." The whole of the business transactad came within the terms of that resolution.

The MAYOR (to Councillor Pemberton) : You cannot go back and discuss those minutes that have been passed long ago. You are simply moving an amendment to certain minutes in the General Purposes Committee. Councillor PEMBERTON : lam showing reasons why the Town Council should do as I ask. - -
_ Councillor ROBER.TS (to the Mayor) : I ask your ruling whether the interpretation I have put on the resolution is correct or not.
The MAYOR replied that it was correct. Councillor ROBERTS (to Councillor Pemberton) : Then what are you making your statement on a falsehood like that for ? _
Councillor PEMBERTON : I say you are wrong. Councillor ROBERTS : I say you are not speaking
the truth when you say that. I have tidied the Mayor's ruling and it confirms my proposition. Councillor PEMBERTON : It b not a queLtion of ruling, it is a question of fact.

Thic TOWN -CLERK ruled that the notice of motian given by Alderman Smethurst was quite wide enough to carry the resolutions then passed. The MAYoit said the Bill would have to be approved by a meeting of ratepayers and it would also come before the Council for discussion. Councillor PEMBERTON contended that the matter had been treated irregularly. Money was being spent but not a single clause of the Bill had been argued in public. The bridge was agreed to, but there had been added clauses referring to the Waterworks, the widening of Horsemarket-street, Buttermarket-street, Sankey-street, and other matters thit could be got though by Local Government Board inquiries without the expense of going to Parliament. Tte expenditure prorosed under the Bill would run to £500,000. (Cries of "Steady.') The TOWN CLERK pointed out that only the draft notice of the Bill hsd so far teen printed The Bill itself would be sent to the members of the Council in about a week and then would be the time to discuss it.

Councillor PE3IBERTON said he had mention* d sums of money in the Council before. On one occasion when he mentioned the probable amount to he c:aimed by a contractor as £50,000 he was called a liar, but when the claim came in it was for £72,000. Councillor WILKINSON : He didn't get it. If he had claimed £lBO,OOO he would have had the same chance of getting it. Councillor PEMBERTON : When we havo widened Buttermarket-street, Horsemarket-street nod Sankey- street, how much will we have leftout of £300,000? _
Councillor WILKINSON : We shall all he dead when that's done. (Laugh-ter). Councillor PKNIBKRTON : In answer to that, let us remember. what happened under the 1899.8i11._

Councillor Rouria : Does Councillor Pemberton take up a position of opposition to everything con- tained in these proposals? If he does, then I can understand the attitude he is taking up to-night, but if there are certain proposals of which he approves and others of which he disupproves, be will have his oppor- tunity when this matter COMO4 before the Wuncil as a definite proposition in the shape of a Bill._ _
Councillor PENIBMTON (to the Mayor) : Is C )uncillor Roberts going to dictate to you as to what is to bo done here?

The MAYOR : I don't suppose for a moment tint Councillor Roberts desires to do so. Councillor PEMBERTON continuing said their last Bill cost £B,OOO and two years after it was passel every contract named in it was in operation. They were in debt on the 1899 Bill and they had not carried out all that they ought to have done. At the present time they owed £22,500 on the water bill. If they had no inten- tion to proceed with all the proposals, why get a Bill of such magnitude? When so many thousands of pounds of public money were involved, everything ought to be perfectly straight and in order. The MAYOR: I don't suppose for a moment you mean to say this Council does not do what is straight. Councillor PEMBERTON : No, I don't say that. I tell you frankly my opinion is that the majority of the Council would not do it if they knew. I challenge any member of the Council to-night. What does he know about this Bill or how far it has gone? Councillor WILKINSON : Say you don't know. Don't infer that anyone else does not know. Councillor PEMBERTON : I will exempt Councillor Wilkinson.

Councillor WILKINSON: That will do, then. It will be strsight, if I know. There will be nothing wrong with it—l will give you my word for that. Councillor PEMBERTON: You have been here when things have been done in which the Council was admittedly wrong. Councillor PEMBERTON, continuing, said he wanted the Council to remember that they had no right to spend the ratepayers' money until they were convinced that they were on the right course. The voting this time would not be taken in the same way as when the last, Bill was promoted end the people were more enlightened to-day. They hid great expenses in front of them—a sewerage scheme. £lOO,OOO for new schools &c.—and be asked the Council as a matter of precaution not to pledge itself to expenditure that had not been placed before them. Councillor LASIIPORD seconded.

Councillor WILKINSON said it struck him that Cuun- enter Pemberton did not know %hat he was talking about. They were applying for a Hill for certain powers, and the chief thing was with regard to the bridge. The other portions of the bill were matters which might come within the province of gentlemen who entered the Council five, ten, or twenty years hence. Whilst they were going to Parliament they might as well get powers for work which they knew would have to be done in the future, but that did not tie the present Council nor any future Council to do it. They had got to make a start with the Bill and the £lOO had been paid to their London agents for •` pre- liminaries "as required by law. Councillor Pember- ton was talking to people who would like to obstruct the good work which 36 members of the Council were trying to do. Some of those people had had great ambitions to enter the Council but had not got in. (laughter). He thought the majority of the ratepayers could safely trust the business of the town in the hands of the majority of the members of the Council. (Hear, hear). If they Went to the Local Government Board instead of to Parliament they would only have 15 years in which to repay the loan. "One gentleman in the audience," continued Coun- cillor Wimurtsox, "says Question," I know the voice, and I know he was an aspirant to this Council, but let that drop. (Laughter). Proceeding Councillor WILKINSON said Parliament would give them certain indemnifications which the Local Government Board could not give them, and in addition they would have 40 or 50 years in which to repay the loan. In reply to Dr. Joseph, the MAYOR said the Bill would be brought before the Council and also the rate- payers for full discussion. Councillor LASHFORD said that if the Bill passed the ratepayers would have no further voice in the matter. The necessary powers for most of the schemes could be obtained from the Local Government Board and then the ratepayers would have the opportunity of objecting at the inquiries. Why was the Council going to take that small right from the rateyayers ? The Mayor :—Yon won't take that small right from them. It will be for the ratepayers to say whether you are to go to Parliament or not. The TOWN CLERK said the Bill would be submitted to a statutory meeting of the Council and the resolution would have to be passed by an abs Auto majority, Then it would be submitted to a meeting of ratepayers who had the right to vote on it and veto any part of it they desired. -- _ _

Councillor Pemberton said if they went to the Local Government Board, each of the items in the Bill would be publicly inquired into in that room and the rate- payers could come there and object. How could they go through a Bill of tbat magnitude at a public meeting in one night? Councillor Howard said be did not think Councillor Pemberton had any objection to the two bridges; it was the other clauses which were creating what he called "obstruction from outside sources" and which required consideration.
The Mayor said they would have plenty of time to consider them. They were really included to save expense.
AN ANGRY SCENE.

Councillor ROBERTS stated that he had not intended to interpose in the dircussion that night, but after the deplorable ignorance generally displayed with regard to Parliamentary procedure by Councillor Pemberton, it was necessary to say something. The assumption Councillor Pemberton had given utterance to was tbat they were going to commit themselves absolutely to the proposals contained in the Bill. They were doing nothing of the kind. They were only giving preliminary notice according to law. Councillor Pemberton had given his caso away by admitting that he was absolutely in favour of the applmation for poor in respect to the Bridge, and he went so far as to say he thought it might be necessary to go to Parliament to obtain that power. They all knew it was essential to go to Parliament because they had already had intimated to them that the Local Government Board would not grant more than 15 years in which to repay the money. Councillor PEMBERTON observed that that only referred to ferro-concrete and not to iron or steel. Councillor ROBEELTS stated that Councillor Pemberton had supported a ferro-concrete bridge all through. Councillor PEMBERTON said that VMS so if they cou!d get 50 years for iepayirent of the loan. Councillor ROBERTS : Vhat is tho purpose of his oppositiocT I don't hesitate to say that he is. here to-night as nothing more or less thin an absolute obst: uctionist.

Councillor PEMBERTON : I don't get anything out of it anyhow. ' • Councillor ROBERTS : His desire is by misrepresenta- tion or suppression of fact to create an impression out- side that this Council is trying to do sotpething unworthy of it and improper. He is cancealing the fact that there is not a single proposal in the Bill that will not be suhrnitted to the Council for a free and frank discussion, and that the ratepayers of Warrington, who. are so largely represented here to-n4ht—anl I am glad to see them—will have their opportunity, through their accredited representatives, of making such suggestions, alterations, amendments and deletions as they like in regard to the proposal, and I would heartily welcome the co-operation .of accredited representatives of the liatepayera' Association in order that we may discuss this matter together and agree upon a Bill which shall he non-contentious. (Hear, hoar.) Ido ohjezt to this obstruction and the waste of time that goes on both here and at the meetings of the General Purposes Com- mittee, which is a disgrace and a scandd, and it is quite time it was st 'pp() I. (Hear, hear.) I deliberately charge Councillor Pemberton with being the greatest obstruction this Council has ever seen in its midst, and it is time that tho business men or the town who are represented to some extent in the Council, nnd the ratepayers outside knew the sort of man he is and the Sort of mischief he is trying to do in connection with the work of the town. (Hear, hear.) We have arrived at a period in our history at which there is absolute stagnation, and we shall never move forward if this man is to have his way. He talks by the hour, importing things utterly outside the question, and makes misrepreslntatiens which are utterly unworthy of him or of an intelligent cit;zen. CoLIDDIIIOr PEMBERTON: IS this on the minutes? It is a personal attack OD me. Councillor ROBF.RTS: Yes, and it is not the last I shall make,if you continue as you are doing. Councillor PrakinErvroN called attention to the rates and made a comparison between whet they were several yeats ago and what .they ware now, without the education rate.

Councillor ROBERIS: Cumcillor Pemberton talks about the rates. flow much does ho pay in rates? Councillor PEMLIERTON : How much d) you pay? Councillor llonsitTS : I represent rating OA extends to over £4,000 a year,
Councillor PEMBERTON : You are only a pt.id servant You don't pay.tbo rates.

. • Councillor ROBERTS : lam a paid servant and .1 am an interested shareholder. The way you ttlk, God bless my soul, you might own the place. There is not a man that talks more and represents lesa than you do. (Laughter.) Councillor PEMBERTON : The public are not fools. Councillor IfowanD asked whether this personal accusation was necessary. Councillor PEMBERTON : lam not taking this lying down. I have no interest in money spent here. The MAYOR: You are never satisfied. __

_ Councillor Ron Etas : Jam going to let the people of Warrington know through the medium of this meet- ing the sort of thing business men have to endure who attend this Council from time to time at the kinds of this man (Councillor Pemberton), and I say withont any hesitation that it is time it was put a stnp to. • We cannot conduct business as we ought to do. - We are not all of us in a position to come at any bour:of the day awl talk until we lira dry in the throat. Councillor PEMBERTON : Is this on the minutes? The MAYOR: Sit down.
Giuncillor RonEnrs : lam getting at you. I find you've got t. skin. Let m 6 put this matter in a very few words.
Councillor PEMBERTON : r don't make anything out of it. It has been a big loss to mo has my public life. I have been here seven years. He has been here about seven hours.
Councillor CUNNDIGTON : You don't mako anything, out of it.
Councillor ROBERTS: Members of the Council bad better mind what they say. Councillor CUNNINGTON: I have said nowt. (Laughter). _

• _ Councillor ROBERTS: You said as much as Ton think and as much as you are capable of thinking. (Laughter.) Councillor Roberts proceeded to state that the expense to which they had gone would be just as necessary if they bad only gone to Parliament for a bridge as for the whole thing. Councillor PEMBRRToN : Nothing of the kind. Lawyers don't do anything for nothing. Councillor ROBERTS: That shows either the dense ignorance or the wilful perversion of facts that Coun- cillor Pemberton is capable of. Proceeding, Councillor Roberts explained that the notices that had to be pub- lished were the Salllo in tiny case, and they were not going to tin ratepayers' meeting until they had got a proper Bill, which they could recommend to them. The ratepayers could demand a poll and refuse to confer upon the Council any or all of the powers that were sought. He sincerely hoped that the commonsense of the Council and the desire the majority of the members had to witness some progress in their life-time would result in the rejection of the amendment. Alderman SMETHURST said that he felt like Coun- cillor Reber's. The obstruction there had been to the Council busintss during the past six years had been disgrace. During the 19 years he had been in the Council he had always done his best for the ratepayers; but if they took the advice of some people they would never be out of litig ition. The kind of scene they had witnessed that night was constantly occurring in com- mittee. He asked the councillors and the ratepayers to look back over the last few years and see how many members of the Council they had lost—good and true men—who did their best for the benefit of the town. There were two gentlemen now whose lives would be endingered if they entered the Council, owing to the conduct and extravagant speeches mide at the meetings. It was time the business was conducted in a business-like manner. They had the best and highest advice the Council could have in the course they were taking over the question now before them. Some people said that grass would grow ender Warrington Bridge before a new bridge was built. (Laughter). He asked the Council, with all his heart and soul, to vote for the minutes for the benefit of Warrington. Councillor TOOLE asked what was the position of the Council if the amendment were carried. It was very important and he regretted the absence of many aldermen and councillors who knew this motion was coming forward. The TOWN CLERK: The amendment has reference to the Parliamentary expenses already incurred and which we will have to pay in any case now. Councillor LASHFORD asked why £lOO was not on the minutes for Parliamentary expenses. _ _
The MA.YOR Slid it was Included in the orders for payment amounting to £653 2s. 9d., which was the usual method.

Councillor LASHFORD: If this Bill is refused are we supposed to pay this £B,OOO ? Councillor WILKINSON: We are only talking about £lOO. If you listen to Pemberton ho will have you all over the show. (Laughter). The amendment was then put and there voted for it: Councillors Pemberton, Lashford and Cunnington. Against: The Mayor, Aldermen Smethurst, Bennett and James Evans, and Councillors Wilkinson, Craik, Steel, Sankey, Hawthorn' Howard, Toole, Wilson, C. Jackson Holmes, Bellian, Roberts, Birtles and Rogers. The amendment was lost by 17 votes to 3. THE ENGINEER'S APPOINTMENT.
Councillor PEMBERTON moved a farther amendment that the Seal of the Council be not affixed to the agree- ment with Mr. Webster.

_ Councillor ROBERTS submitted that the amendment was out of order. Under cover of an amendment to the minutes of the General Puryoses Committee, Coun- cillor Pemberton was trying to introduce his resolution.

_ Councillor PEMBERTON : It is exactly what the Town Clerk advised me to do. Henry Roberta, too, was the very man who got up and said I could do it. Councillor ROBERTS: Henry Roberts said nothing of the kind.

Councillor PEMBERTON : Councillor Roberts com- plains about me-- Councillor ROBERTS: I have got a very good memory and I never made this statement. Councillor PEMBERTON : Councillor Roberts is not the only Man in this room who has got a memory. Councillor ROBERTS: No, but you have got a very bad one. (Laughter.) Councillor PEMBERTON said he did not want the whole agreement to be deleted. He wanted Mr. Webster to go on with his adjudication, but the only course was to move that the seal be not affixed.

Councillor WILKINSON, in saconding, said he did not wish to interfere with Mr. Webster at all. Along with Councillor Pemberton he did not want the seal affixed until such time as they knew the number of years that would be allowed for repaying the loan for a ferro- concrete bridge,and if they did not proceed with a ferro- concrete bride he did not want the Corporation to be liable to Mr. Webster for any damages. The TOWN CLERK said that if they did not accept a tender they would not pay Mr. Webster his 5 par cent. Councillor WILKINSON said that if he had such an assurance he would be satisfied.

Councillor ROBERTS said if they did not put their seal to the agreement they were putting Mr. Webster in an unfair potition, because he would have no legal claim for any work he did. Under the agreement the Corporation were only liable for work done. If there was no accepted tender there was no liability and if they found they could not gat a sufficiently long period for repayment of loan to make it worth their ehile to build a ferro concrete bridge," they could dr9p the matter altogether. . Councillor LOCKER said that if they were exonerated from liability in the event of the work not being pro- ceeded with he did not thihk anyone would object to the seal being affixed. It would, however, be premature to do that if they were not to be freed from responsi- bility if the laricbze were not completed. The TOWN CLERK : You only hied yourself to pay 5 per cent. on the contract which you nocept, if you accept one at all. Councillor PEMBERTON Said he would withdraw the amendment and proceed with his soecial motioa. Councillor ROBERTS (to the tyor) : I call your attention to the fact. that this courae is entirely out of order and ask you to rule accordingly. • The MAYOR ruled th tt Coun illor Pemberton would tilt be in order in bringing for.vard the motion if he could not carry his amcnlment.

Al lernim BENNETT said he was entlrely opposed to Counc7llor Pernherton's argument on the general .ques- Von, but he tholght that if he withdrew tha amend- ment out of regiri to the gen 3r.il feeling of the Council it wolld unf.tir to refine him the right to move his resolution.
The amendm nt •,v.is put to the vote but only Councillor Pembert sn voted for it and it was therefore lost. RESOLUTION RULED our OF ORDER.
Cou,icillor PEMBERTON firm allied leave to move his special Tosolotion rnentionoi above. Tiie MA VOR :It is 0 It or

div.head: WORMA?::„'S METAL POLISH
div.p: WORMA?::„'S METAL POLISH
MR. CHURCHILL AT SOUTHPORT.
SFEE6II ITY
THE TORY CAMPAIGN OF " AUDACITY, RAPACITY & MENDACITY."
HOW TARIFF REFORM WOULD HIT LANCASHIRE.

At the great overflow meeting in the Opera House, Southport, on Saturday, Sir George Pollard, member for the Eccles division of Lancashire, was in the chair, supported by Mr. Astbury, K.C., member for the Southport division • Baron do Forest, Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P. for Warrington ; Mr. J. S. Higham, M.P., for the Sowerby division; and others. Mr. A. H. CROSFIELD, M.P., who was received with cheers,said : I want in the first place to thank the Liberals of Southport for their kindness in sending me an invitation to attend this great meeting. It feel it to be a very high honour to be allowed to take part in the proceedings here to-day on this most memorable and historic occasion. (Cheers). I think it a very good thing Mr. Churchill has come down toLancashire at this time,and that besides giving the County Palatine an exposition of the practical, useful and urgently needed policy of the Progressive Party he should turn the
SEARCHLIGHT OF A BRILLIANT AND POWERFUL INTELLECT

on to the methods of those who think they can run an election on the same lines as some of the influential men •in their own party run a reckless and sensa- tional halfpenny press. (Cheers). Elections it is said, are not fought in the halls of truth, and I dare say we ought all of us make ,allowances for a little exaggeration whether On the one side or on the other in these -moments of excitement. But I am afraid that this time we are in for something a good deal worse than any of the ciistomary special pleading and even the inflated statements of political partisans and enthusiasts. There is to be, or there was to be a whirlwind campaign in Lancashire. Well I hope none of you have suffered in Southport from any little meterological eccentricity of our climate this last day or two—(laughter)--and I am Quite certain none of us in Lancashire have been shaken politically by any such political whirlwind, as we were to anticipate a whirlwind campaign organised on the most approved yellow press methods. I fear we are in for nothing less than a CAMPAIGN OF AUDACITY, RAPACITY, AND

MENDACITY worked by those who seek to gull the public and despoil the nation. (Cheers). The posi- tion of Protectionists in Lancashire of all places in the country is so hopelessly unsound that it seems to me there will scarcely be a pretence at any reasoned defence at all. No, logic will be pitched to the winds, and barefaced appeals to ignorance and prejudice will take its place. People are being told that "-Taxes on corn will not raise, they may even lower the price of bread; moreover the foreigner will pay our taxes; and yet while he continues to do this on his imported articles, by shutting him out there will at the same time be work for all, and two jobs for every man." (Laughter.) Well, to me that sounds just a little too good to be true. (Laughter.) In illustration of his point, Mr. Crosfield told an amusing story of a Scot—one Saundy by name—who had to place himself at the tender mercies of a dentist—McPherson—and before the gas was administered, was seen to produce some silver coins from his pocket. McPherson protested that there was no need to pay in advance and was surprised to receive the reply : "Nae,nae, it's no' that I'm going to pay ye, but before ye gie me the gas, I'm going to coont the shier in ma pocket." (Loud laughter.) "Whenever our Protectionist friends promise you two jobs for every man that wants one" added Mr. Crosfield I do strongly advise any voter, before he allows himself to be drawn into such a trap, to count the siller ' in his pocket." (Hear, hear and laughter).
Continuing, Mr. Crosfield said: Evidently the
STANDING DISH IN THE TORY MENU

is going to be this cry throughout the country," Work for all," and it does strike me as peculiarly odious that one of the great parties in the State should in this way try to make political capital out of the sufferings and too often the miseries of those who are short of employment—(hear, hear),—but none the less it has the sanction, alas, of the Member for West Birmingham, and it is used at street corners and in the gutter press from end to end of the country. I should call it absolutely disgraceful if the Liberal party tried to make capital in the same way and pretended that either fiscal system will of itself enable us to get rid of the whole of this evil of unemployment. Responsible Conservatives know just as well as Liberals do that neither Free Trade nor Protection will get rid altogether of fluctuations of trade, flucuations by the way which are worse in Protected than in Free Trade countries. (Hear, hear.) Well, ladies and gentlemen, if they do throw down the gauntlet to us, and challenge us on this question of unemployment we will accept their challenge—(cheers)—because there is no part of the whole country that stands to lose more in unemployment than the County Palatine if we resorted to the old and evil practices of Protection. It is admitted now by responsible men on the Tory side, it cannot be denied because the evidence is before our eyes all over the world that
PROTECTIVE DUTIES MUST AND DO RAISE PRICES,

and so incidentally the cost of manu- facture for every cotton spinner in Lancashire. What effect must that have on the vast oversea trade which forms eighty per cent of the whole production of the cotton mills of the country? Some of this trade is held by narrow margins, and some of it would unquestionably be lost. Well, we have an old saying in Lancashire that "Eating is like fighting; it only wants beginning,"and that is precisely the casewith your Protectionist. (Hear,hear.) Small duties lead to larger duties, and soon, and we should deliberately run the risk of throwing away, it might be, twenty or twenty-five per cent. or even more, of this wonderful cotton trade of ours, affording as it does to-day the means of livelihood for millions of our popu- lation. Yes, and at the very same time the

COST OF LIVING for all the operatives would be greater; and the operative would object to bear the whole burden himself; he would go and ask the employer to share that burden by giving Mm a rise in wages. But the employer would have to tell him that his output was already reduced owing to his increased cost of manufacture losing Min the command in certain foreign markets; all his standing charges would be increased by this reduced output, and far front raising wages he would say, "If lam to maintain the trade I must reduce cost of manufacture and therefore rather than higher wages I must ask you to accept a lower rate of wages." I say,Mr. Chairman, that inevitably friction would arise between employer and employed. So far as we in Lancashire are concerned, and. many another County too, Protection would take us straight along
THE ROAD THAT LEADS TO IND USTRIAL STRIFE.
And then what about employment? Is there anything that causes more of the pro- fusion and wretchedness of unemployment than industrial warfare?

I hear people say they are sick of the talk of Free Traders about cheapness. They miss what is the very A.B.C. of the question. They miss the fact that cheapness is a most powerful factor in creating employment, for the obvious and simple reason that if by Protection we are going to make everything dearer people will be able to buy less than they do now of the necessaries of life, and they will therefore be able to give less employment to those who produce those necessaries. The balance of argument in favour of Free Trade is simply overwhelming. (Cheers.) And so as the greatest safeguard against unemployment let us stick to Free Trade and get to work with the practical schemes for Labour Exchanges, and Trade Boards, and those contributory schemes for insurance which will be a perfect God-send to the whole artisan class in our country. Lt us go forward with our remedial social reform,—thus helping to reduce unemploy- ment to a minimum—and so far as large sums are needed alike for these and for Imperial defence let us take care that we raise them without putting another penny piece on those articles of food and clothing which are indeed the prime necessaries of life to

that large portion of our population for whom already life is none too easy. Don't let us put on a single tax that will either impair the physique or lower the vitality of our people. That broadly speaking is our policy. It opens out before the progressive party a prospect full, of good hope for the future of our people, and if a group of selfish and short sighted, privileged and prejudiced men choose to block the way, well we must join issue with them. (Cheers.) The House of Lords is playing the usurper, and the time has therefore cbme when we must for ever check their power so that never again will they have the chance to work evil in the State. (Loud cheers.)

div.head: FLAG
div.p: FLAG
„s axed ?
A STIRRING APPEAL

Mr. RbBERT LEWIS, of Manchester; said he had just come from one of the most memorable meetings ever held in the city of Manchester—the demonotration at the Free Trade Hill addressed by Mr. Winston Churchill (Cheers.) One important fact to which. Mr. Churchill had called their attention was that the Bard of Trade returns for November showed that the exports amounted to

div.head: £4,000,000 MORE
div.p: than for the same month last year--(Chee. rs)—and over a million of that was represented by cotton. (Cheers.) "Cotton is going," continued ]Sfr Lewis- amid great laughter; "iron is going; the Lords are going —(laughter)--and will very soon be goue." (Cheers.) He wished them all to realize that never in the history of the country had there been a struggle like this. Their rights, their safety, their liberties depended upon the issue of this election. The Lords had absolutely refused to the Crown the supplies necessary for the maintenance of the army, the provision for the navy, the payment of old age pensions and every other need of a properly regulated State. That was revolution. When the Lord Advocate declared that under Tariff Reform it was impossiple for Mr. Balfour or any Government he formed to provide the money necessary for ()id age pensions, Mr. Balfour said "it was a frigid and calculated lie." But Mr. Balfour could not characterise as a lie the fact that his com- mittee in the Ruse of Lords had absolutely refused the money to pay for old age pensions. It was not a question of raising it; they had refused to pay for them. (A VoteE : " And for the eight they wanted.") The Lords had embarked upon a revolution, but the Lords would not settle it. The people would do that —(cheers)—and the Lords must be prevented from ever again attempting to. control finance. (Cheers.) The marvel was that the people had endured such an anomaly as the present House of Lords so long. The time had come when that state of things must be ended. (Cheers.) With regard to

intr. PROSPECTS IN WARRINGTON, Mr. Crosfield, their present member, had an opinion on the Budget and had not hesitated to express it in the House of Commons. (Cheers.) The man who did that and who was sound on the great questions now before the country, was the kind of man who would lead them to victory. (cheers.) Tariff reform would not mean work for all, but it would mean workhouse for a good many. It would mean handing the mass of the population into the power of trusts and syndicates that would squeeze the life blood out of them. But the struggle meant more than that. The Lords would be able to dictate to the country when the Liberals were in power as to whether they should have a General Election every twelve months, and whether the long established custom of the constitution that representatives government should imply the raising of taxation in the representative Douse, should be abolished and the control of financial matters relegated to 500 individuals who happened to be the eldest sons of their fathers. The Liberals must win in the conflict, for the sake of the poor, for the sake of the aged who were looking to them for help and whose days had been brightened by the gift of pensions.' (Cheers.) The great industries of the country, free and unfettered as they had heon,were looking to them to s'afeguard their interests and those interests were the people's interests. Other ocountries, which had been for so long under the heel of oppression and were looking to England for light and leading, were asking the democracy of this country, for the sake of their freedom, to do right and win in this great struggle. (Cheers). It was no selfish battle of the masses against the classes. The progressives had nothing to gain by it except their freedom ; the Lords had everything to gain and little to lose—but that little they would lose if the workers were .determined to assert their .rights. (Cheers.) • "KING LANSDOWI4E I."

Mr. UPSON, in moving a vote of thanks to Mr. Lewis, said that no doubt if he asked those present under what King they were living, they would reply "Under King Edward VII." They were making a mistake, for they were really living under King Lansdowne I. (Laughter). The House of Lords had done what for 300 years they had never dared to do— they had usurped the right and authority of the Crown. They had declared that from this time for- ward the King was not the first man or the first power in the realm but that their noble selves were to be the supreme rulers of the country. The coming election would be a soldiers' battle, in which the return of Mr. Crisfield would be. but an incident. They were' not fighting primarily to return him but to preserve their own rights—the rights to which they had been born and of which they were now 'being deprived. He (Mr. Upson) had thought the battle of liberty had been fought and won. He was inclined to think the present crisis was a judgment upon us because we had not sufficiently cherished the rights we had inherited from our fathers Where was the passion for nationality which char- acterised our predecessors in the middle of the nineteenth century? We had let little nations go to the wall, oppressed and robbed of their rights of equality by great and powerful neighbours-:—we had even taken part ourselves in that despicable game. Had we cherished as we ought to have done-our rights of freedom and liberty, he believed they would not , have been imperilled this moment. In the coming I election we would be fighting not only for our own rights but for prospective rights. We would be fight- ing for the social programme which Mr. Churchill and Mr. Lloyd-George and other members of the Government had outlined, for insurance against sick- 'less- and accident, for the establishment of labour bureaux, for the time when the workingman would be able to sleep peacefully at night knowing that he was safeguarded against some of the ills which might beset him, and that he would not be so completely at .the mercy of trade fluctuations, epidemics and break- downs in health. The social programme of the Government would relieve to a great extent that terrific sense of an unknown future and make the workingtnan a happy citizen of a happy State. (Cheers). Councillor LoCKER seconded and the vote was heartily passed. A vote of thanks to Mr. Parker for presiding con- laded the meeting.
