div.head: PEOPLE'S CHARTER.
div.p: THE PEOPLE'S CHARTER.
MR. LLOYD-GEORGE'S FIGHTING SPEECH.
" Tax the Man Who Earns Nothing."

A fine fighting speech was delivered on Thursday night by Mr. Lloyd-George to a. great and enthusiastic meeting of his con- stituents at Carnarvon. The Chancellor's first few sentences, were in Welsh, the rest of the speech being delivered in English. , Once for all Mr. Lloyd-George demolished the bogey that the Budget is Socialism In telling sentences and with effective concrete cases he showed that the Budget is merely "justice and equality for all." Here are some of the points of the speech We are in for rough weather. It may be a winter of storms. But there will be something brought within the reach of the people that will give warmth and glow to their grey lives. The common people have gained nothing worth gaining without effort, sacrifice, and suffering. It is not the man who earns who grumbles at the super-tax. I know many of them, and I never heard one of them complain. It is men who never earned a copper of their money who complain. The Lords' claim is a mockery of the democracy. It means annual Parliaments while the Liberals are in power and septen- nial Parliaments while the Tories are in power. Do the Lords really think the people of this country are fools It is not a refer- ence to the people, it is a refusal. Why exempt a man from rendering an account on taxable property purely because he has one man to fix his collar and adjust his tie in the morning, a couple of men to carry a boiled egg to him at breakfast-- laughter, a fourth man to open the door for him, a fifth man to show him in and out of his carriage, and a sixth and a seventh to drive him. The people must struggle if they desire a higher life ; it is stagnation that is the danger. The democracies of the world are watch- ing the present conflict with anxious eyes. Ending his speech as he began it, in Welsh, the Chancellor gave .a homely parable of the " backwoods " days of his boyhood, when he gathered sticks. It was after storms that he got most sticks. "We are in for rough weather," he said, amid cheers, and the lesson of the parable was plain. Speaking, at a wildly enthusiastic after- noon meeting Mr. Lloyd George was at the end- overcome with emotion and sat down abruptly, exclaiming, "I thank you. I thank you."

div.head: FOOD TAXERS
div.p: FOOD TAXERS
COMING INTO THE OPEN.
Mr. Churchill's Reply.

The "Birmingham Daily Post," possibly inspired by Mr. Chamberlain, has this week piovided the Tariff Reformers with a set, programme and some sources of revenue, the chief among which are taxes on food.. No one will believe that the foreigner will pay these, and the electors are faced with the clear alternative of dearer food if they give any support to Tariff Reform and the Birmingham programme. There is no mystery now as to where the Tariff Reformers propose to get their revenue. Imports—food and raw materials— are to be "protected." As a result we should manufacture less, and have to eat. less.
Mr. Churchill replied effectively to the Food Taxers at Liverpool on Wednesday night, when he addressed an audience of 6,000 people, and was received with wild enthusiasm.

div.head: Points for Warrington
div.p: Points for Warrington
Housewives.

Mrs. Crosfield, the charming wife of our Borough Member, is early showing her determination to take an active part in the great struggle between the People and the Peers for legislative and constitutional freedom. She has entered the lists in her husband's constituency with the following 'reply to Miss Brooke Hunt's fallacious Tariff Reform address of last week.
[To THE EDITOR OF THE "EXAMINER," WARRINGTON.]

Sir,—ln reading the speech Miss Brooke- Hunt made in Warrington last week on behalf of the Women's Unionist and Tariff Reform Lekgue I am amazed at what she says about cheapness being " 6.iite a ,seconolary consideration." Let me tell her :that when she next comes to Warrington if ,she takes the trouble to ask the thrifty )house-wives of our town their opinion she will find that they attach very great import- ance indeed to abeapnesq. •

I must also ,point.out to .her that she very ;greatly errs in thinking that cheapness imeans less employment. .Gba,the contrary, it ;stands to reason that the cheaper food and ,clothing are the more the :peop(le can buy of them; therefore manufacturers produce more, and thus more 'Wands are employed. :If on the other hand everything were dearer, 'millions of our ;people ,would 'lame to be eon- -tent With Jess, and so our manufacturers 'would make less. 'Therefore dearness means /less employment, just as cheapness means . more.

That is my answer to Miss Brooke-Hunt's -statement that the best thin in the world is tto secure good 'work and good wages, and 3 that 'thus cheapness should be quite a -secondary consideration—a most unfortu- nate: antithesis.

She then asks " What is the good of bread theing cheap in the shops if there is none in the cupboard " ? Does she think the way to -.replenish the cupboard is to make bread dearer? For an answer to that I will again refer her to the housewives of Warrington. As for the remarks which she addresses -to Trades Unionists, viz. :—" Is it their •principle .that cheapne% is best ? " "What ,does Trade Unionism exist for? To get t better wages for the members and to protect their interests," I fear she has been con- 'fusing wages with the things wages buy. ' Trades Unionists are very naturally in favour of a good rate of wages for their 'labour, but they as naturally have the :strongest objection to spending more on k every single article they buy.—Yours etc* DOMINI CROSFIELD. .Barremman, Hoylake, December 6th, 1909.

div.head: TRADES UNION CONGRESS MANIFESTO. Commons or Lords—Which Shall Prevail ?
div.p: TRADES UNION CONGRESS MANIFESTO. Commons or Lords—Which Shall Prevail ?

A manifesto was issued on Monday by the 'Trades Union Congress Parliamentary, Corn- • mittee calling upon the workmen of England -to accept the challenge thrown down by the House of Lords, which is a menace to political 'freedom. Their action in rejecting the ,Budg'et proposals is described as a deliberate .and unpardonable insult to the duly-elected representatives of the people. The manifesto gives an account of the stewardship of the Labour party during the last four years, and urges workmen on the day of the poll to :support only those candidates pledged to the maintenance of the independence of the House of Commons in all financial matters, and who are prepared to support measures of social reform endorsed by the Trades Union Congress.

div.head: E! THUSIASTIC GATHERING.
div.p: E! THUSIASTIC GATHERING.

The coming electoral campaign will find the Liberal forces of Warrington Well organized to achieve another great victory for the progressive cause. A spirit of enthusiastic determination per- vaded a joint meeting of the Liberal Ward committees which was held at the Liberal club on Monday even- ing, and some stirring speeches were delivered. The attendance was all that could be desired, the large billiard room being crowded. Mr. C. E. Parker (president of the Liberal Association) presided and amongst others present were: Alderman Tinnion, Councillors Wilkinson, Lpcker, Hawthorn, Dicken- son, Skelland, Howard, and Halliwell, Messrs. .1, Dodds,, J. Upson, T. Pemberton, G. Walker, P. Peacock, J. Jarman, J. Critchley, B. Farrar, W. Clegg, G. Weaver, T. Locker, E. England, Jos. Qwen, S. Wright, E. Wynne Jones, J. C. Holland, P. Winskill, N, Cook, W. Haigh, J. Drury, J. Bailey, R. W. Cook, and Mr. Robert Lewis of Manchester. The PRESIDENT announced that letters of apology for non-attendance had been received from Alderman Burton, Messrs. E. J. Guest, J. Longland and F. Maginn. Mr.. GUEST wrote from Colwyn Bay :—I wish I could render vigorous service in the coming campaign against the arrogant assumption of the Lords. They will be re-enforced by the whole power of the liquor traffic, else the victory wohld be an easy • one ' for the democracy. But with the force of" the , trade "behind them., the battle will be fierce. ' Nevertheless there can surely be little doubt on which side the victory will be gained. But it is never safe to despise the enemy, it would seem that the Labour Party will co-operate with us on this occasion and I trust there will be no three-cornered contests to weaken the forces of 'progress. As regards Warring- ton, I think Mr. Urosfield has done well for the con- stituency. He has proved himself

THE BEST MEMBER OF tARLIAMENT WE. HAVE EVER HAD. He has more than fulfilled expectations and seems likely to develop yet more and more so that he may attain a position of some importance. He has done well as a private member and needs only opportunity to secure greater influence in the House. I have every reason to believe that this opportunity will be given him and that he will be returned again in January, with a large majority. The meeting unanimously approved a suggestion by the president that Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., should address a meeting on December 21st, When the ques- tion of selecting him as candidate will be considered.

less ever-flowing expansion of private luxury—here are the foes of Britain, here are the real dangers to the great State we have accumulated by the sacri- fices and the valour of a thousand years. Beware, lest they do not overturn the fabric of British glory. And then look at the other side. Look at the good forces, look at the moral, civic, social, patriotic forces which are advancing to the attack of all this evil. Are not they tremendous too? Why you see them at work from day to day in every town in every creed, in every class throughout our land— strong forces, valiant forces—old England going to the fight for her soul. I think of the state of our country as we bee it now, as if it were two great armies locked together in deadly conflict, swaying this way and that, as the fortunes of the battlefield lead them on, and my belief is strong that in the end the generous forces are going to beat the selfish forces—(cheers)--that in the end the organising forces are going to devour the forces of degeneracy. and that Great Britain is going to emerge fr, all her trials and struggles strengthened by the efforts she has made to guide and 'light the way for the other nations of the world.

Mr. CHURCHILL went on to show that the Budget, so much despised by the Lords, was one of the means by which the evils that he spoke of would undoubtedly be lessened and concluded as follows We do not wish to have power unless the nation wishes us to h.tve it, and we do not intend to under- take the burden and responsibility of Government unless full and effective powers are given to us.— (Loud and prolonged cheering.) We trust the people, and we come to you. The Budget has been murdered ; John Brown's body lies &mouldering in the grave—(laughter),—but his soul goes march= ing along.—(Leud cheers.) A spirit of social service and of social justice, of a larger brother-

the Lords but added: "We have got tlth at last " and he (Mr. Dodds) was reminded of the words of Lord Clive, the great English soldier, who on one occasion when he had got his Highlanders ready for action exclaimed "Up lads and at them." (Cheers.) Mr. Dodds contended that tariff reform would be injurious to the interests of the working- classes and pointed oat that once it was adopted it would be years before they could get rid of it. Con- cluding he urged his hearers to do their utmost in the coming fight for the sake of the great principles which were embodied in Liberal p3licy and declared his, conviction that ,if they worked • unitedly the Liberals of Warrington would maintain their position and even improve upon it. (Cheers.)
ALDERMAN TINNION AND THE MOMENTDITS, ISSUE.

Alderman Tismos said they had an excellent pros- pective candidate in Mr: A. H.. Crosfield. (Cheers). They won handsomely at the last election and if Mr. Crosfield was a fit and proper person to represent them then—as he undoubtedly was . he was more than ever qualified now that he had taken such a charming and excellent lady for his, companion and adviser. (Cheers). The coming fight would be more momentous and stern than he (Alderman! Tinnion) .could remember in his experience—and he. had been engaged in electoral contests in Warrington for over thirty years: Never had the issues been' so tre- mendous as they were this time. He did not hesitate to say that the liberties of the democracy of England were in the balance: On which side were they (his hearers) going to be? Were they going to trust themselves to the
TENDER MERCIES' OF THE HOUSE OF LORDS

(" Never ") to the aristocracy and millionaires—those men who lived not by the sweat of their brows but by the sweat of the brows of others? Were they going to trust their destinies in such hands or were they going to shape their ends for themselves? He hoped that at the beginning, of the new year one of the good resolutions they would make and act upon what be to do their best to secure the return of the Liberal Govern- ment and thus protect their own interests and those of. coming generations. That excellent meeting afforded them great encouragement and could be con- sidered a happy augury for the campaign. The people had now the great opportunity for which they had been waiting. Would they taken advantage-of it, or would they allow it to slip and fasten chains about. their necks which it would take more than twe generations to shake off? (aeerb.) He appealed to

div.head: MR. PARKER'S ADDRESS.
div.p: MR. PARKER'S ADDRESS.

The PRE4DENT, in the course of a brief address, said it was four years since they fought a battle together and won a glorious victory. That victory was somewhat in the nature of a parade, but this time it would be a very difficult fight. The other side were far better organized and prepared than they were on the last occasion, and they ware fighting for what was their trade and their direct selfish interests. The Liberal party were not a wealthy party; they depended—and were glad to depend—upon the democracy—not so much upon money .as upon the service and sacrifice of those who were willing to fight for the good of their country. With regard to the issue, he had in his published appeal ,expressed his opinion about that venerable House which they hoped would, in its present form, pass into oblivion. Mr. Parker went on to refer to the great meeting in Parr Hall on Saturday, December 18th, when that grand and coming man, Mr. Winston Churchill. would address them. (Cheers). A meeting of the Finance Committee had been held, and subject to Mr. Churchill's agreeing to speak at an overflow meeting, it had been decided to engage the Hippodrome. (Cheers). Mr. Crosfield, as the member for the borough, would take the chair at the Parr Hall meet- ing and he (Mr. Parker) would preside at the overflow meeting. The coming fight would be a fierce one, but he believed the leaders of the Liberal party were determined to do their part because they felt that the rank and file, who were the strength ef the democratic forces, would do their share and back them up. They were glad to hear from all parts of the country that the enthusiasm of the democracy was being raised and he had no doubt that they would be able to send to Parliament a
SWINGING MAJORITY

to help such men as the Prime Minister—(cheers)—and Mr. Lloyd-George —(cheers)—in passing into law that great and popular Budget which they had spent six months of arduous labour in passing through the Commons, only to be contemptously rejected by the Lords. Having urged all present to do their utmost to influence publie opinion on behalf of the Govern- ment, Mr. Parker read an extract from Mr. Winston Churchill's speech at Preston—a speech which in eloqutnce and power he (Mr. Parker) con- sidered matched anything that• we had had from the great orptors of the past: Mr. Churchill, referring to the impressions of the Colonial Press representatives who recently visited this country, said : The worst thing they saw here at heme was the contrast between the extremes of poverty and the extremes of luxury. (Cheers-0 The greatest danger in their opinion which ,the British Empire was exposed to was not abroad. It w..s not to be found amongst the great armies of the Continent. It was not to be found in the difficult questions connected with the government of India. It was not to be found in the Yellow peril or the Black peril, or any other peril in all the wide extent of our colonial and foreign affairs. No,, it was here, close at hand, this side of the sea, in our own country, in the crowded cities which are expanding and congesting year by year, and in the deserted, dwindling hamlets of our country districts. In these,in the opinion of these colonial editors,lay the greatest danger which menaced the continued supremacy of the British; race. (Cheers.) The separation of the people from the land, unexampled in any European country, the drifting apart of rich and poor, which finds no parallel anywhere except in the United States, the exploita- tion of boy and woman labour, the physical degeneration which follows so swiftly upon civil- ised poverty, and whie.h has already menaced the British Empire by making it difficult for us even to recruit the necessary soldiers for our small army, the awful havoc created by the liquor traffic, the Insecurity in the means of subsistence and employ- ment, the absence of any established minimum standard of life and comfort for the industrious worker,. and on the other hand, all the swift, cease-

hood possible among men of a conscious and concerted effort towards a better state of things. That spirit lives to-night to vivify and fortify our line of battle, and, I will add, to purify and sanctify our cause.—(Cheers.) And wherever throughout tho land men and women are found doing their, best for their 'fellow-countrymen, willing to make exertions and sacrifices for the causes of the weak and the poor, there we shall find friends and comrades in this struggle; there we shall find enthusiasm and resolves which will support us; there we shall find an inexhaustible and boundless strength, sustained by which we shall surely, conquer now.—(Loud and long con- tinued cheers.) The man who could so express from the bottom of his heart the aspirations of Liberalism, continued Mr. Parker, was well worth going to hear, and the Execu- tive Committee desired to give a chance to as many Warrington people as possible of attending the forth- coming meetings. There would be no charge for tickets, and application must be made to Mr. Howes at the Liberal Club. In conclusion, Mr. Parker extended a hearty welcome to Mr. Dodds who, he said, had always stood true to Liberalism, and asked' him to address the meeting. MR. DODDS AND TARIFF REFORM.

Mr. DODOS, who was enthusiastically greeted, said he had always been a Radical, and so was his father before him. (Cheers.) He agreed with the President that Mr. Winston Churchill's speech at Preston was one of the finest he had ever read in regard to any special subject which had come before the country. Mi. Churchill stated the whole case splendidly, show- ing the necessity for the Budget and the unconstitu- tional position of the Lords, and he (Mr. Dodds) was sure that if the electors thoroughly understood the issue they would see what a magnificent Government we had, and realize how it ought to lie supported through thick and thin. . (Cheers.) Mr. Lloyd-George in his most recent speech spoke of the cunning of

his hearers to leave no stone unturned and to think no sacrifice too great to bring about a successful issue. (cheers.) Mr. W. Haunt said the workers who had rtad about the effects of Protection in the past would not wish to return to it. He would call the attention of the meeting to the conclnding words, of Mr. Lewis HareOurt's speech on Saturday :- "The Peers have proof/dm4d a class war. Very well, they shall have it—(cheers)---and on their heads be . THE BLOOD OF THE CONFLICT.

The toiling millions have too long stood the helpless onlookers at the wreckaae of their hopes and the denial of their rights. (Cheers.) At last your day is dawning. Go into this conflict with deep determination, with grave thought, with unflinching valour, and you will win for yourselves and your children a heritage of which our country will be proud." (Cheers.) , VITAL TO WARRINGTON:
Councillor WILKINSON said it .had been decided to hold
MEETINGS IN EVERY WARD

next week and he hoped the members of all the com- mittees would work their hardest and raise Mr. Crosteld's majority from 1,500 to 2,000. (Cheers.) He could not under Stand how men who read about the questions at stake could be found supporting the other side. The speaker referred to Warrington's industrial progress and pointed to the large number of great concerns which owed their origin to men of Liberal and progressive principles. When they considered the wonderful strides made in the various local industries, dared they,on the word of Mr. Balfour who wfts not a businessman, tamper with what they knew to be right and embark upon tariff reform? Warrington dared not experiment in such a matter. How ,were manufacturers going to continue to compete if a 10 per cent duty were imposed on raw materials. They could not tax raw materials or manufactured articles

without rvi%?ing: priCesi. If the Budget had levied faxes,on tew and other neressaries of-life, instead of tapping new setues c inane, the Lords would not have rejected it With regard to the land question, the Chancellor was simply proposing that the land- j lord should no IcAger escape hiaair share of taxation, I but should contrante•to the need!, of the community whose enterprise and necessitie& helped to enhance the value of his land. (Cheers,) Councillor Wilkinson concluded by urgingthe.assembly to do their utmost to return" our Arthur" triumphantly in the forth- coming struggle. (Cheers-)

div.p: THE NEW GENTLEMANLY PARTY.

They are only a few, of his intimates who always travel with him." JOHN BULL: "Are they? Then I won't have anything to do with any of you. I don't like the company you keep."

Mr. BALFOUR is about BALFOURIAN to issue a manifesto AND It is proclaimed in BRUMMAGEM advance that it will be POLITICS, a stirring document. Perhaps it will; but Mr. BALFOUR has certainly not produced anything very stirring of late. He has been most extraordinarily lacking in inspiration, and for the reason, as is quite evident, that be is being dragged along by the party that he professes to lead. The pace is now , becoming rapid, and must be mentally dis- turbing to a really serious extent in the case of a man with so tepid a temperament as the Leader of the Opposition. The Cham- berlain manifesto issued through the Birmingham Post the other day is miles in advance of any position in which Mr. Balfour can ever have expected to find himself. It is only three or four years since he thought it safe to declare that he would never be the leader of a Protectionist party. He has found that he must be that or nothing. The choice is between retirement from politics altogether or going along with the Protec- tionists, however reluctantly, and with what- ever ambiguity or protestation. The manifesto from Birmingham would be perfectly staggering to any other man in Mr. BALFOUR'S position. It ts, evidently intended to instruct him as to his future course, as was the Chamberlain letter which called upon the Lords to throw out the Bydget, read at his own meeting when he was as yet uncertain as to his own mind and intentions. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is laid aside by physical ailment; but he retains a remarkable capacity for spurring his reluctant pupil. How long is it since the Leader of the Opposition wrote his now almost forgotten pamphlet in favour, or appearing to be in favour, of a policy of retaliation as the utmost possible step in the direction of Protection?. Many milestones have been passed since then. There was the stage at which Mr. BALFOUR would not men- tion Tariff Reform at all, and that at which he would only mention it in a sense entirely different from that in which it was under- stood by the Chamlierlainite section of his party. Then, still with, a difference of interpretation, Tariff Reform was to become the leading item on the Conservative pro- gramme; but there must be no taxation of food. And now ;there issues from Birming- ham a declaration to the effect that there must not only be taxation of food, but taxa- tion of raw materials, and that food taxation must be of wider scope and of larger amount than even Mr. CHAMBERLAIN originally con- templated. What is poor, harassed, Mr. BALFOUR to do now?

The Birmingham declaration should prove enlightening beyond Measure to those who have been honestly hesitating as to the Pro- tectionist policy which is misnamed Tariff Reform. It should prove to them in a wholly conclusi,ve way that Protection never stands still. It is always demanding more. The exposure made by Mr. URE and others as to how little a protectionist policy would bring to the Treasury under the accepted limita- tions has made it necessary to foreshadow a Protectionist Budget with these limitations thrown aside. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S original plan . was to leave our ports open to maize and bacon, be cause to make them dear would injure the poor, especially in Ireland, the plain admis- sion being that taxation or tariff must certAinly raise the price of these commodities.

Maize and bacon are now to be taxed, com- passion for the poor being thrown aside. Raw materials are to be taxed. Everything is to be taxed, more heavily than was at first thought necessary by anybody 'but Mr. CHAPLIN. And thus Tariff Reform will be made to yield a revenue of twenty millions. If the policy were put into practice we should have continual increases of this kind in the height of the tariff wall, as in the case of Germany and the United States. But the present increase in the Protectionist demand is interesting mainly because of the effect it must have on Mr. BALFOUR. What can he say about it in his " stirring " manifesto? If he yields to this latest demand of the Protectionists he is theirs wholly and for ever. If he does not, he cannot honestly rethain the Leader of a Party whose opinions he does not share and whose policy he would refuse to adopt if he were returned to power.

The Conservative A LAMB FOR THE ministry which is .in SLAUGHTER. the happy 'position of holdingoffice in thelocal Parliament has this week ,ventured on the introduction of a Tariff Reform Budget. Councillor Fulton Smith, the Chancellor, estimates generous revenue returns from various taxes•on imports and food stuffs, but the Budget possesses ' all the financial inconsistencies so often pointed out by Mr. Ure in dealing with Tariff Reform as a basis of revenue. You cannot keep imports out by taxation and increase home manufacture, when it is incontestably true that the same imports are paid for by our own exports of manufactured goods. This is a salient feature of fiscal policy which Tariff Reformers persistently ignore. They also fail to explain how the tax on food stuffs is going to ensure cheap food. Will the foreigner pay, or will the extra cost of the necessaries of life come out of the pockets of the con- sumer ?—who, in the main, is a poor and hungry person. The Liberals in the local House have retaliated on the Tariff Reform Budget by moving that it be rejected and an appeal' made to the country. It will be interesting to see with what readiness or reluctance the Tariff Reformers and Food, Taxers swallow their own medicine.
Never did Wartingtoil READY FOR THE Liberals enter upon Et FRAY. canll3algri With highef

hopes or greater enthusiasm than will spur them to victory in the momentous campaign for the big, bold Budget and the people's rights which has now opened in earnest. The joint meet- ing of Ward Committees held at the Liberal Club on Monday evening was an inspiration in itself. Most of the local party leaders were there, the rank and file had mustered in splendid force, and the entire proceedings were characterised by a spirit of determina- tion, begotten of confidence in thetirogressive cause, which presages another triumph for the democratic forces. The speeches were stirring and to the point. The President (Mr. C. E. Parker) gave a whole-hearted lead which was readily taken up by succeeding speakers, and the far-reaching character of the issues that await decision was fittingly emphasised. The liberties of the nation, the right of the peopre through their directed representatives to control finance, are at stake. As Mr. Upson wittily and truly put it, if the preten- sions of the Lords are to succeed we will in reality be governed by " King Lansdowne 1.," for the Second Chamber is stopping the sup- plies which the King calls upon the Commons to vote for the efficient government .of the country. If the :electors do not embrace the present opportunity of putting an end once and for all to this audacious usurpation,they will be delaying the car of progress for another generation. We are certain, how- ever, that they will rise to the occasion and show the Peers that their unjust domination can no longer be tolerated in this enlightened age. Let Warrington play a worthy part in the struggle for freedom by again returning Mr. A. H. Crosfield, who has worthily voiced their aspirations and consistently supported progressive ideals in the House of Commons.

Warrington is indeed MR. CHURCHILL'S one of the favoured VISIT. few among Lancashire to w ns, for it has received the promise of a visit from the Rt. Hon. Winston Churchill, M.P., and the meeting of next Saturday afternoon is cer4ain to be the record gathering of its kind ever held in the ancient borough. Mr. Churchill's Lancashire tour during the past week has been an unparalleled success. Audience after audience has welcomed the young statesman with wild delight, and his expositions of the Budget, his evisceration of Tariff Reform, and his uncompromis ing defiance of the Lords have won votes in battalions., Liberals, Labour men, and moderate men of no party, are present- ing such a united front in the present crisis, that it seems really a misfortune that men like Mr. Churchill, Mr. Lloyd-George and the Premier should be, in the main, speaking to the converted. We could almost wish that Liberals would stay away next Satur- day and give the Tariff Reformers a chance of getting converted by " Winston's " eloquence and logic. But this is not a conceivable possi- bility. .Mr. Howes, the Liberal agent, has already received enough applications for tickets to fill Parr Hall twice over,and we can only counsel those who must, of necessity, be disappointed to remember the greatness of the issue and content themselves with read- ing the speech which they would rather have heard. The strain of the arduous campaign which Mr. Churchill is now in the midSt of is such that he has been compelled to forego the pleasure of addressing an over- flow meeting in Warrington. This will lessen the number of people who will be privileged to hear him, but there is reason in all things and , more could not be expected of Mr. Churchill than he is giving so ungrudg- ingly day after day in the sacred cause of freedom and justice.
Now that Warrington WARRINGTON Bridge is coming within BRIDGE. measurable distance of

re-building, the path- way to the completion of the scheme seems to become more thorny and tortuous every week. The Council has got so far as to give notice of the promotion of a private Bill in Parliament to further the work, and has ratified an agreement with Mr. J. J. Webster as engineer at a remuneration of five per cent. on the, cost of the work. Seeing that Mr. Webster is to have travel- ling expenses in addition, he stands to make a clear £l,OOO on a £20,000 scheme, for the employment of a Clerk of Works will also be an extra for which the 'Corporation will pay. ;There is some objec- tion to sthese terms as being too lavish, but .the main objection is raised to the Parlia- mentary Bill being made an omnibus bill,and including many large and prospective public mprovemen,ts which are not, to-day, within the realm of practical administration. A Bill on such lines would seem like admir- able foresight, were we not reminded that the last Parliamentary Bill promoted by Warrington in 1899 cost £8,012 to get through, and the schemes included were put in hand within two years, thus bringing about a rapid increase in the rates. Coun- cillor Pemberton voices the views of the economists in the town when he points out that these additional schemes could, in due time, be dealt with through the Local Government Board—a method of pro- cedure which has the additional advantage of giving ratepayers full access to a public inquiry in each case. Once the Bill now proposed is passed and we may have another £B,OOO to pay. So far there has been no official estimate of the cost, and the assumption is allowable. Then, most certainly, the Council will be at liberty epter upon any or all of the numerous schemes without remonstrance from outside being of any avail. The Council is not infallibly wise, and we would rather see a
"GOLDEN FLEECE" MARGARINE, Bd. psi pound, or I pounds for ls.—Advt.

greater trust placed in the ratepayers where such vast projects for public expenditure are concerned. The proposed Bill has yet to be submitted to A ratepayers' meeting, and we hope the closest attention will there be paid to every proposal included. This is the only opportunity for the voicing of public opinion and obtaining of information, and it should not be used indifferently. A special Council meeting to consider the Bill in its entirety is advertised for the evening of Thursday, December '23rd. The Ratepayers' meeting will follow at a later date.

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

We wonder if any of our readers have been struck by the strange similarity between Tom Smith's crackers and the political arguments of Mr. Tom Smith (the prospective Conservative candidate for Clitheroe). They are both easy to, explode * *

Tuesday's Council -meeting consisted in the main of a wordy duel between Councillor Pemberton and Councillor Roberts, with the Mayor as a buffer for the two antagonists. The rest of the Councillor wi Akleymen were silent, shocked, witnesses of aft unpleasant scene. Hair-splitting on points of order has developed into a fine art, but of order itself there is not a vestige in one Council meeting out of six. We were glad to note that the general public attended in larger numbers than usual on Tuesday. They were certainly entertained if not elevated. Our hope is that their presence may ultimately conduce to more decorous behaviour in their elected representatives.

* * * Mr. Seddon, M.P„ had better be up and doing. Mr. F. E. Smith has given it forth that the young scion of a lordly house is going to knock him out of his seat. "Allow me," said the member for Walton, to a meagre and unenthusiastic gathering of Conservative bazaarites on Saturday, "to introduce you to my young friend Lord Wolmer, •who is gallantly fighting the Newton Division of Lancashire, where he means to 'relegate Mr. Seddon to that obscurity which he is so eminently fitted to adorn." It is common knowledge that Mr. F. E. Smith says unlikely things seriously, but his words may at least afford some amusement to the good people of Newton Division. It is just possible, too, that the boast may urge the electors to make his youthful lordship's defeat all the more pronounced.

* * * The wooden box on which Mr. Churchill when speaking, rests his notes, appeared both at Preston and Southport in the leather jacket in which it is carried about the country. This box is becoming as familiar an object in the great halls of England as the brass rail which Mr. Balfour, rather more exacting, requires the party managers to erect wherever he speaks, so that his hands may have something to grasp, or as the tall and slender reading-desk from which Sir William Harcourt used to speak. Mr. Churchill's box (says the "Manchester Guardian") generally arrives on the chair- man's table at that moment of acute tension which comes between the singing of the last chorus‘and the arrival of Mr. Churchill him- self, and it is Mr. Churchill's first act when he is in his seat to unlock it and place his notes ready on the flat surface of the box. The papers which he then has to consult are nicely placed for the speaker's eyes, and the box itself forms an elbow rest of which Mr. Churchill makes constant use.

* * Mr. Churchill is becoming wonderfully confident on the platform. When a speaker can take a drink of water and endure with- out flinching the silence and the scrutiny of several thousand eyes during the process he if getting on; on Friday night at Preston. Mr. Churchill not only did this, but after he had moistened his lips, fell for a second or or two into quite a reposeful attitude, elbow on the box, chin in the hollow of his hand, while he looked for the next point on the paper before him. As he surveyed his great audience at Preston on Friday night while Sir John Gorst was speaking, and before his own ordeal had begun, he said quite a lot to Mrs. Churchill, who sat by him about the "fine meeting," and in the middle of the speech two sentences were exchanged between them, probably about the pitch of Mr. Churchill's voice.

* * * In view of the crisis with which the country is now faced, it is interesting to recall a similar crisis in the Colon of New Zealand in the early nineties. It is some- times good for the Mother Country to learn from her daughters, and it may be instruc- tive, therefore, to know how the New Zealanders settled their crisis.

* * * The Liberals in New Zealand had a great xictory at the polls in December, 1890, and ejected a Tory Government which had practically dominated New Zealand politics for twenty years. The, Tory leader resigned on the day of the meeting of Parliament, but before he gave' up the seal of office he appointed seven members of the Legislative Council, of whom he himself, the defeated Premier, was one.

* * * The Prime Minister of the new Ministry was John Ballance—afterwards Sir John Ballance—the famous New Zealand Liberal Leader who preceded Sir John Seddon. He had a large majority in the popular Chamber, and was able easily to pass a ,series of Liberal measures. But whenever these measures were .sent, up to the Legislative Council, which corresponds to our House of Lords, the vital provisions of them were defeated by large majorities—as much as eighteen to five. The members being appointed for life up to 1891 could not be removed, Yet, as the majority included six of the seven members who had been nominated by the Tories after they had been defeated at the polls, these defeats amounted to a defiance of the popular will.

; * Shortly afterwards Lord Onslow retired from his post, but he left a confidential memorandum to his successor, Lord Glasgow, explaining the reasons for his action, and the result was that Lord Glasgow took up the same attitude. In other words, the Tory peers tried to force on New Zealand the same form of Government that they want to try and force on the British people at the present time.

* * * But the Governor at that time was Lord OnSlow, whom we in this country now know as among the most reactionary of the enemies of the Budget. Lord Onslow refused to take the democratic line. There had been six deaths and one or two vacancies in the Chamber, and he was willing to appoint eight substitutes: But he would not appoint any more. The dead- lock continued.
* * * It wa4 impossible that Ballance should go on with this,state of affairs if Liberalism was to survive at all. Ballance was not at all the sort of man to acquiesce. During the

reggs§, after A §dr4eo or &feats, he advised the Gdireffidr tO dipdhit tWel-V-e nie mbers to the Legislative Council ds the least number thought necessary to allow the Government to be fairly represented in the Second Chamber.

* * But 'happily, there was a more enlightened man at the head of affairs in England. The Conservative Government was still in power although it was in its last stages, and Lord Knutsford was Colonial Minister. But this is what Lord Knutsford wrote to the New Zealand Prime Minister:

The existence of an Upper House largely dis- proportionate to what appears to be the present political feeling of the Colony may be imperilled unless a more even balance of parties is secured. That was the view of the Conservative Colonial Minister at the time, and it shows how far backward the Conservative Party has travelled since.

*** A month later a Liberal Government came into power, and one of its first actions was to give Ballance the necessary leave for the creation of Councillors. Lord Glasgow was instructed by Lord Ripon, the new Colonial Minister, that he must accede to Ballance's request. * * *

• The despatch which Lord Ripon sent on September 25th is so good that it is worth quoting. It. lays down the lines on whick a representative of the Monarchy in the Colonies ought to act in such cases—and the lines on which, by the same argument, the Monarch himself may be expected to act if a similar situation occurs in this country. I had no hesitation in advising you by tele- graph on the 24th inst. to accept the recom- mendation of your Lordship's Ministers. I think it is right' to add that a question of this kind, though in itself • of purely local iinportance, presents also a Constitutional aspect which should be considered on broad principles of general application. When questions of a Con- stitutional character are involved it is especially, I conceive, the right of the Governor fully to discuss with Ministers the desirability of any particular course, that may be pressed upon him for his adoption. * *

The Constitutional duty of the Governor was finallyi to accept the advice of his Ministers on this as on otHer Constitutional questions': He should frankly state the objections, if any. which may occur to him, but if, after full dis- cussion, Ministers determine to press upon him the advice which they have already tendered the Governor should, as a general, rule, and when Imperial interests arp not affected, accept that advice, bearing in Mind that the responsibility rests with the Ministers, who are answerable to the Legislature, and, in the last resort, to the country. Lord Glasgow then, of course, wah-ed his objections, and made the appointments, and the Liberal reform policy, was launched. The New Zealand crisis was settled in precisely the sane way as the crisis of the British Reform Bill in 1832.

div.head: Confirmation at St. Ann's Church.
div.p: Confirmation at St. Ann's Church.

The Bishop of Liverpool (Dr. Chavasse) administered the rite of confirmation at St. Ann's Church on Tuesday evening in the presence of a large congregation. The candidates numbered 160— 71 females and 89 females— and came from the following parishes: St. Ann's, 29 (10 males and 19 females) ; Sr. Paul's, 54 (18 males and 36 females) ; St. Peter's, 27 (10 males and 17 females; and Hollinfare, 10 (4 males and 6 males). The follow- ing dlergy were present: The Rev. J. Davies, who conducted the service; Rev. W. Bracecamp, Rev. E. E. Peters, Rev. J. H. Banks, Rev. J. H. G. Hollingwortb, Rev. J. W. Glendenning, Rev. B. Percival, Rev. J. H. Garnett and the Rev. A. F. White. Before and after the laying on of hands the Bishop gave an impressive address. Mr. W. Miller presided at the organ. '

div.head: Bewsey-road Wesley Guild.
div.p: Bewsey-road Wesley Guild.

The members of the Bewsey-road Wesley Guild assembled in full force on Monday evening in the Lecture Hall adjoining the Church to hear the Rev. W. Bracecamp, vicar of St. Pauls who was down to address them. The Rev. E. R. Keeling presided and extending a welcome to him remarked that he at any rate was sufficiently broad minded to come amongst them.—The Rev. W. Bracecamp gave an address on Prayer. In his introductory remarks he considered it an honour to he asked to come. It was a great pity that those who met under different shibboleths should not come together more often. Instead of talking about their little differences they should help each other to form a great army against the enemy. If they were more broad minded and helped each other their work would progress a great deal more.—Miss Elsie Walters and Air. C. Sinclair gave a good rendering of "Love Divine."

FOUR MONTHS FOR THEFT.-Arthur Longshaw, of no settled abode, was charged with stealing from outside the shop of 30-32, Mersey-street, a rocking chair and rwo kitchen chairs,valued at about 9s. on 2nd December, 1908, the property of Ann Houghton.—lnspector Williamson stated that Mrs. Houghton carried on busi- ness as a pawnbroker. The chairs were seen safe out- side the shop on the 2nd December last year, by one of the assistants. Three-quarters of an hour later they were missed. From inquiries bp the police, it seenited that at six o'clock the same evening prisoner went to the shop of Mr. Hibbert, Hamilton- street. and offered for sale the rocking chair. Mr. Hibbert in consequence of prisoner's piteous story, bought the chair. Later it was discovered that the other two chairs were s3ld by prisoner to a Mrs. Morris in Egerton-street for 3s. Prisoner was arrested last Frick?, in town.—Prisoner said it was a case of mistaken identity.—The magistrates, nevertheless sent him to gaol for four months.

FOOTBALL IN THE STREETS.—John Dunbobbin, 22 Robson-street; John Brooks, 5, Stephen-street; William Wrench, 18, Portland-street, were charged with playing football in Fennell-street on the 29th November.—The Chairman, in fining defendants in the coats, said they had got to understand that the streets were not to play football in. He did not want to do away with football, as it was a very good thing, and he advocated an indulgence in it to the fullest extent. He would not record a conviction against defendants that time.

£90,000,000 worth of manfactures' excluded by the tariff would have to be made by British labour. Wages represent 50 to 75 per cent, of the value of manufac- tured goods. Manufacturers profits, however spent., can only be spent on objects produced by labour, there- fore the whole of £90,000,000 worth of goods secured to British labour by an import duty or tariff would be paid away in wages to British workers, except tbe value of foreign raw material contained in them. If 33 1-3 per cent. be allowed as the value of the foreign raw material contained in these manufactures, not only will the revenue be benefitted to the extent of £90,000,000 but £50,000,000 will go annually in wages to the British worker. Referring to clause 3, the Chancellor said it would not, affect the workingman, but the rich. With regard to the export of coal be said that we were giving away one of the most valuable assets that we had in this country. To give away something :that was of vital importance to us and to place it in the hands of those who might some day become our enemies was certainly cutting our throats and would be a danger to us in time and war. With regard to clause 6 he observed that when tbe tax was put on it would not have any effect upon the selling price of bread. (A Liberal member: "Question.") Well, when it was on before they did not Complain so much. (Opposition cries of "Oh" and Government applause.) Mr. E. ENGLAND (Warrington and ex-Cbaucellor of the Exchequer)moved : "That this House is not justified in passing the Budget until it has been submitted to the judgment of the country." He said tha.t the Budget stated certain sums which could not be realised. A Budget meant either the lighting of the burdens of the people or of placing more burdens upon them. Employment and trade and even their lives were affected by a Budget. The Conservative party alleged that they could raise revenue and at the same time improve the trade of the, country by creating tariffs which they said the foreigner would pay. (Laughter.) On the other hand they opposite said that to raise up tariffs will not only injure trade, but would seriously affect the social conditions of the people. (Hear, hear.) When Free Trade was introduced our navigation went up tremendously, and the social conditions of the people had since been wonderfully improved. The hon. mem- ber gave statistics representing the various death-rates in protectionist countries and in England. England's death rate was shown to be by far lowest and he attributed this in a great measure to our fiscal system. This country bad grown richer under Free Trade, but unfortunately a great portion of those riches had gone to the persons who never made them and had been obtained in a way which was burdensome to the nation. (Hear, hear)—and they as a party were determined to adjust that position. (Applause). Did the foreigner or consumer pay the tax? To show that consumer paid it he said that a few days ago wheat was quoted in Mark-lane London at 335. per quarter and in Berlin at 455. The latter had a tariff of us. 10d. or it. Not only did Germany put a tax upon foreign wheat but also upon home grown wheat. The recent House of Commons increased the duty on whisky and beer. He wanted to know who paid the tax? Did the seller or the consumer? Not only did the consumer pay the tax, but he was charged considerably more. (Hear, hear). There were croakings about the nation going to the dogs. One would think that this nation had very little foreign trade but what about our fcreigu trade? He said that the population of the United States was 83 millions, Germany 63 ,millions and England 41,000,000, He thought it should follow that the other nations should he doing a foreign trade considerably more than we. If tariffs assisted trade, how was it it had not assisted them? In 1907 the foreign trade of the United States was £395,00,000, Germany, £338,000.000 and England £426,000,000. (Applause.) Through Free Trade our shipping trade had gone up so much that we practically had half of the shipping trade of the world. Since 1851 our exports had gone up from £97,000,000 to £426,000,000 millions. Mr. Joseph Chamberlain in 1903 said that our foreign trade was going. Since then it bad increased by 1.00,000,000 millions. Mr. Chamberlain was, therefore, a false prophet. (Laughter and applause.) If goods were stopped from coming in,where were they going to get the money from? If the goods came in how were they going to benefit the trade? If we made the goods ourselves we at once destroyed the purchasing power of the foreigners; because trade was not carried on by gold but by exchange. (Applause.) Mr. DARRYSIIIRE L., (Davenport) formally seconded the amendment.

div.head: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
A TARIFF REFORM BUDGET.

The Tariff Reform Budget introduced by Councillor J. Fulton Smith (Chancellor of the Exchequer) at the Warrington Parliamentary Debattng Society on Tuesday 'evening in the Conservative Club, Assembly Room, provoked an interesting discussion. The ASSISTANT CLERK (Mr. N. Cooke) read the Budget as follows : • It is the duty of the Treasury to make provision for the discharging of the yearly increment of National ,expenditure (estimated at £16,000,000) and to meet this amount it is proposed as follows I. That an average duty of 10 per cent. be imposed ..on all goods of foreign (not Colonial) manufacture: further, that silks, motor-cars, jewelley, hats, pianos and similar articles of luxury bear a '2O per cent duty; altogether, to provide £9,000,000. 2. That foreign,not Colonial, poultry, game, salmon, lobsters, grapes, almonds, chocolates and mineral waters •carry an import duty of 20 per cent. to provide £1,000,003. .

J. That raw materials now classified as, ostrich feathers, furs, sealskins, precious stones, &c., when 3rted, carry a 20 per cent. tax to provide £1,000.000. 4. By* graduated tax on high-class tobaccos, cigars, rcigarettes and high class wines and spirits to provide £1,500.000.

5. By an export duty of 2s. per ton on all coal shipped from Great Britain to provide £5,000,000. 6. Re-impose the Registration duty on corn, to pro- vide £2,000,000. 7. Remission of 2d. per lb. duty on tea, which will cost £2,400,000.

£BO,OOO Surplus.

The CHANCELLOR in introducing the Budget said: 'The popnlation ef the United Kingdom is estimated at 44,000,000 and of that number it has been stated there are 13,000,000 on the brink of destitution. This being a ,commercial community it follows that the first con- sideration to be determined by those at the head of the nation's affairs is the removal of this inequality in the condition of the (*pie. Employment, remunerative and regular' is acknowledged to be essential to secure the desired amelioration of this large section of the population now dependent upon the help of the State or the benevolence of others. A crisis has been developing for a long time and is threatening to deprive us of our own home markets and •excluding us from the markets of the world. Surely the time has arrived when the economic government of thi& country should be placed in the bands of practical captains of industry conversant with the intricacies and exploitations of trade and commerce, under the guidance of a Minister of Commerce rather than given over to the emperical deliberations of political partisans. (Hear, hear.) The imposition of taxes .on foreign articles of Commerce brought into this country is no new feature in England's fiscal policy. This being so, the proposal to extend import duties to cover a wider range of articles (more especially manufactured as against raw materials) should be looked upon as a fair and reasonable method of preserving to our countrymen that share of employ- meat to which they are entitled and which was theirs in former years. Most of you are familiar with t figures which make up the sum total of goods imported. Dining the last three years an average of £180,000,000 value of goods manufactured abroad has been landed on ,our shores annually. The goods formed the staple industries of our leading towns and villages for many years. If we assume that an average duty of 10 per cent. would keep out one half of these foreign manu- factures it would produce a revenue of £9,000,000. The

ported the Budget before them that night. His only criticism was that it did not go far enough. He really liked his own better and he would put a 10 per cent tariff including food and raw material with the object. of encouraging those who worked under the British flag. But he would impose a 5 per cant, duty on colonial goods, because it would give us some bargain- ing power. Concluding he said that he did not think that the foreigner would pay, in every -case, but it was certain that he would in some. (Applause). Mr. J. JARMAN (L., Burton-on-Trent), said that if we were to raise revenue by the means Inid'clown we must of necessity allow the goods to come in and therefore it would not benefit employment. In that House members opposite had said that it was"goicg to do something for employment." In the country they were told that it was "going to cure unemployment."He wished that they would have the courage of their indoor convictions. outside, and then they would take the placards that were on that building down.(Opposition Applatise.)lf we were going to help unemployment we must keep the goods out, but we were going to lit them into get revenue.(Laughter) Referring to Alderman Bennett's speech he said that that gentleman was going to show his kindness to the Colonials by imposing a duty of five per cent., whereas their goods came in free now. (Applause and laughter.) If we were to give a preference to the Colonies we must tax food. (Alderman BENNETT : Hear, bear. Immediately we started preferential treatment we restricted our markets and we did the same as was done with the sugar bounty business—the prices were raised. (Opposition applause.) Referring to the coal tax and the statement that the price went up when it was taken off, be asked how many households used Welsh Steam coal? He maintained that the Registration duty on corn would affect the selling price as no miller would pay it and not increase his price. (Opposition applause). Mr. F. G. TAYLOR (Attorney-General) said that be did not knew whether the export of coal was confined to Welsh steam coal, but if it were he would like to remind tbe House that the tax was paid by the foreigner and also that the Liberal Government bad put a tax on coal.

Mr. JARMAN: It is a tax on royalties. Mr. TAYLOR: That is aidegree of difference which will requires very great deal of explanation. Continu- ing, he said that if a tax of 5 per cent. were put upon Colonial goods they would still have the advantage of 5 per cent. over others. Mr. J. HAWTHORN (L,Montrose Burghs) said that he thought they now knew what Tariff Reform meant. They heard a good deal of what it was to be, but he thought it was the first concrete example of what they might expect. He found that Tariff Reform was simply their old friend Protection in a new guise. They bad resorted to the old taxes on food, and the necessities of life wbizh our forefathers struggled against and terminated. The country had not gone backward under Free Trade, but forward. (Opposition applause.) The chief argument in favour of the preferential tariffs for the Colonies bad been that we ought to have preferential treatment with each other. In the Budget there was no provision made. The Colonies could doiwhat they liked and receive a preferential treatment from us but we did not from them. There was no guarantee made. It would benefit, the Colonies without giving us any compensating advantages in their markets.
On the moiion of Ali-. JOHNSTON (C, Scotland Division of Liverpool) the House adjourned.

div.head: MR. CHURCHILL'S CAMPAIGN.
div.p: MR. CHURCHILL'S CAMPAIGN.
Impressions of the Overflow Meeting at Southport. THE BOROUGH MEMBERS TELLING SPEECH.
;An " Examiner " representative who attended the overflow meeting in the Opera House, Southport, on the occasion of Mr. Winston Churchill's visit on Saturday after- noon writes :

It was a remarkable overflow meeting—a mighty and inspiring demonstration in itself. The great gilded theatre was literally packed from floor to ceiling, from the comfortable stalls and boxes to the giddy heights of the "gods." Surely this must have approached the record in the way of overflow 'meetings in the north, for it excelled in numbers and enthusiasm many gatherings with much more pretentious designations. The portals of the buildings were zealously. guarded by police and stewards, for the übiquitous suffragettes who appear to regard Mr. Churchill as legitimate prey, have applied themselves to the cheerful task of harrassing him as much as possible during his Lanca- shire pilgrimage. When these irrepressible advocates of "votes for women" declare war they are as good as their word, and it needs firmness as well as ingenuity to thwart their designs. However, it would have been as easy to pass through the eye of a needle as to enter the Opera House without the necessary pass- port and, save on the platform, the fair but militant sex was quite unrepresented. To keep its spirits well attuned to the memor- able occasion and to relieve the tedium of waiting for the meeting to begin, the huge assembly sang lustily a number of Liberal songs with good rousing refrains. "When the Baron comes marching north "—Baron de Forest is the Liberal candidate for the division—sung to the tune of " When Johnny conies marching home" went with a rare swing but most popular of all was "A song of the People" winding up with " Glory, glory Hallelujah " ! A harmonium and cornet supplied the necessary lead and when the audience had nearly sung itself breathless, a young gentleman who had been conducting with some vigour from the plat- form, laconically observed "' Very thin, gentleman," whereupon the stirring strains of the Liberal March were taken up with renewed energy, and the time passed enter- tainingly enough. A great cheer heralded the arrival of Sir George H. Pollard, M.P.—recipient of one of the recent birthday honours—and Lady Pollard. The picture of geniality Sir George, who is an ex-Mayor of Southport and the Member for Eccles, seems to regard public speaking as one of the pleasures of life. His resonant voice reached all parts of the build- ing with ease and his crisp, clear-cut phrases were instinct with conviction and determination. Sir George has a pretty wit and flavoured n admirable fighting. speech with delightful humorous touches which were keenly relished. One of his happiest hits was the allusion to "Pitt the great Commoner,and Balfour the little Commoner." The jovial knight put the political situation in a nutshell :

"'['he Peers are simply fighting to protect their own pockets. This will go down to posterity as the meanest electoral fight on record. A more despicable, a more miserable set of motives never animated a political party in the State than those which have moVed the Lords to this fight. We Can no longer rely on an unwritten Constitution. It will be the duty of the Liberal Government, when it returns to power, to define by statute the relationship between the two Houses of Parliament, so that never again will there be any question of the supremacy of the Commons in matters of leaislation as well as finance."

Then we had a long and really eloquent address from Mr. J. H. Astbury, K.C., the retiring representative of the division, and the tumultuous cheering which greeted him showed how unquestionably he retains the confidence of the electors of a, constituency which prides itself upon its traditions. Tall, alert, and confident, Mr. Astbury is quite at home on the platform and he has the ready flow of language that one expects from an advocate of his standing. He dealt compre- hensively and incisively with the questions which await the' decision of the voters and showed, by damning quotations from Mr. Balfour himself, how utterly indefensible is the action of the Lords. He waxed scornful at the pretence that the Second Chamber was animated with a desire to ascertairf the will of the people, "to save them from being oppressed by their own representatives in the House of Commons." " There never was," he declared, " piece of more absurd and hypocritical cant and sham." Coming to tariff reform, Mr. Astbury demonstrated by the force of logic and irrefutable statistics that Free Trade is the safeguard of Lanca- shire's industrial prosperity and that a Pro- tective policy would be fatal to its great

enterprises. Mr. Astbury warmed to his subject and, like some preachers, was disposed to indulge in a "thirdly," "lastly," and "finally." When in embarking upon the last of the numerous phases of the situation which he touched he exclaimed for the second time, "Just one word more" the audience laughed good-naturedly. "It shall be one this time" said Mr. Asbury, appreci- ating the joke, and he promptly wound up his fine speech with an effective peroration which roused enthusiasm to a high pitch._

While Mr. Astbury was holding= forth, Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., who had been listening to Mr. Churchill in the principal meeting, took his place on the platform and he was now called upon to speak. Our member was iil. very good form and the thoughtfulness, cogency and directness of his remarks obviously created a favourable impression. The audience signified unmistakable agree- ment when he forcefully stigmatised the methods with which the progressive forces will probably have to contend in the coming struggle as 'a campaign of audacity, rapacity and mendacity." A typical Scotch anecdote which the member introduced, served pleasantly to emphasise his contention that the specious promises by Protectionists of " Work for all" are to be regarded very dubiously.Mr.Crosfield told the story well, his simulation of the Northern vernacular being capital, and the audience laughed heartily. The most important part of the speech was that in which he showed how disastrously tariff reform would operate in Lancashire for, by increasing the expenses of production to the manufacturer and the cost of living to the operative, it would inevitably tend to industrial strife. In conclusion Mr. Crosfield took up the clarion call of the campaign with the unhesitating declaration that the Lords must no longer be allowed to block the path to reform. The speech, which was atten- tively followed, must certainly rank as one of Mr. Crosfield's best efforts.

Barqn de Forest, the candidate for Southport, who next addressed the meeting, was obviously labouring under the excite- ment of the occasion and it took one some time to get accustomed to his nervous mannerisms. A small body of Conservatives manifested their presence by raising a mild cheer when the Baron happened to mention Lord Curzon. The Speaker neatly turned the tables on the noble lord's admirers by pointing out that Lord Curzon had said that the Budget would mean cheap land—which is one of the crying necessities. for the proper development of a place like Southport. Mr. J. S. Highaqi, M.P., a bluff Yorkshire- man, was belabouring the Lords in thorough- going ' fashion when a tornado of cheers announced that Mr. Churchill had at last arrived. The multitude rose en .masse in welcome • and the acclaims continued for several minutes. Mr. Churchill is a striking and fnagnetic personality. He is, in fact, somewhat of a paradox in himself. Young, as leading politicians go—he was thirty-five last week—he has the grave visage and calm, collected demeanour of the experienced statesman. Not the flicker of a smile crossed his face as he stood before the wildly enthusiastic assembly—indeed he gave one the firm impression that this Lancashire campaign is an eminently serious business with him and that he regards the issues at stake as vital to a freedom-loving people. Mrs. Churchill, looking charming and radiant, accompanied her husband. After the exertions of a fine masterly oration at the chief meeting, Mr. Churchill was naturally inclined to reserve his resources for the concluding meeting at Waterloo in the evening, and his speech was therefore very brief. It was, however;choicely worded and one could hardly have wished for a better illustration of that marvellous power of compression of which the President of the Board of Trade is a past master. He put the issue succinctly and convincingly :

"You have to decide in the next few weeks whether your country shall be governed by a great representative assembly, elected by millions of people and in the choice of which almost everyone has a chance directly. or indirectly of being consulted, or whether the predominance of Parliament is to pass to a hereditary assembly of titled persons who use their power, not at all in the inteTests of the nation as a whole, nor even impartially between the two great parties; but who use their power to play a shrewd, vehement, aggressive party game in the interests of the Tory party. (Cheers.) That is the great issue you have to settle, and I. am sure we may rely on Lancashire men, who have always taken such an honourable part in achieving for the masses of the British people their political rights and enfranchisement, not to fail in this momentous hour. .(Cheers). We must remember that not only is a great constitutional question at stake. The Conservative party have openly avowed and their leader in the House of Lords has brazenly prcclaiined that it is the intention of the Conservative party, if returned to power, to impose a protective tariff; to raise money for public needs by taxes on your bread and meat and foreign imports. Such a policy as that would bring evil upon all parts of the country, but most certainly upon Lancashire, for Lancashire stands to gain absolutely nothing from protective tariffs/ or any variation of the proposals of Tariff Reform, whilst it must lose in all the markets abroad by which the marvellous proscerity of the Palatinate has been built up." (Cheers.)

With a gracefully-framed tribute to Baron de Forest, Mr. Churchill concluded an impressive little speech, which for the terseness and lucidity with which the case was stated, could hardly have been excelled. Some inconsiderate individual in the audience was disposed to cavil at the brevity of the utterance and, called out "What about the Budget ? " Mr. Churchill rose and simply remarked i` I bid you good-night, gentlemen." Then to the accompaniment of more ring- ing cheers, the young Minister, whose rise to the front rank of orators and men of influence in the counsels of the nation has been one of the most notable features of our later political history, made a triumphal exit. Warrington people are expecting a rousing lead from ." Winston " when he. visits the old town on Saturday next and, fudging from the brilliant series of speeches which has so far distinguished the Lancashire- campaign, their hopes will be fully realised.. • j

div.head: "TWAS IN TRAFALGAR SQUARE."
div.p: "TWAS IN TRAFALGAR SQUARE."

Between twenty and thirty thousand persons tcok part in the demonstration in Trafalgar Square on Saturday afternoon organised by the National DemocraUc League. A resolution condemning the action of the House of Lords in refusinl to pass the Finance Bill was carried with enthusiasm, and _subsequently the "Land Song" was sung by the huge assemblage. The speeches were of a somewhat fiery nature, but although the crowd was one of the largest that has ever b?en gathered together under the shadow of the Nelson Monument there was no disorderliness or disturbance. The speakers included Dr. Clifford, Mr. W. C. Steadman, M.P., Dr. Rutherford, M P., Mr. W. P. Byles, M.P., Captain Hemphill, and Bart Kennedy. Our illustration shows the sea of faces turned towards the main platform.

div.head: HOPE OF HOLLAND.
div.p: THE HOPE OF HOLLAND.

The world that awaited with so much interest the birth of Holland's Princess will be glad to learn that little Juliana is progressing wonderfully, well. The photograph we reproduce is the latest taken of Queen Wilhelmina and her daughter, and it will be seen that the hope of Holland is a particularly plump and healthy child, Mtg./ugh Princess Juliana the succession of the House of Orange to the Dutch throne is assured, for if no son is born to the Queen and her Consort, this little Princess will one day rule over Holland with forty million subjects at home and abroad. _

div.head: S WARRINGTON CHAPTERS.,2
div.p: S WARRINGTON CHAPTERS.,2
GLIMPSES OF BY-GONE STOCKTON
HEATH.
Stockton Lodge and Some of its
Inhabitants.

Standing by the roadside on the North side of" London Bridge" and familiar enough to both natives and travellers is the fine old house known as Stockton Lodge. The making of the canal and the modern growth of the village have deprived it of its dhcient surroundings and left it a somewhat solitary object, but to the imaginative eye that can place the homestead amid the quiet scenes of two centuries ago and people it with its former inhabitants the old place is alive with interest.
Of its builder we have not been able to obtain any knowledge, nor do we know of any tenant earlier than the one of whom we are about to write.

div.head: JOHN DE BEAUVOIR.
div.p: JOHN DE BEAUVOIR.
The persecution of the Hugenots in France drove many Protestant families to seek refuge abroad. Among thQse who fled from his native land was John de Beauvoir, a native of Marsailles, who was born

possess miniature copies, and the picture is one of striking beauty. Yet from her legion of lovers, Maria—the baptismal register records her as Mary —failed to secure the right one, and she died at Stockton Lodge in January, 1810,to be laid with her sisters in Grappenhall Church. Her nephew, Rev. Edward Hinchliffe, who had a close knowledge of the family, wrote, "She was never married, not because she had no offer of marriage, for many proposals were made to her, and twice by men of rank; but an attachment—" like a worm i'th bud " nestled in her heart, and, though fervently returned by the object of it, was never per- mitted to reach its long cherished hope."

div.head: MISSES GASICELL.
div.p: THE MISSES GASICELL.

It would almost seem that Stockton Heath has had an unusual share of the radiance of female beauty, for the poets—and perhaps they are the best judges—have sung the charms of other fair residents in lines as melodious and enthusiastic; and whilst we are touching the subject we may record that the same Sir William D. Evans also visited at Birchdale—now the home of Mr. Vere Davies—and thus sang of another fair one Rebecca Gaskell.
Shall .here my falt'ring MUSO to sins forbear
Another Gasicell like 'her sister fair?
The sweet Rebecca, beauteous as the day, For ever lovely and for ever gay : Whenier she speaks what sounds enchant the ear ! . . _
When'er she moves what matchless charm appear ! For her unnumbered youths shall heave their sighs. And doubt the charms which strike their wand'ring eyes. Miss Rebecca G-askell has two sisters who

div.head: STOCKTON LODGE
div.p: STOCKTON LODGE

about the year 1714. His first foreign home was the Channel Islands but h 3 afterwards (am 3 to England and beceme a naturalised Englishman. In doing so he anglicised his name and became Boyer. Entering tho Navy, John Dover attained the rank of Post Clptain and served England in several campaigns against his former countrymen. He was with Admiral Byng when. that ill-fated commander was sent to intercept the French Fleet and in the expe- dition which brought Byng to a traitor's death. Boyer was in service on the war- ship "Buckingham." This bit of history concerns us here because the expedition brought into friendship two remarkable men who because of their friendship came to live together in our neighbourhood, Admiral Hoare and Captain Boyer. It was on being appointed Naval Superintendent of the Cheshire district that Captain Boyer came to live at Stockton Lodge, but previous to his sea battles he had married a Cheshire lady of good family, Mary Malbon of Bradeley Hall: The worthy couple were married at Dares- bury Church in 1752, and now comfortably settled at Stockton Lodge they enjoyed the advent of their thirteen children.
shared the home at Birehdale with her,
Two sisters Gvskell, nymphs adorned with sense, With wit, with beauty, and with innocence, And for these also local poets vied to find the true superlative.

div.head: BOVER FAMILY.
div.p: THE BOVER FAMILY.

Most of the family lie buried in Grappenhall Church and the visitor may read their names upon a memorial tablet of white marble which bears the Boyer crest, a goat's head with fleur de lys. Captain John Boyer does not, however,rest in the family vault. A Government appoint- ment was given to him at Newcastle and after enjoying the great honour of the con- ferring of the freedom of the City he died there in 1782 and was buried in St. Nicholas Church.
Stockton Lodge continued to shelter the Boyers for Captain George Boyer, shis son continued to reside there with his si ters.
THREE FAMOUS BEAUTIES.

These last made the name of Boyer famous. By something they could scarcely help—such is the nature of this curious world—the sisters Dover brought more fame to the family name than all the hard fought battles ot their father and the no less faithful naval service of their brothers. It was the sisters whom the Duke of Gloucester came to visit and who drew to the shelter of Stockton Lodge a long list of visitors that would have done no dishonour to a royal home. Perhaps this is a case where we can appropriately call in the poets to explain the reason why. We quote from the outpouring of a local bard:
Blow soft, ye winds ; ye waters ceaw to move ; Lo ! , Boyer conies the sweetest child of Jove, _
Blest with a form'all harmony and grace,
While heaven's own goodness- brigh,tens in her face Adorn'd with ey'ry grtlce which virtue gives, Ador'd and innocent here beauty lives; ,If seas and beauty claim a mortal's care _ _ _ _
Let wondering millions guard this matchless fair. All heaven to form her perfect frame combined,
And made her loveliestof the lovely kind, Each power to deck her all their skill employed, . .
_ Stamped her divine, and then the die desiroied: Then strive no more to rack thy tortured brain To find her likeness, since the attempt were vain.
But stop, and let her right in triumph sit O'er bankrupt nature and exhausted wit; _ _ . _ _ _
For to be nic-ely and exactly known ... . _ . _ __ _ .
Sophy can only- by herself 'be shown.
Lo! why sweet Fanny pass unnoticed by! Who in good temper doth each mymph outvie.
So mild her looks, her heart more pure than snow, Words from her lips like fragrant honey flow • _ _ _
Is't form alone in this fair M.-aid we find?
No • she has all the beauties or the mind. WI; soar so high? Hence all attemyt forbear
To Paint the Veauties of these matchless fair. ,

Lest this tribute should appear extra- vagant we quote another from a rhymster who attained great fame in his profession of the law. "Sir William David Evans, as he afterwards was, served his articles of clerk- ship in Warrington afterwards becoming vice-chancellor of Lancashire and Recorder of Bombay. Sir William wrote: Another Boyer comes! her charms belie
The tale that nature broke her sisters die

"Could nature cast" admiring youths exclaim "In differing moulds two forms so much the same?" Aught can I add to this? In Ann we find Maria's beauty joined with Sophy's mind. Ann, Sophy and Maria, but the most winsome was Maria. Her charms were transferred to canvas by the Court painter Hoppner, of which the Academy and Museum

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH NOVEL.
div.p: A STOCKTON HEATH NOVEL.

Stockton Lodge has another memory which we must not omit to mention. Turn- ing back a period of fifty years we find it sheltering Mr. James Grant the novelist. That 'talented Scotchmen spent considerable time here as tbe guest of the then occupant and within its walls wrote his "Lucy Arden or Hollywood House," an h;storical novel dealing with the period of the rebellion of 1715. Those who care to turn the pages of this story will discover that its author had a close acquaintance with the neighbourhood in which he had made his temporary home. Walton Old Hall figures in the narrative and so does Stockton Heath, referred to even then as open and Uncultivated land. Captain Errington the hero also knows Bold Hall and the shades of Delamere Forest and give the information that on the day of the death of King James 11. the bell in Warrington Church steeple tolled of its own accord. One brief dialogue from the novel is worth quot- ing. Captain Errington is a Jacobite envoy and falling under suspicion of having come to enlist men for the exiled king,' he is cross-examined by his prosecutors and asked.
"Do you pray for the King?" "I do." "Which king ? " "I never knew there were two." "You quibble; you know well that he whom you style Elector of Hanover is our King."
To which Captain Errington says: "God knows best who is king, and I need not name him in my prayers to ono who knows the truth."

Which reminds us of the delightful squib of John Byrom, God bless the King, the faith's defender, God b!ess—no harm in blessing—the Pretender. But which is the Pretender, which the King-- God bless us all, that's quite another thing. . A.M.
