div.head: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
div.p: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
By Philip Snowden, M.P.
THE WORK OF THE PRESENT PARLIAMENT.

The Parliament which was elected four years ago has finished its work, and in a few days it will cease to exist. There were great hopes entertained among ardent reformers when the General Election of 1906 was over. For the first time in history there was an independent Labour group in the House of Commons, sufficiently strong in numbers to make its influence felt. The Liberals, too, were expecting great things from their own party, and believed in their reforming zeal apart from any spur which the Labour mem- bers might apply.

div.head: VARYING ESTIMATES
div.p: VARYING ESTIMATES

The estimate of the work of this Parlia- ment will vary according to the ideas which one held and the expectations one had formed. The young enthusiast who expected the Labour members to storm and take the citadel of capitalism after one or two attacks will be disappointed, if he has not become wiser in the meantime, without losing his enthusiasm. But the grey bearded politician, who had seen Parliaments come and go for fifty years, and who had been chastened by disappointments, and who in consequence, expected but a very slow move- ment in the wheels of progress, will have his youthful zeal and hopes rekindled, and his faith in the possibility of achieving great reforms restored to him. ' A RECORD PARLIAMENT.

There never has been a Parliament which has done and attempted so much. I should be neither human, nor partisan, nor fair and just to the Labour Party and the Labour movement outside Parliament, if I were not to claim some considerable credit for them for the legislative record of the last four years. If there had not been a sympathetic or an impressionable • Government in power the efforts of the Labour Party might have been exerted, but not to the same effect. I frankly admit that this House of Commons has been more truly representative of the reform spirit of the times than any Government of this generation. But I still claim that the Labour Party has done the main part of the work in the country in making that reform opinion, and if the impelling force of the Labour Party were removed the reactionary elements in the Liberal Party would again dominate the policy of the Government. A great Liberal journalist spoke the truth to me last week when he said "The only hope of success in this great crisis is that the Labour Party will maintain and increase its power and influence." - A LIST OF MEASURES.

I have been going through the list of measures passed by this Parliament in these four years. The record ,when seen at one glance is surprising to one who has seen that record made bit by bit. The Parliamentary machine moves so slowly that one who watches it often wonders that it ever turns out any finished article. There has been an enormous output of legislation from this Parliament,and it is of an exceptional quality. I cannot name even the measures which have been passed. It would take a - page of this paper to give their titles. I call only call attention to a few of the more important, especially those in which Labour is deeply interested. SOME LABOUR MEASURES.

I may have to repeat much which has been written and spoken for the Labour Party during these four years, but when the Party is restoring the talents to its lords it must point to the increase made. The Trades Unions have been re-established; their funds, which for years were insecure, have been legally protected ; the right to picket it has been conceded by law; in short, the whole trade union demand of the last election has been granted so far as the legal position of the trades unions is concerned.

div.head: VALUABLE MEASURE.
div.p: A VALUABLE MEASURE.

The Workmen's Compensation Act, and a far better Workmen's Compensation in every detail now applies to millions more work- peoplq than was the case four years ago. Even minor amendments in the law, which have been made, have doubled the amount of compensation paid. The workpeople who now have the misfortune to get injured are receiving every year millions of pounds more than was.payable under the old Act. If there is no gratitude in politics, an instinct to dis - cover where future favours may come from should gain for the Labour Party renewed support on this one item in their record alone, for the Act would not have been what it is had it not been for the practical experience which the trade union members were able to bring to bear on the consideration of the Bill. THE CHILDREN, TOO.

The children have not been neglected. Power has been given to local authorities to feed them when hungry, and a system of medical examination has been introduced into the schools which, when followed up as it will be, by and bye, by the public provision of medical treatment, will save tens of thousands of children from growing up physical inefficients. The children have been protected in a great many ways by an Act of Parliament which is all their own, and one which shows great advance in the recognition by the State of its duty to the uprising generation. THE OLD FOLKS.

I need say little about what has been done for the aged poor. Everybody knows of that. This Parliament would forever stand out as remarkable if it had passed no other measure than the Old Age Pensions Act. If it could have continued its course to its natural end the great blot on that Act would have been wiped out, and the aged poor 'now excluded through their deeper poverty would have been brought within the Act.

div.head: MINERS' ACT.
div.p: A MINERS' ACT.

It was in 1868 that the miners began their agitation for an Eight Hours' Day. Four- teen times in previous sessions had a Miners' Eight Hours Bill been brought before Parliament. But it has been the work of this Parliament to put that demand into an Act of the Legislature. The question of Sweating has been dealt with, and next year there will be Trades Boards established which will have the power to fix a minimum wage for the sweated industries, with the power to enforce the payment by law. There was before Parliament, when it was prorogued, a Bill for reducing the hours of Shop Assistants, and that Bill would have becoine law if the Lords had left the Commons to come to a peaceful end. OTHER MEASURES.

The Housing Question has been dealt with as well as the Peers would permit, and the building of back-to-back houses is pro- hibited, and futurb towns will have to be built after an ordered plan. A great step towards keeping the labourers on the soil has

been taken by the Small Holdings Act, which is bringing a new hope into the rural parts of England. South Africa has been unified, and India has had some measure of repre- sentative Government conferred upon her.

div.head: UNEMPLOYED.
div.p: THE UNEMPLOYED.

The Unemployed Question has been kept continuously before Parliament, and annual grants have been made under the Unem- ployed Workmen Act. A system of Labour Exchanges is being established and in the Budget were financial arrangements for financing next year a system of insurance against unemployment. The Development Bill has become law, and under this Act £2,500,000 can be spent on purposes of national development, such as afforestation, reclaiming waste land, and the like. In addition to this, it is proposed in the Act to spend the £600_,000 a year from the motor and petrol taxes on the improvement of roads. If the Budget is ultimately defeated this valuable Development Act will be a dead letter.

div.head: IN FULL CONFIDENCE,
div.p: IN FULL CONFIDENCE,

So I might go on piling up the record. I might make a list • of rejected measures which went through all their stages in the House of Commons, but were throWn back by the other place. I have said enough to prove my opening ~f.tatement that this Parliament's record of work is one which has never been equalled. But, after all, what has been done is only just the beginning in a small way. If the people like the samples they can have more. That is their business. So far as the Labour Party is concerned, it submits its four years of apprenticeship in the sure hope that it will qualify for and receive renewed confidence and support.

div.head: OUR CELLfI
div.p: OUR CELLfI

In our article of last week which dealt with Warrington printing mention was made of the first book which bears the name of a Warrington bookseller. The volume so described merits further reference because of its intrinsic interest. Its full title is "Spiritual wickedness in High Places or the corruption and oppression of the spiritual courts laid open in the case of Peter Slynehead," and it is described as being printed by R. Tookey and sold by H. Eires, bookseller, Warrington.

This Peter Slynehead was a member of an old Sankey family of yeoman rank and it was his misfortune to become the victim of a false charge which led him into litigation and controversy which embittered his last years and led to his death. The charge was of a breach of the seventh commandment and was made by a churchwarden of Prescot, of which parish Sankey formed a part. The charge was heard before a Judge at Chester who believed the charge and condemned him after the manner of the _times to punishment. He appealed to the prerogative court at York, but was referred back to the former Judge at Chester. He next appealed to the Queen's Judges at London and took 25 witnesses to prove his case. The court had three law Judges and three spiritual Judges and these found him innocent and allowed him .£lOO for costs. It is the story of this litigation that fills the pages of his " Spirituel Wickedness" and he tells us that the suit lasted five years, that he travelled more than three thousand miles at the loss of .£2OO.

But one booklet was not enough to contain his outpouring of woe. He published a second, "England's Misery for want of Godly discipline," and followed it with a third, "The Damnable Doctrine of Church Discip- line by the Bishops' laws and their deputies in Spirituals against the Health of our Souls." These are dated 1704, 1706 and 1709, and all bear the imprint of "H. Eires, Warrington." .

It would have been well if Peter Slynehead had borne his injustices in silence for in the attacks made in his books—and the reader may judge from the titles that they were spirited productions—he libelled some person (probably his accuser) and was prosecuted. The punishment was that he was placed in the pillory at Warrington, Wigan and Newton. He was subsequently imprisoned in the Fleet Prison, London, and died there. He left two daughters and his estate at Sankey was sold to meet the liabilities incurred by his 'law suits. With him the old family and estate came, to an end. The old house has since been demolished and with it a relic of the former unhappy Peter Slynehead carved on the granary: PETER SLYNEHEAD IS MY NAME, AND WITH MY HAND I MADE THE SAME. Nov. 6th, 1688.

div.head: OUR SERIAL STORY.
div.p: OUR SERIAL STORY.
[ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.]
HIS FATHER'S SON.
BY TOM GALLON
Author of " Tatterlcy," "Dicky Monteith,* "Kiddy." "A Rogue in Love," "Fate's Beg- gar Maid," -" The Charity Ghost," Ste.
CHAPTER X.

London in due course went mad over the arrest of John Baxendale; shouted itself hoarse in the Press over the double life led by this young country gentleman (this point i being rubbed n a little in certain newspapers read by the masses), and exhausted itself in comparing him with this, that, ard the other notorious scoundrel of the past. John Baxen- dale had been proved, beyond the shadow of a doubt, to be not only John Baxendale, but Rufus Cridge ; and while the pedigree of the Baxendales was given on the one hand, the prison records of the scarcely less notorious Rufus Cridge were set out in detail cn the other. Long before the trial the moral -les- son of it all was hinted lit, and John Baxen- dale was, in a sense, doomed from the be- ginning. The case womised to be one of rio ordinary interest. John Baxendale held a stake in the country, and had but recently succeeded to his property. MoreoVer, he was to marry a very .charming girl of good pesitien. On the other hand, he had had a low intrigue with the girl he had killed, the girl who had. in so dramatic a fashion, written his accusation at the very moment of her death. John Baxen- dale was to be -tried for he life, and there were but few prepared to say that he was innocent.

Of the few we may mention one or two at least. Evelyn Kaylor, who was not to be turned from her allegiance to him, even when everything pointed clearly to his guilt; and old Felix Goode, who knew the story, and yet saw the hopelessness of getting_ the man out of the tangle in which he had involve himself. For the horrible part of the busi- ness was that John Baxendale, in the hope to draw Rufus Cridge out of his hiding-place, had been outmatched by the cunning of the other man, and had stamped himself as the murderer, with, as it seemed, no possibility of the real truth ever becoming known. There had been a John Baxendale and a Rufus Cridge_, and in one mad moment John Baxen. dale had consolidated the identities of the two men. Johanna Cridge was prepared to declare that this man, John Baxendale, had again and again come to Middleton's Rents; had even suffered imprisonment for sordid crimes committed while a mere youth. Strangely, too, it happened that two of these periods of imprisonment fitted in with jour- neys abroad made- by John Baxendale. The evidence was overwhelming; and Felix Goode sat many and many a day and many and many a night at his desk, seeing himself, in imk.,,ination, openly derided in court when it should happen that -he stood up to tell the story of that mythical second son. There was no record of the boy, no possible scrap of paper that had not been destroyed by the dead man, the better to hide his own shame- ful part in the business. For the rest, Felix Geode was working hard, and was almost hopeful of the result. Above all, he had secretly set about to try td find the real Rufus Cridge. Loudon was being scoured and searched in...an endeavour to find the fugitive.

The ordinary sordid business of the coroner's court and the police proceedings need not be detailed here. Suffice it to say that in the one case a verdict of wilful mur- der was brought in against John Baxendale, alias Rufus Cridge, and in the other that the prisoner was fully committed to take his trial at the Assizes.

All efforts to discover Illfus Cridge had been in vain; the man seemed to have disap- peared utterly. Felix Goode was at his wits' end to know what to do. He was the more perplexed because the counsel he had in- structed shrugged his shoulders, and smiled at that-feeble defence set up, of the unknown brother, whom no one had ever seen apart from John Baxendalc. The barrister, indeed, pleaded that some other suggestion might be made—some taint of possible madness pleaded in regard to the Baxendales gene- rally, and to this one in particular. Naturally enough, he demanded evidence of what this most careful lawyer had to tell him; shrugged his shoulders again helplessly when told that there was no evidence to be had. However, he had been instructed, and he would carry on the defence on the lines suggested. .So we come to that day when John Baxen- dale stood up in a crowded court to stand trial of his life. Faces about him that he knew, friendly hands to touch his own now and then when opportunity offered. Above -all, one white, girlish face that ,never seemed to turn from his for a moment; for now it seemed that the life of Evelyn Kaylor was so bound up in that of the man, that if they sentenced him, so must they sentence her. A cry for silence, and the Judge is in his place and the trial has begun. In the first place, the setting out .of a very strange and yet a very ordinary story by the prosecuting counsel. He began by tracing the history of the Baxendales back through the years, shewing what they had been, and how in particular this one had fought and bled for his country, and this man had chosen the more peaceful paths of politics, dnd so on, and so forth. Finally, he came down to the present Baxendale, whom everyone would be disposed to regard as a very fortunate young man. He had been bred in luxury, and brought up as the heir to a great estate, and to all appearances had led a blameless life in the sight of the world and of his neighbours. . But, as men of the world, the jury would not need to be told that some men had in them a taint of wickedness that could over- ride training and environment, and every- thing else. Such a taint this man must have had—this fortunate young man, endowed with all that the world regards as riches, for he chose to step out of his life, and, under another name, to live in the most sordid sur- roundings, and to take his pleasures in the vileet company. The John Baxendale who travelled abroad as a gentleman of position and fortune, had seized the earliest oppor- tunity, on more than one occasion, to slip back to London, and so to appear among the scum of a great city as Rufus Cridge, burglar and common thief. In due course it would be proved, that this young man lived an apparently blameless life on his own estate, and among his own people, yet disappeared occasionally to take up that other life in London. To so great lengths had he carried that double existence that he had suffered imprisonment as Rufus Cridge, while he was supposed to be taking his ease in a foreign country. In two cases the dates of that imprisonment and that period of foreign travel absolutely coincided. They would be told an absurd story abopt there being not one man, but two—of a brother so like the man now before them as to have been mistaken again and again for the prisoner. Yet they had to remember that at the time of the prisoner's arrest, when roused from sleep • and taken by surprise, his own words were, "I am Rufus Cridge"; ii statement afterwards varied by him, when he claimed to be what he really ,was—John Baxendale.

No man could touch pitch without being defiled,, and. this man, descending into the depths; had touched a story as sordid as his surroundings. The unfortunate girl, for whciso death he was to be held responsible, had, in her fashion, loved this man she be- lieved to be Rufus Cridge. There would be those in court to-day who would tell how she had been heard to declare that the man had promised to marry her. But the gentlemen of the jury would understand at once that in that promise the man had exceeded what it was possible, for him to do, for John Baxen- dale, of Baxendale Hall, could scarcely mate 'himself with such a woman as this. Perhaps the vilest part of the story was contained in the fact that this John Baxendale was abso- lutely engaged to be married to a young girl in his own station of life, and who lived near to his own estate at Deepington. stiv.gve.lyn kept her eyes fixed upon beg

lover; sun sue seemea to smite, as though in encouragement. Counsel for the prosecution, proceeding with his speech, began now in- dustriously enough to tighten the rope about the neck of the prisoner, beyond possibility of its ever bein2 loosened again. It would be clearly understood that this un- fortunate girl, Bella Ogden, knowing the man as Rufus Cridge, and desirous of knowing Tot more about him, had at last fathomed tne secret of his double life, which accounted for her presence in the neighbourhood of Baxen- dale Hall at the time of her death. She. had been seen about there, and in that quiet place had been noticed as being a stranger. What more natural than that she should have there discovered t. t her apparently humble lover was not RufLis Cridge at all—thief and ex-gaol-bird—but John Baxendale, betrothed to another woman. The gentlemen of the jury had to remember that the body was found quite near to the house. Was it not possible that the wretched girl had pleaded with the man, perhaps even threatened him, and that in a frenzy, lest his secret should be discovered, the man had killed her? But the girl by this time had learnt who the man really was, and so, in the end, with her last dying strength, had written wonderfully enough upon the white wood of a blazed tree, the name of the man who had killed her. It would be proved that the un- fortunate girl had died some time after the stroke had been delivered. There had been time for, her to crawl to that tree, and to write her message to the world that was to condemn John Baxendale. Surely never in the history of the world had such a message been written, almost as it were by the dead; to accuse the guilty living! Had the unfortunate girl written the words, "Itufns Cridge lilted me," it might have been possible that the two men really did exist; but this dying declaration, made in the fuller knowledge that had come to the woman at the last, put the matter beyond dis- pute. "John Baxendale killed me, and it was as though, counsel urged, the dead wo- man stood before the jury-box and spoke the words to them.

_ There was a movement in court, and a whispering, while a photograph of the tree as passed round among the jurymen; a craning. of necks on the part of the general public m the hope of catching a glimpse of it. It would be shewn, counsel proceeded, that, after the murder and its subsequent dis- covery, a crowd of indignant people went straight to the Hall, in the hope to find the prisoner, that they did find him there, and that he actually appeared at a window, and shouted defiance to them. Whether in fear, or in some gudden madness, the man had actually set.fire to his own house, and so had caused to be consumed the pictures and heir- looms and valuables of centuries. And after that had contrived to escape, and to remain for a long time hidden. But the habits of years were not to be lightly flung aside. To what place did this man of the double life turn in his extremity as a hiding-place? Not back to Deepington, where he had friends, but to that other place where, most mistakenly, he felt he might hide as Rufus Cridge. Among thcoe, squalid friends he was found; and even then he thought to escape by declaring that he was Rufus Criclge. There was, however, some spark of honour and good feeling even among those with whom the prisoner had thought to hide. They had declared readily enough that, although known among them by the one name of Rufus Cridge, he was, in reality, John Baxendale. Evidence was called as to the first dis- covery of the murder. That frightened ser- vant, who had walked with his rustic sweet- heart through the woods, and had come upon the body of poor Bella Ogden, stepped into the witness-box, and created some whispering by touching his forehead respectfully to the prisoner. He told what he had seen with a clear and simple directness, that added, if anything, to the horor of it; and he was followed by the girl who had been with him, and who had run down to Deepington to tell the news.

After them came the stolid country con- stable, and a nervous little doctor who had known John Baxendale all •hie life, and we obviously dejected and apologetic. He had seen the body. There was no doubt whatever that the girl had not died at once on receiv- ing the blow with the knife, but had con- trived to drag herself to the tree, and, hor- ribly enough, to write that mcosage with her own blood. The doctOr was very sure about this. He only wavered a little when, in cross- examination, he admitted the possibility that another hand might have written that mcs- sagea suggestion ridiculed by the prosecu- tion in a sharp question or two in re-examina- tion.

Various witnesses followed, each of them having something to say as to the extra- ordinary changes they had noted in John Baxendale from time to time. The first of these was the landlord of the Baxendale Head, in Deepington, and he had a word to say concerning a night when Mr. John Baxendale had come into the place unex- pectedly, and had created something of a sensation.

"It wasn't as if it was young Mr. John at all," said the man, with a melancholy shake of the head. "It was Mr. John, of course; but he made free with everybody, even to the labourers off the roads, and ended up by get- ting drunk and smashing things. Fortunately for me, Mr. Goode came past, and succeeded in quieting the young gentleman." The worthy man gave a circumstantial ac- count also of another night when that\con- duet had been repeated; only on that occa- sion he had managed to get rid of his unwel- come visitor, and had seen him go staggering away towards the Hall. And no amount of cross-examination could shake his testimony that it had been Mr. John Baxendalc, and no other.

The appalling thing was that one witness after another who came up there and faced the prisoner, swore to the same thing. Old familiar servants, who had known John Baxendale in his boyhood and young man- hood stood up there, and, with drooping heads, whispered the same thing. This one had let him into the house in the condition described by the landlord of the inn; this other had seen him in the morning, when John Baxendale, "most surprisingly, sir," had sworn at him.

There came a, bearded warder from the prison in which Rufus Cridge had served his last term of imprisonment—in this particular case for a rather mean sort of fraud. He faced John Baxendale,, and waited, with his inscrutable official face turned to the pri- soner, for the questions he would be asked. "Now, warder, look well at the prisoner, and don't make any mistake. Who is he?"
"Rufus Cridv. I can't make 'any mistake about him,'; said the man. - -

- "He wa; under your care, I believe, in Stonyhurst Prison,, for some months in Alia year 190—, was he not?" "Yes, sir. A very quiet sort of prisoner, though a bit sulky at times." The warder, a little bored with the pry- ceedings, and a little surprised that anyone should dcubt his testimony, looked at the ceiling, and covered his mouth to hide a yawn. Counsel for the defence, a little jaded and worried, got up to cross examine.

"Just reme-mber; warder, that a man's life may hang on your words. There is no doubt in your mind Fle to the prisoner? " The man shook his head. "Not the faintest. It's my business to remember mem and remember faces; I can't forget that one.

He glanced at the prisoner for a moment, its though wondering at his audacity in sug- gesting, even through another man, that they had never met before. Counsel for the presecution now dealt his master-stroke. He was to. introduce iat this point three most unwilling witnesses—three people who had. been dragged out of the somewhat secluded lives they led to this place; three people who were, and had been, the accomplices of t;l'4; John Baxendale in his disguise as. Rufus Cridgc..., One of them would have a strange tale to tell, a- tale reaching back to the boyhood of the prisoner, and sup- plying the very last link necessary to connect him with this crime. "Call Johanna.

Johanna Undge, of the calm and stately manner, and clad completely in black, pre- sented a striking picture. She answered the questions in a low and refined voice, and with obvious reluctance, and her story was a re- markable one.
She had known the prisoner for many years; in fact, all his life. She had known his mother.
In what relationship did you stand to Mrs. Baxendale7 " she was asked. "A confidential friend, one might almost nay a sister. in tnat way I knew donn as a baby." _ _ _

believe that you, left Mrs. Baiendale, and that since then the world has not been kind to your.- • "That is so. I fell upon evil days, ati it was only by the merest chance that I found John, when he was living under another name." "Is ii true that you. befriended him?" "It is. Remembering his mother, and my great love for her, I ,endeavoured to wean him away from the men with whom he was associating. In that I Was unsuccesful; but I tried not to lose sight of him." At this point the prisoner would hays vigorously -protcsted, but was stopped by .his counsA, to whom 11,2 whispered agitatedly. "When you first heard of this murder what did you do?" _ _ .

" Nothing. I had formed my own opinion about it, because I knew the girl, and she had confided to me—,as one woman to another —her story. I knew that in all probability John Baxenclale would fly to me, and that is exactly what happened. I would have saved him if I could." witnees created a somewhat painful sensation by breaking down, artistically enough, at this point, and hiding her face in her hands. 'Evidently some deep sympathy had been stirred for her, and things were going hard with the prisoner. "You have not the slightest doubt the) John Baxendale and Rufus Cridge are one and the same person?" The witriess smiled through her ts-ars. "I have known him since he was a baby," 6he said, with a little catch in her voice. Counsel for the defence confined himself te a few questions dealing with the possible pri- vate life of this woman, and what it was that had brought her down in the world. Ski answered simply and, with dignity that a little annuity had been swept away, and that she had had to live under poverty-stricken conditions. She denied sadly but emphati- cally that she had had anything to do with the prisoner's companions. These companions enlivened the proceed- ings a little when, in their turn, they stepped one after the other into the witness-box. Mr. Ames Voles looked so highly respectable that the record of his crimes, with which he wat endeavoured to be tainted, seemed altogether out of keeping; nevertheless, in cross-ex- amination, they were proved up to the hilt. Not that that did very much good to the pri-: goner, because it Seemed also to be proved that the amiable-looking Mr. Voles had been a chosen companion of John Baxendale in that lower half of his life._

_ Mr. Voles lied freely and well, as one hav- ing long experience. He had always had a suspicion that Rufus Cridge was sometmi. better than Rufus Cridge. He was not in the least surprised to find that the young man had turned out to be, after all, "a gentleman born." Certainly Mr. Voles had been in trouble, owing to unfortunate circumstanced and much adiscriminate swearing away of character by unscrupulous persons. In this particular instance, however, be claimed, in- dignantly enough, to be 'telling the truth. For the rest he could only detail the several occa- sions on which he had worked hand in glove with Mr. Rufus Cridge, and most certainly the prisoner in the dock was Rufus Cridge. You might as well have expected Ames Voles to deny his own mother, had .that lady been still alive. Saul Tuttle, following him, was equally emphatic in another way. Saul whimpered a little when his past was laid bare before him, and muttered something about British justice and the working man. He, it appeared, had been merely unfortunate. But he left, if any- thing, a worse impression upon the minds of the jury and of those in court generally, by reason of his avowed connection with the prisoner, than Voles had done. Some rebutting evidence had to be called, something to. be-said by those who had known John Baxendale all his life, and to whom this thing was incredible. Men who had lived in the same county with him, and had ridden to hounds with him, and had dined with him men who knew him for a good fellow, anti were prepared to assert, though vaguely enough, that this thing was impossible. They, too, carried but little weight. But they said what had to be said, and stepped down again, with kindly nods of recognition to the prisoner. Lastly, Mr. Felix Goode. Curiously enough, when that name was called, the prisoner shewed some excitement, leant over from the dock to call to the old man, and to whisper to 'him urgently. "You must say nothing of the old scandal. In the first place, they wouldn't believe. They would demand that the man should be produced, and we can't produce him. More than that, no one has ever seen us together. We shall find some other way. Rufus may yet be laid by the heels. I charge you—not a word about my father."

The old man whispered vainly to the prisoner, and at last shrugged his shoulders and stepped into the witness-box. A 6 a mat- ter of fact, there was very little that he could say, now that the very groundwork of the de- fence had been stripped away from him. He- could only tell, in .his precise way, all that he knew of John Baxendale ; of his boyhood and his youth; of the impossibility that the man should be guilty of such a crime as this. John Baxendale had never had any secrets from him (whereat those in court glanced ab each other, and smiled a little incredulously,. and his life had been like an open book. There was an explanation, but not one that could be given in that place. Here the old man glanced at the prisoner pleadingly, and then lowered his eyes.

"It is underste-ojd, Mr. Goode, that the original suggestion as to another man who had masqueraded as John Baxendale came from you?" Thus the prosecuting counsel determined to dispose of this myth at once and for ever. . .

" Yes," replied the old man, with another glance at the prisonr. "And you believed that this other man ac- tually existed, and that he took the place of the prisoner, of the blamelessness of whose life you were convinced?" " I—l did believe it," said the old man, moving his hands nervously. "I do believe it." "So that you see, Mr. Goode, you also have been deceived. You understand that 'zhis fraud has been carried on so cleverly that even you have been hoodwinked?" "I don't admit that,". said the old • man.' "I can say nothing more. Everything will be explained—some -day." He got out of the box and went away, mut- tering to himself. I3ut he must have left some instructions secretly with the counsel for the prisoner, for the next name called Caused John ilaxendale to turn his head sharply, and to look anxiously towards the, witness-box. - "Mr. Richard Munby."

Dick stepped into the box and smiled at his friend, and it became obvious in a moment that he had something to 6ay that would put another aspect on the case. In all pro- bability Mr. Felix Goode, bound by his own oath, felt .that he might get another to tell the truth about the matter, and so save John Baxenclale. But that was not to be, after all. The first questions referred solely to the friendship of Dick with John Baxendale, of their lives together in his schooldays, and afterwards in various places, and then came an astounding _outburst from Dick before he could be checked.
"I tell you I know that there was another man, another man co like Baxendale as to be abcolut?ly mistaken for him. I can prove it. I know for certain-"
*" Stop! Stop! You nwst not speak!" broke in tlic‘ priGoner, in a stern voice. "For the love of Heaven, Dick, be silent)"
There was considerable uproar before the counsel for the prosecution could silencti both men, and could put those clear and biting questions that chould settle the matter once for all.
"Did you ever see th.is other man?" asked the prosecuting couno3l. "Yes," rePlied Dick Munby, unhesitair ingly, "I saw him at Itaxendale Hall, ill John Bazendale's clothes—,—"
" Wait a minute. Where wa6 John Baxen- dale at that lime?"
" I—l don't know," faltered Dick; "at least, I heard afterwards." -
"One point at a time, please. Have you ever in your life seen the prisoner and this other man side by side?"

"No," said DiCk, a little miserably. "Have you ever in your life had one man under your eyes, and kno‘ln with certainty, unpuestismablv, where the other man • .No,' replied Dick again, after a mo- ment's hesitatien. "But I tell you I know--"
"That will do, sir, and tlit completes my ease," said the other, triumphantly, as he sat down.

It was decided that John Baxendale should enter tile witness-box and give evidence on ,his own behalf. He stood the ordeal very well, but even there he was compelled to make damaging admissions. He had known the dead girl, but only very slightly, and in the most accidental fashion. Pressed to say bow he had known her, or why, he could not answer, or would not. On the night o; the murder he had certainly been in the grounds of Baxendale Hall, which adjoined the woods where the body was found, but he did not know the girl was there, and he had not seen her. He had confessed to being Rufus Cridge on the impulse of a moment; lif7 had not understood what the COII6CCILICIIC,.; would be.

There were the usual speeches for the pro secution and for the defence ; a cl!)self thought-out summing up by the judge. far as the latter was concerned, lie had word or two to say about that much-vexed question—a law for the rich and one. for the poor—and was emphatic that that idea should be dismissed from .the minds cf the jury. The whole case was built up on circum- stantial evidence alone, and on that meet par- ticular, and, as it 'seemed to him, conclusive piece of evidence, the writing on the tree. The duty of the jury was clear before them. and they must not hesitath in its performanu. They hesitated a matter of half-an-hour, while the court buzzed and hummed and speculated on the verdict. And when the mo- ment came for the giving. of that verdict, and the prisoner stood up to face the men who had his life in their bands, there was no breath of sound in all the crowded court. The usual questions, cutting the still air— and then the one word necessary. " Guilty !" Asked if he had anything to say, John Raxendale shook his head in a dazed fashion, and seemed not quite to comprehend what had happened. In a fascinated way he gazed at the Judge, and at the black-robed chap- lain behind him; heard the solemn words pronounced that were to take away his life. Then he turned and stretched out a hand as though he would have spoken, then let the hand fall to his side.

So he passed out of sight; so he looked, it') the last time as it seemed, into the eyes of a woman who stretched out her arms to him, and fell fainting into other friendly rale as he disappeared from view. Ore be continued.)

div.head: ALDERMAN BENNETT AND LE GALLIENNE.
div.p: ALDERMAN BENNETT AND LE GALLIENNE.
Some Personal Reminiscences.

Another of the series of lectures by members of the Warrington Society was given on Monday evening, when Alderman Bennett read a paper entitled" Reminis- cences of Richard le Gallienne.' Mr. E. J. Hall pre- sided:and thete was a good attendance. The speaker sketched le Gallienne's early life described the intimate acquaintance which existed beta een himself, Mr. E. J. Hall, Mr. Theodore Craig London, Mr. Richard le Gallienne and Mr. James A. Weleb, the celebrated actor, and referred to Mr. le Gallienne's early visits to Warrington and the meeting of the Booklovers' Club at Birkenhead, which he and Mr. Hall attended. Alderman Bennett quoted several paksages from the poems and other writings of Mr. Is Gallienne, which were addressed to Warringtonians, or related to the town, and gave extended extracts from "The Romance of Zion Chapel," which is based upon part of Mr. London's early life. Although, he said, Mr. is Gallienne had, to some extent, fallen short of his early promise, some of his best writings were worthy to rank with the choicest literature of our time, and ,slthough the reputation of .the gifted young poet had, of recent years, to some extent been upon the wane, as one of his old friends, he (Alderman Bennett) had not lost faith in him. He hoped Mr. le Gallienne might even yet do work which would give him a secure posi- tion among the foremost poets of our time. (Applause). The CHAIRMAN also contributed some personal reminiscences of Mr. le Gallienne._
_ Mr. MADELEY proposed a vote of thanks to Aldermen Bennett. _ _ .

Mr. T. E. GIBSON seconded, and said there must be something in common between the two men which could bring forth such a paper from Mr. Bennett, and in honouring Mr. le Gallienne, Alderman Bennett had honoured himself.
e. The vote of thanks was heartily accorded.

div.head: WATCHING A STOMACH DIGEST FOOD
div.p: WATCHING A STOMACH DIGEST FOOD
WAS THE MEANS WHEREBY SCIENCE MADE POSSIBLE THE CURE OF INDIGESTION.

The Abbe Spallanzani was the first scientist to study systematically the chemical powers of the gastric juice, but it was by the careful and con- vincing experiments of Beaumont that the founda- tion of our exact knowledge of its composition and action was laid.

Beaumont was an army surgeon located at an obscure military post in Michigan while it was yet a territory, and was called upon to treat a gun-shot wound in the stomach of a Canadian voyageur—Alexis St. Martin. When the wound healed a permanent opening was left by means of which food could be placed in the stomach and gastric juice taken from it. Beaumont made scientific experiments with his crude means and wrote a book, which to-day is recognised among the classics of physiology. Beaumont showed the way for other scientists, so that to-day medicine knows what the stomach does with food and what food does to the stomach.

Science also knows what the gastric juices are and how to make them best for the system. Alderman Smethurst said ho was sorry they could not comply with the association's request, but they had no power to do what was suggested. The minutes were approved. TRADES COUNCIL AND TnE EMPLOYNENT OF OU ES] DERS.

At a meeting of the Paving and Sewerage Committee a letter was road from the Warrington Trades and Labour Council with reference to the employment of local men for street paving. Councillor Pemberton Laid the Trades Council said they had received information that a I3irkenhead firm whose tender had been accepted for street paving were employ- ing Birkenhead men 03 the job. They asked that in face of the fact that so many local men were unemployed,this should not be allowed to occur again._ _

Councillor CHANTLER said he believed the Local Government Board were asked to expedite the grant- ing of the loan for the work on the ground that work would be found for Warrington unemployed. Councillor PEMBERTON said the committee had accepted the lowest tender in every case and by far the majority of the work had gone to Warrington firms. Councillor HAWTHORN said he believed the Council had no right to impose a condition that contractors should employ only local men.

The minutes were approved. PROPOSED ACQUISITION OF ORFORD HALL. The following resolution has been passed by the General Purposes Committee : that Alderman Bennett and Councillors Birtles, Fulton-Smith, Jenkins, and Wilkinson be appointed with the town Clerk to report upon the advisability of acquiring Orford Hall and some of the adjoining land. This was approved.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
ANOTHER "SCENE."

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Town Council was held on Tuesday evening in the Council Chamber, the Mayor (Alderman Forshaw) presiding. There were also present :—The Deputy-Mayor (Alderman Smethurst), Aldermen A. Bennet and James Evans ; Councillor A W. 11. Bellian, T. Birtles, T. Chantler, J. G. Craik, E. Cuunington, J. Dickenson, J. Halliwell, J. Hawthorn, C. Jackson Ifolmes, G. C. Hoc% ard, F. T. Lashford, J. 'l'. Locker, J. Pemberton, H. Roberts, J. Sankey, J. Skelland, T. S. Steel, J. Fulton Smith, 0. Toole, J. Wilkinson and W. J. Wilson; Messrs. L. Whittle (town cleric), A. T. Halloway (deputy town clerk), 'l'. Longdin (borough surveyor), F. V. L. Mathias (electrical engineer), J. M. Murray (director of education), and Dr. J. C. Ilibbert (medical officer).
CO-OPTATIVE MENIBERS OF"ndli EDUCATION
COMMITTEE.

Mr. F. R. Roberts was, on the motion of Councillor Furirobi-Smunt, seconded I.)y Councillor HOLMES, appointed a co-optative member of the Education Cora- mittee,•on the recommendation of the Association of the Unsectarian Elementary Schools in the borough, in place of the Rev. John Youge, resigned.

div.head: COMMON COURTS AND YARDS.
div.p: COMMON COURTS AND YARDS.

The Sanitary Works Committee have passed the following resolution :—" That the following members be appointed to represent this committee on the Joint Committee to take into consideration the report of the Medical Officer of Health on the condition of the common courts and yards of the borough: The Chair- man, the Deputy-Chairman,and C.nurcillor Dr. Joseph." The 'Paving and Sewerage Committee have also appointed a sub-committee to deal with the question. BOWLING' GREENS DURING THE •WINTER.

A letter from the Amalgamated Union of Cabinet Makers with reference to the provision of bowling greens during the winter was read at a meeting of the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee and ordered to "lie on the table." _ . _ _
_ The miuutes were passed on the motion of Alderman SMETHURST, seconded by Councillor BIRTLES. A CONTRACT QUESTION.

At a meeting of the Sanitary Works Committee, on the recommendation of he sub-committee, appointed to consider tenders for second-hand bags, it was resolved that the tender of Mr. H. T. Harding for the supply of large bags at 2d. each, and of small bags at each, be accepted. Councillor LASBFORD moved an amendment that this minute be referred back. He contended that there was another tender considerably lower. Councillor PEMBERTON seconded. Alderman JAMES EVANS said the Committee did what they thought was best at the price. Eventually the minute was withdrawn.

div.head: BREEZE.
div.p: A BREEZE.

When the minutes of the Cemetery Committee came up for confirmation, Councillor CHANTLER raised a strong protest against the appointment of Councillor Birtles as vice-cbairmarfof the Cemetery Committee. He said Councillor Birtles was elected by a snatch vote. (A Voice: "Who snatched it ?") The few who were present. Several members of the Committee had more service to their credit, and Councillor Birtles was elected through a misunderstanding. It was about the shabbiest piece of work he (Councillor Chantler) had seen since be joined the Council. It only showed what some men wohld do to get a handle to their name. Councillor ROGERS said he must object to the language of Councillor Chantler. He (the speaker) was a member of the committee and he proposed Councillor Chantler for the deputy-chairmanship. Afterwards Coun- cillor Chantler spoke to the chairman and asked if it would not be wise to elect Councillor Skelland. The latter, however, declined to stand as he would not be able to attend regularly and proposed Councillor Birtles. He (the speaker) was surprised at Councillor Chantler attempting to say anything shabby was done. It was all lair and above board. Councillor PEMBERTON said it was a well known custom in that Council that these appointments should go by seniority and some members were very jealous of that seniority. It would therefore be unfair to over- look that principle. If the rule were once broken, it would be broken all 1.3 und.

Councillor CHANTLER : I lost the appointment through trying to act honourably by our old friend Councillor Skelland. Because I refused to do a dis- honourable act I lost the vice-chairmanship. I would not have it under the conditions Councillor Birtles holds it, under any consideration. _

Councillor Butii.Es: I cannot allow the remarks of Councillor Chantler to pass unchallenged. I say he is telling a deliberate falsehood ; I say it advisedly. Councillor Skelland is the oldest member of the com- mittee and I proposed him myself.Do you think I would take any position, especially on a committee like that, by a snatch vote? When Councillor Skelland refused the position he said to me "You take it. You are better able to take it thairrayself." I appealto Coqn- cillor Skelland, if that, is not correct. Ho proposed me. i As for voting for myself,' never did so. It san absolute lie. 4 _

bouncillor CHANTLER : Who said you did? Councillor BIRTLES : Yon inferred it. If it comes to merit, I have attended to all my Committees and I have been there when that man has not. 1 hurl his statement back at him and say it is a lie. Councillor PEMBERTON : 1 don't think any member ought to address another member as "that man." Councillor CRAIK said Councillor Birtles' election was in perfect order. Councillor Ckantler was pro- posed, but he had no seconder. In the course of further discussion, it was stated that only four members were present at the committee meeting. The minutes were approved. div.head: DISTRICT NEWS.
div.p: DISTRICT NEWS.
Grappenhall.

WRIST DRIVE.—A uhist drive and social —the fourth of the present season—was given in Miss Spinks' schoolroom, Ferndale, Grappenhall, on Thursday even- ing. The party was well attended and passed off with great success. Mr. Sbakeshaft efficiently discharged the duties of M.C., and the ilriza-winners were : Ladies: First, Miss Goulden ; 2nd, Mrs. Mounfleld. Gentlemen : First, Mr. Mounfleld ; seccnd, Mr. Few.

div.head: Culcheth.
div.p: Culcheth.

INDEPENDENT METHODIST CfrAPEL.—Tb e usual monthly P.S.A. was held on Sunday last, the chair being taken by Mr. W. Kenyon. Solos were rendered by Misses Runcorn and E. Kenyon and Mr. E.Barton. Mr. R. Taylor delivered a short address to the children and Miss Bickerstaffe gave a very interesting reading. Mr. H. Griffiths officiated at the organ.

div.head: Hatton.
div.p: Hatton.

THE INSTITITTE.—A Committee meeting was held on Tuesday in the Parish Room in connection with the Institute, the Vicar (Rev. T. T. Lee-Jones) presiding. There were also present :—Mr. W. Blackshaw, Mr. J. Hayward, Mr. L. Leach, Mrs. W. W. Leach, and Mr. W. Dooley (secretary).—The minutes of the lost_ meeting were read, and a bellows of over asi as shown in the books.—lt was decided to have the billiard table re-covered.—At this point the Budget was introdnced, and the meeting ended in a lively and rather heated controversy on its different aspects. The general view of the Committee seemed to be that the Liberals would be returned to power. though with n4t so great a majority. Moore.

ADVENT SERVICES.—The first of these services, which are held on loridtly in each week during Advent, was held in the Milner Cuurch Institute on December 3rd. —The Vicar, the Rev. T. T. Lee-Jones preached, and, considering the inclement weather, the attendance was very good.

- - WOMEN'S SOW L.—On Tuesday evening a special social evening for ladies was held in the Church Insti- tute. There were about 70 present. The first part of the evening was spent in gatnes of various kinds, under the superintendence of Mrs. Burder. After this light refreshments were served, and this part of the pro- gramme had been very creditably arranged by a com- mittee of local ladies. After the refreshments, dancing was indulged in for a short time, and after a very pleasant evening thd party broke up about 10 o'clock. WESLEY GUILD.—At the meeting of the Wesley Guild on Wednesday evening a good audience assembled to hear a lecture on " Tennyson " by Mr. H. Cartwright. Miss B. Dutton presided and introducing the work of the evening congratulated the audience on having so able a speaker to deal with such an interesting subject. Mr. Cartwright in choice sentences gave a detailed epitome otf the events, aims and work of the poet's long life. ma showed an appreciation of Tennyson's spirit and writing which had rendered the preparation of the lectute a labour of love. Not the least interesting portion was the account of Tennyson's touching friendship with Hallam and his contact with many famous men of literature from this and other lands. The chairman and Messrs. Jackson and Jas. Banner expressed their gratitude to the le6turer for one of the most attractive " papers " of the season and their satisfaction tkat Mr. Cartwright and other local members of the Guild were in the most spirited way, rendering talented and painstaking aid to the work it was doing.

div.head: Croft.
div.p: Croft.

CONCERT.—A very snccessfril concert was held in the Council Schools last Saturday evening, given by the Twiss Green Pi@rrots. Mr. W. J. Bate presided. The school was crowded, and a splendid programme was gone through. Mr. R, Fletcher sang "The Old Kentucky Home" and "I must go home to-night," which were very much appreciated. "I couldn't keep from laughing" was very well sung by Mr. W. J. Bate; Mr. William Kenyon caused great merriment by his piece entitled "The Lecture" and "The Pierrot Band " ; "The Redwing" was tastefully rendered by Miss M. A. Howard; Miss B. Kenyon's rendering of "The Lagoon" was appreciated; Mr. John Sutton left an indelible impression by the songs "John Willie come on" and "I knew 1 got something to do " ; "Let's have a song about the boys" was given by Mr. E. Everton ; Miss Runcorn sang " Boys in scarlet and Gold " with very pleasing effect; " Somewhere" and "A Pal of Mine," by Mr. H. Overton were much enjoyed; Miss M. Barton sang in a very taking manner "Willie's got another girl now " ; an excellent render- in F of "The Gondolier" was given by Miss Elsie Willocks; Mr. E. Barton caused much laughter with his song "I want to see-my girl "; a trio by Messrs. W. J. Bate, Win. Kenyon and Miss B. Kenyon wrs well executed, The jokes by the Pierrots were new and original, and put the audience into convulsions of laughter. Mr. W. J. Bate was the accompanist.—Tho proceeds were in aid of the school building funds.

div.head: Stockton Heath."
div.p: Stockton Heath."

BEGGAR SENT TO GAOL.—At the Warrington Occasional Court on Monday, before Mr. James Hepherd, Thomas Walker who said he was a native of Yorkshire, was sent to gaol for seven days for begging alms in Mitchell-street, Stockton Heath, on Sunday morning.—P.C. Barber said prisoner had is. 40. in coppers and a quantity of bread and cheese in his possession. At two houses prisoner was given a breakfast.—Prisoner said he had been out of employ- ment fer nine months and was destitute. HILL CLIFFS AND STOCKTON HEATH UNITED BAND OF HOPE.—The Rev. J. S. Hughes presided at the I third entertainment of the session which was bald in the Wesleyan Schoolroom on Monday evening and was supported by Mr. 0. Whitfield (secretary). The Rev. J. S. Hughes, who is about to leave the district for Coventry, referred to his connection with the society, which he formed about 15 years ago and in which he had taken a deep interest up to the present time. He appealed to the members and workers to rally and make the society even more vigorous than it had ever been. A good programme was provided, and it was much enjoyed. Recitations were given by Gertie Cliff e, Elsie Roughsedge, Frances Phelps, Tom Lloyd, Reggie Grounds and Edward Phelps. Miss May Isher- wood contributed a solo in capital style and Miss Doris Welsby, who is only six years of age, delighted the audience with three songs. She showed a surprising amount of confidence. A duet by Elsie Whitfield and Dolly Cain was well received, and the action song, "The doll's complaint," by N. Barber, E. Pollitt, L. Gerrard, E. ;farms. SI. Pollltt, L. Isherwood and E. Lloyd, and M. Mounfield, M. Cain, D. Bairsto, T. McDermid and E. Pearse were much enjoyed. Mr. Bert Spruce created much amusement with.a couple of humorous songs. The event of the evening was tbe performance of a sketch by the local Baden-Powell Boy Scouts. It showed how the Scouts may be useful, and justified their existence as an aid in training boys to be goocicitizeus. Mr. G. A. Whi•field and Miss Welsby acted as accompanists. On the proposition of Mr. 0. Whitfield, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Hughes and all who had taken part.

div.head: Penketh.
div.p: Penketh.

WESLEYAN CH APEL.—The men's bible class held their open service on Sunday in the Chapel after a h)nnt had been sung and prayer offered. Mr. C. E. Parker president of the class read a part of a chapter from the Book of Ruth and in doing so he said it was appropriate to the address Mrs. Leathby was going to give as she would speak of the Land of Moab. Mrs. Leathby widow of the late Rev.W.Leatbby gave a graphic account of their work as missionaries ;n the Land of Moab which was most interesting and greatly appre- ciated and will no doubt, have the effect of making the Book of Ruth more fully understood by those who bad the pleasure of hearing Mrs. Leathby. LIBERAL CLIJB.—An interesting debate took place at the above club on Tuesday evening. Mr. J. Isherwood opened the debate which was on the present political crisis, in a most able manner. Mr. Isherwood explained many reasons why the workers should rally round the Liberal and Labour men and send back to power a Liberal Government so as to deal the too long delayed blow to the House of Lords. Mr. F. Dendy took up the opposition but did not get many to follow him. Mr. Deady having much the greater task took his part well. Mr. D. Ridyard, of Warrington, presided with great tact. At the close a hearty vote of thanks was passed to the speakers and chairman. MEETING OF THE SANKEY PARISH COUNC IL .—A meeting of the Great Sankey Parish Council was held at the Council Schools on Monday evening, • Mr. H. Fair clough presiding. There were also present : Messrs. W. Furness, W. H. Ireland, Ditchfleld, J. W. Walters, and J. Smith (clerk).—A letter was read from Mr. F. Salisbury, G.P.O. surveyor,stating that "circum- stances did not warrant the establishment of telephone or telegraph facilities at tho Great Sankey sub-oftice, as„the business which would be transacted would not be sufficient to cover the expense incurred."—The Clerk read a letter from 41r. W. S. Haddock, the engineer to the Gas Committee of the Warrington Cor- poration stating that the committee were prepared to reduce the charge for street lamps to 50s. per lamp on the assumption that the Parish Council will be putting down extra lamps. If they erected a sufficient extra number of lamps the committee would be prepared to reconsider the price.—On the motion of Mr. Furness, seconded by Mr. Walters, the Clerk was instructed to write a letter expressing his appreciation at the amicable way in which the gas officials had met the Council and for their substantial redaction in price.— It was decided that the lamp near the end of Huntley- street in Hood-lane be Amsted to the end of Huntley- street, and that another lamp be put in the centre of Huntley-street; also to erect one lamp between the canal bridge and the first gas lamp at present in exist- ence. The position was to be selected by Messrs. Furness and Ireland.

div.head: Padgate.
div.p: Padgate.

WESLEY GUILD.—The monthly devotional meeting of the Wesley Guild was held on Monday evening last presided over by the Rev. T. Gladding. A very inter- 'eating paper was given by Mr. J. H. Mason on the "Relationshiß, twist God and man." A solo entitled "Light after darkness" was very ably rendered by Miss L. Duckworth. In spite of the inclement weather there were a large number of members present and the meeting throughout was very enjoyable.

div.head: Stretton.
div.p: Stretton.

CONCERT.—A highly successful concert was held in the school on Thursday evening in aid of the Church funds. The Stockton Heath Choral Union, under the conductorship of Mr. H. Berrey, gave their services and the Vicar (the Rev. the Hon. C. F. Cross) announced that the society, which had just commenced its winter session, would welcome recruits. The choir snug with good effect "By Babylon's wave" (Gottnod), "Queen of the night " (Strtai/), "The parting kiss" (Pinsuri) and "He watching over Israel" (Mendelssohn). The lady members gave a bright ren- dering of "Come away elves" and a part song for male voices was acceptably interpreted ' by Messrs. Murby, Conway, Tonge, Ellison, Ratcliffe, Parker, Grounds, Grice and turton. The following songs were given :—Miss Elsie Hewitt," When the heart is young "; Miss Bancroft, "Allan water" and "The flight of ages" ; Miss Ethel Mounfield, "Tit for rat " ; Mr. W. H. Grounos, "Asleep in the deep"; Mr. Jas. Turton " Glorious Devon " ; Mr. W. M urby "Oh, that we two were maying." Duets were creditably rendered by Messrs. J. Conway and G. Ratcliffe, Miss Monntleld and Mr. W. H. Grounds. An amusing trio "Three maids of Leigh" by the Misses Dutton, Leigh and Mrs'. Tongs was well received. Mr. H. E. Tone played a violin solo with taste and skill. Miss Atkinson ably accompanied the soloists on the pianoforte and also gave a selection

div.head: Lytytm
div.p: Lytytm

LYMM FREE CHURCHES.—The united week-night service V 4 as held on Wednesday in the Wesleyan Church. Mr. William Mort conducted the service, his address dealing with Paul's trial, and heieg amen appreciated those present. Mr. H. S. Brown presided at the organ.

LYMM POLLING DISTRICt.—A public meeting open to the Liberals of the Lymm Polling District was held on Tuesday evening in Hirst's Pavilion. Air. R. H. Gotobedpresided. A strong representative committee was elected to the Central Council. .

CONGREGATIONAL GUILD.—The weekly meeting of this society was held on "1 hursday evening and was devoted to"lmpromptu Speaking" and a variety of subjects were discussed. SUGGESTED LADS' CLUB.—A movement has been set on foot to provide a Lade' Cluo for Lytton. A com- mittee has been formed with the Rev. G. B. Thurston, M.A., as president, Mr. Becket, treasurer, and Mr. J. G. L. Farrar as hon secretary. On Monday last an open meeting was held when a priinastic display by members of the Anooatis Lads' Club and the Salford Lads' Club was given, Arrangements have been made for the use of the Drill Hall, three nights a week.
0 ITG R INOTON MUT UAL TM P RON' EM ENT SOCIETY.-

Mr. F. .1. Wright gave a lecture to the members of this society on Monday evening on "Ancient Rome" illustrated with some very fine lantern slides. Con- sidering the inclemency of the weather there was a very fair attendance and Mr. Wright's lecture was heartily appreciated. It has been desired to abandon the next meeting which should have taken the form of a mock trial. The next meeting will be held on January 7th, 1910.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the'above Board was held on Tuesday at Dutton Workhouse. Mr. T. Baxter pre- sided, and there were also present : —Messrs. J. Spruce, T. Wright, S. Woodward, C. E. Linsker (senr.), C. E. Linaker (junr.), H. Mynekyme, G. Egerton-Warburton, G. Pilling, J. H. Davies, P. Booth, A. R. Norman. J. H, Chadwick, A. H. Talbot, H. Mawdsley, J. Hallows, T. Watson, Fryer, A. Broome, J. Stokes, with Messrs. T. Cooke, W. R. de Prez, J. Pearson (relieving officer), G. F. Ashton (clerk), W. E. Hough (deputy clerk), E. Partous (master).

div.head: CHRISTMAS RELIEF.
div.p: CHRISTMAS RELIEF.

Mr. Liriaker moved that each adult over GO years of age and every child in their district on receipt of out- door relief be granted Is. and Gd. reseectively during Christmas week. The increase of expenditure will be about £2O.
This was agreed to. A COMPLICATED SUBJECT.

The =flop of Mr. .1. Spruce to advertise for an all- roupd man to do plumbing, fitting, and steam boiler work, and "make himself generally useful," which wits before the Board for discussion at a previous meeting was again brought forward by Mr. Spruce, who trutved that a married man be advertised for to reside outside the House, and have a general knowledge of plumbing, fitting, and steam boiler work; candidates to be not less than 25 years of age; to state salary. Mr. Spruce said that they would raise the man's salary by the saving caused by him doing the work instead of outside workmen.

Mr. Linaker asked if there would be sufficient employ- ment to keep the man going? Mr. Spruce replied that from previous bills for work done by outside workmen, there should be enough wotk Mr. Woodward said the matter required considerable. consideration. Before advertising for a man they should fix a maximum age of condidates. Mr. Watson asked what wages it was intended to give the man? Mr. Spruce replied that the amount bad not been fixed.

Mr. Norman moved that the matter be deferred until definite figures could be arrived at, with regard to the average quarters of expenditure, for work done about the house, in order to compare it, and see if by employ- ing a man there would be a saving. Mr. Linaker seconded, and this motion was agreed too.

div.head: OFFICERS' PARTY.
div.p: OFFICERS' PARTY.
Mr. Spruce Sa id that the annual officers' party would be held at the House on December 27th. Each officer oeuld invite one friend.
RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The fortnightly meeting of the above Council was held on Tuesday at Dutton Workhouse. Mr. T. *right presided and there were also present :—Messrs; T. Baxter,. J. Spruce, S. Woodward. J. H. Chadwick, C. E. Linker. C. E. Linaker, jun., H. Mynekyne, G. Egeltort Warburton, G. Pilling, J. H. Davies, P. Booth, A. R. Norman, J. B. Chadwich. A. El, Talbot, H. Mawdsley, J. Hallows, T. Watson, J. Fryer, A. Broome, J. Stokes, with Messrs. W. Diggle and J. Swinton (surveyors), Dr. Adams (medical officer of health), J. Farrington (Enspector of Nuisances), G. F. Ashton (clerk), W. E. Hough (deputy clerk).

div.head: _FOOTPATH CONTROVERSY.
div.p: A _FOOTPATH CONTROVERSY.

A matter which was discussed at a prev:ious meeting was again broached by the clerk. The subject was whether there was a public) right of way through the Bird Wood and across the railway at Aston. The London and North-Western Railway had written tç the clerk instructing him to make enquiries and report. The Clerk ?laid it was going to be a very -serious ques- tion. He proposed that a committee be formed to probe into the subject. In response to a query by Mr. Hallows the clerk said it was a matter of public safety. Mr. Woodward n,oved that a committee be formed to discuss the matter. He proposed the following as a committee :--Messrs. Warburton, Chadwick, Pilling, Stokes, Broome, Harrison and himself. Mr. Hallows seconded and the proposal was agreed to. INFECTIOUS DISEASES. • _ CLOSING OF SCHOOLS.

Dr. Adams reported that theWw-ere ten cases of scarlet fever at Frodsbam, one at Five Crosses and two at Overton. The infant schools at Manley lvicl been closed for three weeks from Monday last, chiefly owing to whoop- ing cough; also the infant school at Frodsham for a similar period, owing to (scarlet fever. The attend- ances had lowerel at both schools by over 50 per cent.

div.head: NORLEY WATER.
div.p: NORLEY WATER.

Mr, R. H, Cbrimes, wrote agreeing to take a supply of water to Moss Farm, Norley. At the same time he strongly objected to it on the groundi that there was slready a never-failing supply of good water. ,

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
STRONG BIINERAI, WATER.

At St. Helens, on Monday, John Henry Richardson, of Parr Mill Farm, was charged with being drank on licensed premises. Sergeant Gleave said that Richard- son was a labourer at the farm < On Saturday night witness visited the Princess Royal, Park-road, and on entering the bar saw accused staggering about. He at once came to the conclusion that the man was drunk.— Accused said he was only drinking a bottle of mineral water when the °Meer came in and said he was drunk. He denied that he was drunk. The Bench imposed a fine of 10s. and costs or fourteen days. MANY MEN AT ST. HELENS CHURCH.

The twenty-first anniversary of the formation of the St. Helens Parish Church Men's Bible Class was cele- brated on Sunday afternoon, when 1,003 men assembled to hear an address by the Rev. Canon J. W. Willink, a former vicar. The class was founded during the vicariate of Archdeacon Eyre and as a result, of mission services by the Rev. Canon lay Aitken. Each of these gentlemen sent messages.

WARRINGTON DRAMATIC SOCIETY.

div.head: "A Pair of Spectacles" and "The
div.p: "A Pair of Spectacles" and "The
Idler."

The Warrington Dramatic Society has never been lacking in eitherambition or enterprise throughout its long and creditable career, and this year a new line has been struck in the difision of the seastAt's work between the production in one week of "A Pair of Spectacles" and "The Idler." There is a •marked dissimilarity between the two pieces, thus ensuring a sustained interest which cannot always be counted upon when the same play is performed for six nights in succession. We think the Society adopted a wise course, for several reasons, in thus dividing the work. An important consideration is that the study and pro- duction of two works gives opportunities on the stage to a larger number of members, thereby developing the Society along the proper lines. From all appearances this season's experiment has proved a success, and there is no doubt that the general public has enjoyed the humorous and dramatic fare provided for its entertainment.

The first three nights Of this week have been devoted to the production of Mr. Sydney Grundy's well-known comedy "A Pair of Spectacles." It is a question whether any comedy, either old or new, is superior to this in the spontaneity, refinement, and genuineness of its fun. There is a fund of enjoyment in -!,` A Pair of Spectacles" which nothing but the rankest of rank bad acting could cause to pall on the public taste, and fortunately we are in no danger of such a martyrdom at the hands of the Warrington Dramatic Society. The Society has certainly been stronger from a histrionic point of view, but it cannot be denied that it has to-day in its ranks some of the most accomplished amateur performers who have ever donned the paint in Warrington. We unhesitatingly give the highest award possible •to the work of the tw.o men who practically carry the comedy of " A Pair of• Spectacles " on their shoulders, i.e., Messrs. Sidney Wellhead and H. G. Mosley as the Brothers Goldfinch. Round these two widely differing characters the rest of the company revolve like planets round the sun. As Benjamin Goldfinch, Mr. Wellhead gives perhaps the finest character study of his career, and this is no slight testimonial. He seems to really become a man of sixty, oozing with benevolence and a sublime faith in humankind, and not merely to act the part. Sir John Hare is the greatest Benjamin Goldfinch the stage has known among many, and even he would, we firmly believe, take pleasure in witnessing the humour and insight with which Mr. Wellhead endows the role. It is perhaps hardly necessary to add that Mr. Wellhead looks what he is represented to be to the life, and this alone is no small accom- plishment either of make-up or self-repression. What we have said of the one might be said with equal truth of the other brother, were the characters not so essentially different. While Benjamin is gentle, courteous, and generous, G,regory is narrow, dog- matic and self-righteous in the extreme. He comes "fm' Sheffield" and is typical of that city of hard steel and sharp cutlery. Mr. Mosley hnows Uncle Gregory like a near relative and personates hin7( per- fectly. He has never, been better suited with part and he has never scored a greater among many triumphs. Voice, action, and demeanour all go to make up perfectly the hard-headed North-country ironmaster who has so dominated everything and , everybody during a life-time of money-making that even his spectacles seem to be imbued with his unyielding and su4picious personality. Certainly they distort the vision of poor Benjamin to a most laughable extent when borrowed by the dear old -gentleman for the time being. Miss Dorothy Browne plays the chief lady's part in the comedy, a great advance on anything she has previously undertaken under the aegis of the Society. Miss Browne has the enviable and pardonable fault of being young, and she is not free from those little failings which are inseparable from inexperience, but she has an inherent grace and charm of manner which should serve her well in the future. If we may allude to one fault which has been previously noted it is Miss Browne's uneven articulation. Pauses in speech are either for effect or expression of emotion.. A predominance of them tends to render the spoken words colourless. We can however honestly congratulate Miss Browne on a considerable improvement, and give her credit for making an attractive Mrs. Goldfinch. Mr. 17 W. Richmond was quite at home in the lighthearted role of 'Percy," and acted with a piaiseworthy naturalness. Miss Bessie Pierpoint had little opportunity of displaying her talent for light humour as Lucy Lorimer, the inconspicuous daughter of Goldfinch's friend, but she made the best of the part. A character which did not seem very well fitted to its interpreter was that of "Dick," the scapegrace son of Uncle Gregory. Mr. W. H. Brown needs opportunities for the display of robuster acting, and did not seem cenfident in the unenviable situations of the penurious barrister. Mr- Walter Young did well as Bartholomew, the shoe maker who paid rent in leather, and Mr. John Craik always raised a laugh in the lifelike representation of the funereal, faithful family butler. Mr. R. P. Johnson appeared creditably as Lorimer, and Miss Rose Wellhead made a smart parlourmaid. The comedy was preceded each night by e mirthful comedietta entitled "Mrs. Hilary Regrets," in which Mr. Geoffrey Dodd and Miss Mary Brundrett acted with spirit. The former was capital as a blunt Irish physician, and Miss Brundrett showed skill in her representation of the spoiled Society widow with an eye oh the main chance. "The Idler" undoubtedly ranks among the greates successes which the Society has achieved. This is the second time it has been performed, and well as it was done some! few years ago we think that in the last three nights of this week the members of the Society have 'excelled, even themselves. It is a fortunate circumstance that practically the original cast kas been secured, and while this company is available we feel we must retract the assertion than the Society is not so strong as it- once was. Certainly, nothing more artistic and finished that the production of Mr. Haddon Chambers' great play could be wished for from amateur sources. There is not a part—and there are many good ones—of which it could be fairly said that adequate interpretation was lacking. Mrs. Redmayne Jones (more familiarly known as Miss Margaret Pierpoint) demonstrates herself a 'consummate actress of the restrained emotional type every time she appears as Lady Harding, and the role is one which she should be pfoud to fill. It affords ample scope for her undoubted talent. Mr. Mosley, too, seems never more at home than when playing Simeon Strong though the difficulty- would be to find him an incongruous role. The keynote of his acting is always apparent—that perfect ease and self-possession which betoken the, born actor. Surely, the stage missed a devotee who might have been distinguished when Mr. Mosley betook himself to commerce. Nothing but a complimentary reference is once again due to Mr. Wellhead, who skilfully pourtrays Sir John Harding, though we do not consider him best suited in the part, which requires a more essentially masculine and vigorous personality than his. Miss BessiePier- point is perfect as the precocious but dainty and amus- ing daughter of General Aferryweather. She has a gift for light, subtle comedy, and the scene between her

and Simeon in theblast act is a triumph of flirtatious fun. Mr. Geoffrey Dodd is very convincing as the much-married general, and shines in the matrimonial duel with Mrs. Glynne Stanmore (Mrs. F. E. Griffiths), who contributes much to the humour and enjoyment of the second act. Mrs. Griffiths has a penchant for the refined burlesque, and -never fails to make the most of the subtlest point in a difficult role. Little need be said of Mr. C. H. Wood as Mark Cross. He plays" the lead" and plays it well. The " Idler " has long been one of his greatest successes, and calls forth alibis capacity for dramatic power and effective characterisation. A word of praise is due to Miss Constance Broadbent, who appears very success- fully as Mark's mother, and demonstrates a fine per- ception of the pathos of her concluding scene with Mark. Mr. Walter Young is quite confident as Bennett, Mark's servant. As a •play "The Idler" is remarkable, not only for the grip which it has on the attention, but for the wonderful mingling! of light and shade in action and dialogue. The Warrington Dramatic Society makes of it an all-engrossing performance. Acknowledgments are due to Mr. Norman Latham and his orchestra for some delightful musical selec- tions, among which was to be noted a tuneful inter- lude entitled" Spanish Memories," specially composed for the occasion by Miss Lucy Wenham,a local lady whe has also distinguished herself in comedy. The Dramatic Society renders noble service in the cause of charity, and is to be commended as much for this as for the excellence of its stage productions. Generous public support is its due.

div.head: Confirmation at St. Ann's Church.
div.p: Confirmation at St. Ann's Church.

The Bishop of Liverpool (Dr. Chavasse) administered the rite of confirmation at St. Ann's Church on Tuesday evening in the presence of a large congregation. The candidates numbered 160— 71 females and 89 females— and came from the following parishes: St. Ann's, 29, (10 males and 19 females) ; St. Paul's, 54 (18 males and 36 females) ; St. Peter's, 27 (10 males and 17 females; and Hollinfare, 10 (4 males and 6 males). The follow- ing dlergy were present: The Rev. J. Davies, who conducted the service; Rev. W. Bracecamp, Rev. E. E. Peters, Rev. J. H. Banks, Rev. J. H. G. Hollingworth, Rev. J. W. Glendenning, Rev. B. Percival, Rev. J. H.. Garnett and the Rev. A. F. White. Before and after the laying on of hands the Bishop gave an impressive address. Mr. W. Miller presided at the organ.

div.head: Bewsey-road Wesley Guild.
div.p: Bewsey-road Wesley Guild.

The members of the Bewsey-road Wesley Guild assembled in full force on Monday evening im the Lecture Hall adjoining the Church to hear the Rev.. W. Bracecamp, vicar of St. Penis who was down to address them. The Rev. E. B. Keeling presided and extending a welcome to him remarked that he at any rate was sufficiently broad minded to come amongst them.—The Rev. W. Bracecamp gave an address on Prayer. In his introductory remarks be considered it an honour to be asked to come. It was a great pity that those who met under different shibboleths should not come together more often. Instead of talking about their little differences they should help each other to form a great army against the, enemy. If they were more broad minded and helped each other their work would progress a great deal more.--Miss Eli Walters and yr. C. Sinclair gave a good rendering o "Love Divine."

On Tuesday —evening the Rev, C. Harvey-Cook addressed the members of . this class on the subject "Does the stand primarily for a spiritual or material millennium." A discussion followed, in Which Messrs. W. Lowe, Watson, Highley, Randles, Jackson, and Williams took part. Mr. W. Lowe presided. Latchford Baptist Church. _ _ _

A very sucoel;sful Sale of Work and Christmas Tree was held on December 2nd in aid of the above Church and Sunday School. The sale was opened at 2.30 p.m, by Mrs. Robert Henshall, and Councillor C. Jackson Holmes, J.P., officiated as chairman. Although the weather was unfavourable the amount realised was nearly £5O.
