Mr, W. H. J. Jenkins very —kindly mail- a paper entitled." A concise sketch of woman's position in Jaw " at a meeting of the Warrington Women's Suffrage Society at the Winmarleigh Cafe on Tues- day evening. There was a large attendance, Mrs. J. A. Ransome presiding. The paper was much appreciated by the audience and gave rise to some lively discussion. 'Penny Popular Concert. _ .

'On -8 a turday evening an admirable programme was submitted by Mr. Bert Hollingsworth's party of five artistes, the Bold-street schoolroom being crowded with a most appreciative audience. The first item was the action song, "The boys in scarlet and gold," following which came such humorous pieces as 'The village pump," "If I had a nice little girl like you," and 'Grow, little mushroom, grow." Individually, as well as collectively, the artistes proved themselves most accomplished, and such songs as "Put me on an island where the girls are few," "Sea, sea, sea," "The masher," "The man with the single hair," and "Hr. w the bargee saved tbe barge" created great merriment. During the interval the Chairman (the Rev. T. Mill:r) delivered an address. Wycliffe Young People's Society. - --

At the weekly meeting of this society held on Monday evening in the Memorial Buildings, Mr. Arthur *Wallington presided. Mr. James Gauld read an interesting paper entitled," The oldest book in the world." At the outset the essayist pointed out that the book was not the Bible but was called "The Instruction of Itah-Hotep," which was written by an Egyptian in the year 550 B.C. The exposition of the book proved very interesting and instructive in view of its historic value, and also for the man?, themes which it contained. An interesting discussion followed, Miss Swindells and Messrs. C. Eccles, A. Millar, and A. Wallington taking part. A vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Gauld for his paper. Death of an Ex-Town Councillor. Many Warrington people will regret to hear of the death of Ur. William Pollitt, who passed away at his residence at Buxton, at the age of 77 years. Mr. Pollitt for many years carried on business as a grocer at 1, Sankey-street, a shop which has been demolished for street widening purposes. In 1871 he was elected a member of the Town Council for the South-West Ward, and he continued his membership for nine years, when be retired. He was a Churchman and a Conservative. The funeral took place on Monday at St. Thomas' Churchyard, Stockton Heath, the Rev. James Collins officiating. The, chief mourners were Messrs. James A. Pollitt and W. F. Pollitt (sons) ; Messrs. F. Gibson (Manchester), T. Truslove (Warring- ton), F. Booth (Warrington), and W. Blair (Redhill, Surrey), (sons-in-law) ; and J. H. Smith (Sheffield), (brother-in-law). Amongst those who sent wreaths were the church choir of St. Mary's (Buxton), Alder- man Gibson (Manchester), and the relatives. PEAT FOR 1101./SE FIRES, 3s. 9d. per 1,000 blocks, delivered free..—J. S. GARLAND, Kitchen Range and Stove Warehouse, 51, 53, & 55, Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt. Rylands' Workmen's Recreation Club.

-On Wednesday evening the committee of the above club provided the members, their wives and friends, with an excellent concert, which for variety and talent was excellent. Miss E. Taylor with "Serenade" and "Come sweet morning," Miss Plinston with " Within your heart and" The Valley by the sea," and Miss Hewitt" Dear heart "and "May.Morning " brought down the house. Mr.J.Draper who sang"Thora" and Flower of all the world" was in fine form, and so also was Mr. George Gough in "Lighterman Tom" and " The young Royalist." The humorous side was provided by Master W. Farririgton and Mr. Harry Sutton of Bolton. The latter in "Funny side of things," " Funniosities," etc., kept the audience in roars of laughter. On this occasion the committee secured the services if two turns from the Theatre Royal by kind permission of the Manager, Mr. Waters, namely, the Sisters Terry, character duettists and mimics, and Mr. Mannix in his coon song and dance. These artistes met with a- splendid reception, which proved to be well deserved.
AIILLEn. & Co. (opposite Trinity Church), for Whist Drive Prizes. Large Stock.—Advt. Warrington Women's Circle.

The meeting on Sunday was a "Snowdrop" lesson for the girls. The subject " Sweethearts" was taken by Mrs. Letheren. Visa Isherwood gave two solos. —On Tuesday afternoon (8.W.T.A.) a delightful talk was given by Mrs. Gladding on "The grace of cheer- fulness" ; not the aggressive quality possessed by some people 'which has the same effect on others as a " cheerful " wall paper. An imaginary school of cheerfulness with Charles Lamb as Principal, R. L. Stevenson with his gospel of good humour in another chair of office, resulted in the question : is cheerfulness an art to be learnt,or are some born with a bias towards cheerfulness, a homely herb which will grow in any garden. Yet cheerfulness is not an English virtue nor a modern one. The tendency is to be intense. The Master saw the sorrows of the world as no one else ever saw them and His heart was broken over its f•in, but he was wont to still the storm and pardon sin 3 with a word of cheer. The speaker referred to the different outlook of Byron at 33,and Whittier at double his age, who was as blithe as a bird. Cheerfulness is not the prerogative of youth. She askod the members to give to the world the service of joy, social, miselfish and diffusive.

div.head: Warrington Cycling Club.
div.p: Warrington Cycling Club.

At the-first annual dinner in connection with the Warrington and district Motor Cycling Club, held at the Lion Hotel, on Saturday evening the President (Mr. W. V. Baxter) distributed the prizes as follows: Competition.-1 (Triumph Co.'s gold medal), Dr. J. A. Howard; 2 (presented by Mr. H. N. Gandy), Mr. Cartwright, " Triumph" ; 3 (presented by the Warrington Club), 4.r. Wilding, "Triumph." Club Prize.—Fastest time on bill, Mr. Jordan, 9 h.p. "Bat." Inter-club Prizes.—Warrington v. Stockport M.C.C., won for Warrington by the following team :---Dr. Howard, 31 h.p. " Triumph "; Mr. Joalan, 9 h.p. "Bat " ; Mr. Cartwright, 31 h.p. " Triumph " ; Mr. Lowe, 3} h.p. " Triumph " ; Mr. Oliver, 6 h.p. "Matchless." During the evening the following toasts were honoured : "The King," proposed by the President; "Motoring as a sport," Mr. McClure ; "The Club," Mr. J. L. Oliver, responded to by Mr. K. T. Hardman (secre- tary) ; "The Visitors," Mr. C. H. Wood, responded to by Mr. Sixsmith (Wigan). Dr. Howard gave an interesting lecture on magnetos, illustrated by sketches. A good musical programme was gone through, Mr. H. S. Saville, junr.. of Lymm, proving himself a capable accompanist. He also contributed a pianoforte solo. Songs.svere given by Mr. McClure, and Mr. T..Critchley, and Mr. Kendrick contributed a recitation. .

div.head: Warrington Victims in the Ellan Vannin.
div.p: Warrington Victims in the Ellan Vannin.

The whole nation was shocked on Saturday morn- ing last when news came of the disaster that bad befallen the Ellan Vannin, the mail steamer due to arrive in Liverpool on Friday evening from Ramsey. But it came as a most painful surprise to Warrington and district when it was learned that Mrs. Allen (aged 46 years) and her son Ernest, (aged 16 years) of Liverpool, and late of Stockton Heath were on the illfated vtssel. The boy's body was recovered on Thurs- day. He was found by divers lying in his bunk with his clothes off and looking at perfect peace, The conjecture is that he was asleep when the catastrophe occurred. The deceased lady's body has not yet keen recovered, but the divers report that there are b'odies in the cabins and it is expected that she will soon be identified, Mrs. Mary Allen was daughter of the late Mr. Gandy, of Cairo-street and brother of Mr. John Gandy who carries on business as a shoemaker and clorger in Horsernarket-street. Prior to Mr. and Mrs. Allen and family taking up their residence in Liverpool they resided in Earlestown hiving left Stockton Heath six years ago. While in Warrington Mr. and Mrs. Allen were very much interested in the Emmanuel Reformed Church in Bold-street.

MILLER Sc Co., 10, Sankey at., Jewellers. Xmas Presents. great variety, from ls.—Advt. Parish Church Choristers' Association. The Warrington Parish Church (Past and Present) Choristers' Association held a musical festival at the Parish Church on Thursday evening when the greater part of Mendelssolin's oratorio " St. Paul" was per- formed by a choir of upwards of eighty voices. A large cingregation listened attentively to a devotional rendering of this majestic work which,while not being so intensely dramatic as" Elijah," presents vivid pictures of the martyrdom of St. Stephen, the conversion of St. Paul and striking events in the mis4ionary efforts of the great apostle. Considering the numerical limitations of the forces engaged and in particular the fact that there was no orchestra, the performance was most satisfactory and evidenced a high degree of careful and intelligent practice upon which all con- cerned are to be congratulated. The chorus was well- balanced and sang with precision and good taste, the interpretations of the thrilling "Stone him to death," the beautiful and ear-haunting "How lovely are the messengers" and the massive "0 great is the depth "—the latter sung as the finale—being particularly praiseworthy and effective. The soloists were :—Master Greenough (treble), Miss E. 'Taylor (soprano), Miss J. Armstrong (contralto) Mr. J. H. Draper (tenor), and Mr. J. B. Poole (bass). All entered sympathetically into the spirit of their respec- tive parts and sang with marked expression. Mr. F. M. Darby, Mus. Bac., played the exacting organ accompaniments with his customary skill and the success achieved was in a large pleasure due to his admirable and painstaking work at the rehearsals as well as at the finished performance. The .collection was on behalf of the choristers' association which is doing a commendable work in the interests of the choir boys of the Parish Church.
Miss Brooke-Hunt's Fallacies About
Food Taxes.

feel it my duty to pen a few lines in answer to Miss Brooke-Hunt, as I consider her remarks about cheapness to be a slight upon the housewives of War- rington. We must be 'devoid of judgment from her point of view. Now she stated that under Tariff Reform the Foreigner would pay the Tax. How so? I cannot understand, as she distinctly tells u# when we purchase a pound of tea we pay sd. tax, and so on in everything that is, txed. She would take this tax off our tea and put it on Bread, thus causing me an extra expense, say moderately one halfpenny per two pound loaf. I should use 48 loaves of bread for one pound of tea, I save 6epence on tea and lose two shillings on the bread, and the same in all other things, making my sovereign's purchasing power not more than seven- teen shillings. I consider her judgment of the abilities of us Lancashire housewives to be greatly at fault, and I trust that the housewives will use their persuasion and effort to cause their husbands to vote for the Liberal p trty which has always ,been the party to pass laws for the benefit and welfare of the working classes.—Yours,
A HOUSEWIFE.

div.head: Eyres' Press.
div.p: Eyres' Press.

Sir,—l was interested in reading the account of " Eyres' Press " over the initials " A.M." in your issue of Saturday last. Most of it I had read before in a pamphlet written by Mr. H. Stuart Page. To refresh my memory, I referred to it again and on comparing the two I was somewhat surprised to find such a striking likeness, so much so that if there been some acknowledgement from "A.M." of his indebtedness to Mr. Page I should not have marvelled much. The phraseology is only slightly varied, whilst the framing of the article is the same from beginning to end. There is no reference., however, in Mr. Page's pamphlet Ito the " Murdei of Maria of the Red Barn" which" A.M." introduces into the list of Chap Books of the 18th century. Seeing that Maria Marten was not murdered till 1827 there could scarcely have been a Chap Book dealing with the crime in the 18th century, and one cannot help thinking that if your writer" A.M." bad continued to cling to Mr. Page's pamphlet for support and had not let it go, even for a moment, he would not have fallen. - I should just like to add that the two blocks used for Mr. Page's pamphlet and now re-introduced to our notice in " A.M. s ' article appear to be none the worse for wear. Thanking you, &c.—Yours truly, EDMUND OSBORNE. Padgate, December 10th, 1909.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

The "Bill of fare" this week is the best seen for a long time, the programme being a regular " pot-pourri " of patter and cross talking, juggling, singing and instrumental music. The Elliot Savonas take the palm with a marvellous musical scena entitled "The Palace of Orpheus." The setting of the piece is magnificent, illustrating a palace stateroom, lit up by myriads of electric globes of all the colours of the rain- bow, while on either side of the structure are two magnificent organs with their numberless brass pipes which emit the most charming music. Amid this splendid scene the artistes, eight in number, i the ladies n riding habits and the gents in cavalier costume play, different sets of music on innumerable kinds of instruments, and finish up by the playing of a grand March, which earns merited applause from all parts of the building. They introduce a novelty in the music Hoe by playing a tune on small motor horns. Lovers of club swinging should pay a visit this week and see the Juggling Geraldos in their original speciality act, which includes club swinging of the most intricate and artistic kind. There are many sparks of humour introduced In this act by one who is the most funnily constructed youth yet seen on the variety stage. He appears to be all legs and no body. Ada Gatley gives a good show with a mixed turn of slack rope walking, juggling and contortion. The Melba twins sings some enjoyable duets, and further items of a meritorious order are given by Albert Barraclough, descriptive vocalist, Blair and Allen, comedians and dancers._ • -
, Next week's programme lea varied and excellent one and includes Fred Kam's company of comedians in "The Casuals."

div.head: RELIGIOUS INSTRU CTION.
div.p: RELIGIOUS INSTRU CTION.
Local Churchmen Dissatisfied. STRONG DENOMINATIONAL CLAIMS.

A conference of the clergy and lay representatives of the Rural Deanery of Winwick was held at tbe Church House on Thursday afternoon, the Rural Dean (Rev. Canon Penrbyn) presiding over a large attendance. At last year's conference an instruction was given to the Committee of Church School Managers to take action in the matter of religious instruction in the Secondary School and if possible, in the Arpley Street school.

The Rev. G. Vale Owen asked what was the outcome of the instruction? The Rev. James Davies said the matter was con- sidered by the Executive Committee. With reference to the Arpley-street schools they would be treading On dangerous ground if they called upon the local educa- tion authority to interfere with the managers. They would not like the committee to interfere with their own schools. As to the Secondary School, it was for the Parents to make application for the religious teach- ing which they desired their children to receive, and the matter did not rest with any association. The association tried to get permission some time ago but failed.
Thd Rev. J. H. G. Hollingworth : Does the law allow the Education Committee to grant the right of giving definite religious instruction during school hours in a Secondary school?

The Re-v. James Davies: The law is that they may do so if they wish, if the parents ask for it. The Rev. G. Vale Owen moved: "That the mem- bers of this Conference view with much regret the fact that there are more than 1,000 scholars attending day schools in Warrington who receive no adequate instruc- tion in the Christian religion. They sincerely hope that the Education Committee may see their way at an early date to procure in the Secondary School to which their authority extends that every child shall receive such instruction in religion as the parents desire in school hours by teachers duly qualified to teach it." Were they unduly interfering in passing such a resolution? He thought not, for our Lord left them the command—not merely the request or advice —to feed His lambs, as well as the sheep, and they were not doing it in Warrington. Mr. R. Carpenter seconded. •_ _ _

The Recto': said he was thoroughly in accord with the principle of the resolution but he saw two great difficulties that might arise. Firstly the Education Committee would probably say that if they brought in the question of religious education as taught by the staff, it limited thbir choice of teachers, and secondly they would probably not agree to the arrangement if tbe committee were expected to pay the teachers for giving the instruction. He therefore moved an amendment as follows: " That the members of this conference view with deep regret the fact that there are more than 1,000 scholars attending day schools in Warrington who receive no adequate instruction in the Christian religion. They sincerely hope that the Education Committee may se their way to allow religious instruction according to the beliefs of the various denominations to be given in the Secondary School by accredited representatives at their own expense during school hours to all children whose narents request it." He was inclined to think that' the Nonconformists would be willing to have the same religious Instruction in the ease ot the Wesleyans, Baptista and Congregationalists, and that would remove the difficulty of further accommodation. The Roman Catholics would require one room, the Church of England another, and the Nonconformists wonld perhaps agree to a third. The • . •E. Rev. E C E Carleton seconded. __ _

The Rev. Canon Stevenson explained that if the parents of children attending the Secondary School requested it, the Education Committee had power to grant the request contained in the Rector's amendment, What that conference had to do was to inform public opinion and get parents to make the request. Colonel Buckton Is it mit a fact thAt they read prayers in the schools in question? The Rev. Canon Stevenson said he was not clear about Wycliffe school, but at Arpley-street school the Bible was read. At the Secondary School a portion of the Bible was read, a hymn sung, and prayer said. A similar condition of things obtained in the Beamont and Bolton schools.

The Rev. H. A. Lester urged the importance of a united demand being made by Church parents in War- rington and district. It ought to be realized that the best children in Warrington—the children who ought to fotm the baokbone of the Church for the future— were being brought up to-day without definite religious instruction The cream of the children went to the Secondary School and they were having no religious instruction worthy of the name. The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton suggested that the same course be adopted at the Secondary School as obtained at the Grammar School

The Rev. J. Davies said some people would object to declaring that they belonged to a particular denomination The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton: If anyone objects to designating himself what kind of Christian he is the public should know. Continuing, he considered the difficulty arose from the tact that some Nonconformists would not accept the Apostles' Creed as simple Bible teaching. If they could be got to see that the Creed was simple Bible teaching they could unite in the work. The Rev. J. H. G. Hollingworth said that when they found Church children in their respective parishes who went to schools where there was no religious teaching they must not try to stir up the managers to give undenominationalism but endeavour to form outside classes and teach the children. He therefore moved a further amendment : "That the members of this conference view with much regret the fact that there are many children of Church parents attending elementary day schools in Warrington who receive no instruction in the Christian religion in the schools which they attend. They sincerely hope that the clergy and other lay workers of the Church of England will use every effort to secure for the children of Church parents in those schools definite Church teaching on week days out of school hours. That this Conference urges the clergy to stir up the parents of children attending the Secondary, school to ask the Education authority to grant per- mission for their children to receive definite religious instruction."

The Rev. J. W. Glendenning seconded. Tee Rev. G. Vale Owen said! the Rector's amend- ment was if anything too liberal. They had already paid for that instructlon when they paid their rates and taxes and when they asked for their rights they were not asking too much. The Rector: I want to be fair to all parties—to give to them what we want ourselves.

Colonel Buckton said he thought the alternatives suggested by Mr. Hollingworth were the only ones they could legally take up. On a vote being taken, the Rector's amendment was carted and the following committee was appointed to cansider the means of putting it into operation : The Revs. G. Vale Owen, J. H. G. Hollingworth, H. A. Lester, and B. Percival.

div.head: EMPIRE RINK.
div.p: EMPIRE RINK.

A highly successful whist drive took' place at the above rink on Thursday night. About 120 took part in it and all had an enjoyable evening. The winners are as follows :—Ladies, 1, Miss Carpenter, prize silver cruet; 2, Mrs. Welsby, fflegree bowl • booby, Miss Ince, miniatura teddy bear. Gents, 1, dr. div.head: AN INSECT NEW TO SCIENCE.
div.p: AN INSECT NEW TO SCIENCE.

So many collectors are at work in all corners of the British Isles that it is seldom that an entirely new moth of any size is discovered nowadays ; but such a cue has just been reported. The lucky captor is Mr. Esson of Aberdeen, who took the stranger at " sugar " on a fir tree in July last. It is a moth of considerable size, not only, new to the British list and, apparently, to science, but belonging to no known genus, so that a new genus will have to be found for it, though in external appearance it closely resembles some of what are known as the Agrotidre—the common "white under- wing" moths, of which the turnip moth, the caterpillar of which is so destructive to root crops, is the best and most unpleasantly known representative. The srteci- men has been bought by the Hon. N. C. Rothschild, and by him presented to the Natural History Museum. The chances are that next July there will be a rush of col- lectors to Aberdeen, and the trunks of the firs for miles around will be sticky with sugaring mixtures.— "Country Life."

div.head: LATCHFORD WESLEYAN CHURCH. Successful Bazaar.
div.p: LATCHFORD WESLEYAN CHURCH. Successful Bazaar.

By means of an attractive bazaar the Weslevans of Latchford have this week been making an effort to raise a substantial amount towards the liquidation of the debt of £450 on the Sunday school, which was erected in 1907 at a cost of £1,150. These premises have met a need which was felt and acknowledged for a number of years, and the successful work amongst the young, which has been accomplished since the new building was erected, justifies the con- siderable expenditure which has been incurred. The arrangements for the enterprise had been entered into with commendable enthusiasm by a strong com- mittee with the Rev. Thomas Gladding as President, Mr. John Strange as treasurer, Messrs. J. Atherton Smith and David Maile as secretaries. The stalk were very pleasingly arranged in the schoolroom and the large display of useful and fancy wares was eloquent proof of the splendid work done by the ladies in pre- paration for the event. div.head: OPENING BY MRS. A. H. CROSFIELD.
div.p: OPENING BY MRS. A. H. CROSFIELD.

Mrs. A. H. CROSFIELD opened the bazaar on Wednes day afternoon in the presence of a large gathering. Mr James Dodds presided. The Rev. T. GILA DD LNG, in the course of an intro- ductory statement, said the building in which they had gathered together, with the fine set of class rooms, had been erected at a cost of £1,137 13s. 3d. On July 31st 1903 the balance of debt was £469 ]6s. id. Since then they had had to add £3O for interest, making a total of .E 499 16s. id. On the credit side they had £45, the proceeds of the collection on the occasion of the open- ing of the new organ. There was no debt upon the chapel and the organ was the generous gift of a lady whom they all knew perfectly well. The Sunday school, which was doing an excellent work, was well officered and organized. There were 256 scholars (including men's and women's Bible classes) on the books with an average attendance of 125 in the morning and 190 in the afternoon. Most of the children who went to school in the morning also attended service at the chapel and that was one way by which good Methodists could be made of the coming generation. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN said he rejoiced to be present on that occasion. He well remembered being invited by Mrs. Hartley—and he regarded it as a signal honour— to preside at the opening of the organ so generously given by Miss Hartley. At that time he expressed the hope that they would soon get rid of the debt on the schools and possibly that suggestion had something to do with the bazaar. His pleasure that day was much enhanced by the fact that he had to introduce to them Mrs. Arthur Crosfield, the wife of their worthy and respected member. (Applause,) Wherever she had been in Warrington she had won all hearts by the charm of her graceful manner and her simple sincerity —for sincerity, after all, was a characteristic of all good people—and he was sure that when that gathering had heard her, she would have completed the con- quest as far as Latchford was concerned. He had the sincerest pleasure, deeming it indeed an honour, in asking Mrs. Crosfleld to declare the bazaar open. (Applause). Mrs. A. H. CROSFIELD, who was enthusiastically received, said : I do not intend to make a speech to-day, because in the first place I am sure that in the course of a few weeks you will have so much speechify- ing that you will be grateful to me not to give you a foretaste of it now. (Laughter.) But I must thank Mr. Dodds for the very kind remarks he has made about me, and which I do not at all deserve. (Laughter.) Then, in looking round I see so many pretty and useful objects that I am certain no eloquence will be needed to persuade you to buy because you will all be anxious to encourage the workers who have spent their time, talent and energy in this admirable cause. If it be necessary to use persuasion lam sure the ladies in charge of the stalls will be quite equal to the task—in fact they will be able to plead the cause very much better than I could. In looking through the bazaar handbook I came across a very appropriate quotation—and the book is full of amusing and suitable sayings upon which those who made the selection are to be congratulated. The one to which I refer is from Shakespeare "Shake out thy gold And smiles from ladies fair shall be thy portion." (Laughter). Of course, lam addressing this especially to the gentlemen, although it would be unfair to hint that they need any such bribery to buy. (Laughter). But, on the other hand, could they desire any greater recompense than the one Shakespeare mentions? Those who have spoken before me have told you of all the work the Sunday school has done, and how successful it has been since its erection. In declaring the sale open I wish it, with all my heart, every possible success. (Applause). Mr. R. H. MELDRUM proposed and Mr. James Gandy seconded a vote of thanks to Mrs. Crosfield and the Chairman.

The Rev. E. B. KEELING in supporting said he was not inclin6d to apologise,for bazaars. If he had to apologise for anything, he gave it up. Bazaars did a great deal of good in bringing the workers together and at the present juncture, when they were likely to be flying at one another's throats before many weeks were over—(laughter)--it was as well that they should begin with a little honey. (Laughter.) The vote was heartily accorded and Mrs. Crosfleld briefly returned thanks. The Rev. T. GLADDING announced the receipt of the following donations :—Mr. William Walker, of White- haven, .£lO ; Mr. and Mrs. Wheatley, £5 ; Mrs. Posuett, Runcorn, ,£2 2s. ; Mr. Francis Boston, Runcorn, £1 is.

div.head: SECOND DAY.
div.p: SECOND DAY.

Mrs. C. E. PARKER declared the bazaar open on Thursday in the presence of a good number of people. Mr. E. J. Guest, in the absence of Mr. J. G. Within- sbaw presided. Mr. JOHN STRANGE announced that the proceeds for the previous days sale amounted to £136 3s. 10d. and included donations, one being from Mr. James Dodds of .E 25. (Applause). The CHAIRMAN said that Mr. Withinshaw !found it impossible to come, but with his usual generosity he had I sent a contribution. lie (the speaker) thought that he was getting out of public work altogether, but when Mr. Smith asked him to preside he could not refuse. (Laughter). He had been wandering about for the last 6 months seeking rest and finding none, but where-ever he went he found that two things were want- ing—religion and morality, the worship of the true God and love of one's neighbours. God was worshipped by all people in various ways, but He was worshipped. There was a code of morality amongst all people yet wherever he had gone he had found no form of worship more suited to him than that of Methodism. (Hear, hear.) In introducing Mrs. Parker he said thet,she was one of the most eloquent ladies he had ever heard. (Applause.) Mrs. PARKER prior to declaring the Bazaar open spoke highly of Mr. Smith one of the secretaries and congratulated those at Latchford on having such a worker amongst them. She and her relatives owed a great deal to the church to which she belonged. However strongly they might feel about the brotherhood ot all the churches, they should ally themselves to one church and do what they could for it. Referring to the 'aim of the blzaar—to clear the debt of! the Sunday school—she impressed upon them the need of doing all that was possible for the training in that sphere. She bad much pleasure in declaring the sale open. (Applause.) On the proposition of Mr. J. A. SMTTH seconded by Mr. ATKIN and supported by the Rev. Thomas Wadding a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mrs. Parker and Mr. Guest.
The total on Thursday evening was £2ll. __ _ YESTERDAY.
Yesterday the bazaar was opened by Mrs. GUNNELL Mr. George Weaver presiding. The total proceeds amounted to £ 285 12s. ENTERTAINMENTS.

An excellent series of entertainments had been arranged. During Wednesday and Thursday afternoon Mrs. W. B. Roberts' ladies orchestra played light selec- tions in pleasing style. On Wednesday evening con- certs were given in the guild room by the following: —Misses Dulcie and Olive Gladding, Lena Duckworth. G. Hensball, May Isherwood, Messrs. J. W. Willett. John McArthur and J. Foster. A humorous sketch " The Geese "was given by Miss Bessie Forshaw and G. Hensball. On Thnrsday evening the pupils of Miss A. Lloyd Williams (winners of three prizes) submitted two action songs "Maids of Seville " and " Chinese Lantern," an operetta "The Girton Girl and Milkmaid" and the juvenile cantata "Playmates," On Friday evening the artistes were Misses Violet Brown and A. Bancroft, Messrs. W. Warburton and Burt.
A capital bazaar souvenir of quotations and recipes had been edited by Mr. J. A. Smith, and printed at the "Examiner" Office.

div.head: FREE TRADE LEAGUE.
div.p: FREE TRADE LEAGUE.

The Committee of the Warrington Branch have decided to take vigorous action in the forthcoming, election contest. At a well-attended meeting of the Executive held on Thursday evening last a unanimous, feeling was expressed that there must be even greater energy in this fight than was displayed in the 1906, election.

Next week there will be two meetings, one in Messrs. Greenings' Dining Hall, Bewsey-road, on Wednesday evening, and the second in Brick Street Schoolroom on Thursday. Good speakers will be on the platform and the cause of Free Trade will be well explained. Any friends who are willing to join the branch, and lend a helping hand, will be heartily welcome. The, movement Anon-political;all shades of opinion being represented.

div.head: WHO KILLED THE BUDGET P
div.p: WHO KILLED THE BUDGET P

Who killed the Budget ? "I," said the Peer, "With assistance from Beer,. I killed the Budget." Who saw it die? "L" said the nation, "With great execration, I saw it die." Who'll he chief mourner? "I," said Lloyd George, With a lump in his gorge-,, "I'll be chief mourner. • Who'll sing a psalm ? "WE," said the Party, With emphasis hearty— "A rousing good psalm,"' Who'll toll the bell?
